01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Mo.html:
Carbohydrates

Biological Chemistry › Molecules of Life

Source: Molecules of Life gallery (drawn for these notes)

Sugars: fuel, structure and part of DNA and RNA. Many hydroxyls and, when sugars join, a glycosidic link.

Maltose, lactose and cellobiose are all two six-carbon sugars joined by a 1→4 glycosidic link. Drawn flat they look the same; they differ only in the 3D arrangement at certain carbons, and enzymes can tell them apart.

α-D-glucose: the OH on carbon 1 points down (ring drawn flat). Groups: hydroxyl

β-D-glucose: the OH on carbon 1 points up: cellulose is built from this. Groups: hydroxyl

Fructose: a 5-membered ring sugar; a ketone in its open form. Groups: hydroxyl

Ribose: the sugar in RNA and ATP. Groups: hydroxyl

Deoxyribose: the sugar in DNA: no OH on carbon 2. Groups: hydroxyl

Sucrose: glucose + fructose: table sugar. Groups: glycosidic link, hydroxyl

Allolactose: the real inducer of the lac operon. Groups: hydroxyl

IPTG: a lab inducer of the lac operon that E. coli cannot break down. Groups: hydroxyl

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Panel 2–4: An Outline of Some of the Types of Sugars Commonly Found in Cells, Monosaccharides (Alberts 7e, p. 100)

Panel 2–4: An Outline of Some of the Types of Sugars Commonly Found in Cells, Disaccharides (Alberts 7e, p. 101)

Questions

How do ribose and deoxyribose differ?

Deoxyribose lacks the OH on carbon 2, so it has one fewer hydroxyl. DNA uses deoxyribose and RNA uses ribose.

What is allolactose and how is IPTG used?

Allolactose is the natural inducer of the lac operon. IPTG mimics it but can't be broken down, so it keeps the operon on in the lab.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Mo.html:
Amino acids

Biological Chemistry › Molecules of Life

Source: Molecules of Life gallery (drawn for these notes)

The 20 building blocks of proteins. All share an amino group and a carboxyl group; the R group makes each one different. Proteins use the L-form, not shown here.

Glycine, as a zwitterion: how amino acids exist at pH 7: NH₃⁺ and COO⁻. Groups: carboxyl, amino

Alanine: R group: methyl. Groups: carboxyl, amino

Serine: R group has a hydroxyl: a common phosphorylation site. Groups: carboxyl, hydroxyl, amino

Aspartic acid: an acidic R group: negative at pH 7. Groups: carboxyl, amino

Lysine: a basic R group: positive at pH 7. Groups: carboxyl, amino

Phenylalanine: aromatic ring: UUU codes for it. Groups: carboxyl, amino

Tryptophan: absorbs UV at 280 nm: how proteins are measured. Groups: carboxyl, amino

Histidine: its ring gains and loses H⁺ near pH 7. Groups: carboxyl, amino

Proline: the R group loops back onto the amino group. Groups: carboxyl, amino

Methionine: coded by AUG: the first amino acid of proteins. Groups: carboxyl, amino

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 116

Some of these side chains are nonpolar and hydrophobic (“water-fearing”), others are negatively or positively charged, some can readily form covalent bonds, and so on.

Panel 3–1: The 20 Amino Acids Found in Proteins, The amino acid (Alberts 7e, p. 118)

Panel 3–1: The 20 Amino Acids Found in Proteins, Nonpolar side chains (Alberts 7e, p. 119)

Panel 3–1: The 20 Amino Acids Found in Proteins, Uncharged polar side chains (Alberts 7e, p. 119)

Panel 3–1: The 20 Amino Acids Found in Proteins, Acidic side chains (Alberts 7e, p. 119)

Panel 3–1: The 20 Amino Acids Found in Proteins, Basic side chains (Alberts 7e, p. 118)

Questions

Which functional groups are in serine?

Amino, carboxyl and a hydroxyl in the R group.

How do amino acids exist at pH 7?

As zwitterions: the amino group is NH₃⁺ and the carboxyl is COO⁻.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Mo.html:
Lipids

Biological Chemistry › Molecules of Life

Source: Molecules of Life gallery (drawn for these notes)

Fats and membranes. Long non-polar hydrocarbon chains, joined to glycerol by ester links.

Palmitic acid: a saturated fatty acid: straight chain. Groups: carboxyl

Oleic acid: a cis double bond puts a kink in the chain. Groups: carboxyl, c=c double bond

Glycerol: the backbone of fats and phospholipids. Groups: hydroxyl

A phospholipid (phosphatidylcholine): polar phosphate head, two fatty acid tails (drawn short). Groups: ester, phosphate

Cholesterol: four fused rings; stiffens membranes. Groups: hydroxyl, c=c double bond

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 51

This makes the hydrocarbon as a whole hydrophobic—a property that is exploited in cells, whose membranes are constructed from molecules that have long hydrocarbon tails, as we shall see in Chapter 10.

Panel 2–5: Fatty Acids and Other Lipids, Fatty acids (Alberts 7e, p. 102)

Panel 2–5: Fatty Acids and Other Lipids, Phospholipids (Alberts 7e, p. 102)

Panel 2–5: Fatty Acids and Other Lipids, Steroids (Alberts 7e, p. 103)

Questions

What does the cis double bond in oleic acid do?

It puts a kink in the chain, so the chains pack less tightly and the fat stays liquid.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Mo.html:
Nucleotides and energy carriers

Biological Chemistry › Molecules of Life

Source: Molecules of Life gallery (drawn for these notes)

Base + sugar + phosphate: the units of DNA and RNA, and the cell's energy and signalling molecules.

AMP: base + ribose + one phosphate. Groups: phosphate, hydroxyl

ATP: the energy currency: three phosphates. Groups: phosphate, hydroxyl

GTP: the energy source in Nirenberg’s cell-free system. Groups: phosphate, hydroxyl

cAMP: cyclic AMP: the signal that switches on CAP at the lac operon. Groups: phosphate, hydroxyl

NAD⁺: carries electrons in metabolism (as NADH). Groups: amide (peptide bond), phosphate, hydroxyl

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 70

The activated carriers store energy in an easily exchangeable form, either as a readily transferable chemical group or as electrons held at a high energy level, and they can serve a dual role as a source of both energy and chemical groups in biosynthetic reactions.

Alberts 7e, p. 70

The most important of the activated carrier molecules are ATP and two molecules that are closely related to each other, NADH and NADPH.

Alberts 7e, p. 72

As the most abundant activated carrier in cells, ATP is the principal energy currency.

Panel 2–6: A Survey of the Nucleotides, Nucleotides (Alberts 7e, p. 104)

Questions

How do ATP and cAMP differ?

ATP has three phosphates in a chain on carbon 5 of ribose. In cAMP a single phosphate bridges carbons 3 and 5, making a ring.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Mo.html:
Metabolism

Biological Chemistry › Molecules of Life

Source: Molecules of Life gallery (drawn for these notes)

Landmarks of respiration, all small carboxylic acids or ketones.

Pyruvic acid: the end of glycolysis. Groups: carboxyl, carbonyl

Lactic acid: made from pyruvate without oxygen. Groups: carboxyl, hydroxyl

Citric acid: starts the Krebs (TCA) cycle. Groups: carboxyl, hydroxyl

α-Ketoglutaric acid: a Krebs cycle intermediate. Groups: carboxyl, carbonyl

Oxaloacetic acid: joins with acetyl-CoA to make citrate. Groups: carboxyl, carbonyl

Butyric acid: a short-chain fatty acid made by gut bacteria. Groups: carboxyl

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 58

Two opposing streams of chemical reactions occur in cells: (1) the catabolic pathways break down foodstuffs into smaller molecules, thereby generating both a useful form of energy for the cell and some of the small molecules that the cell needs as building blocks; (2) the anabolic, or biosynthetic, pathways use the small molecules plus the energy harnessed by catabolism to drive the synthesis of the many other molecules that form the cell. Together these two sets of reactions constitute the metabolism of the cell (Figure 2–14).

Figure 2–14: Schematic representation of the relationship between catabolic and anabolic pathways in metabolism. (Alberts 7e, p. 58)

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Mo.html:
Buffers and lab reagents

Biological Chemistry › Molecules of Life

Source: Molecules of Life gallery (drawn for these notes)

Molecules from the bench: buffers that hold pH steady and reagents from the practicals.

TRIS: the most common biology buffer. Groups: hydroxyl, amino

Acetic acid: pKa 4.7: acetate buffers. Groups: carboxyl

H₂PO₄⁻ and HPO₄²⁻: the phosphate buffer pair, pKa 7.21. Groups: phosphate

EDTA: grabs metal ions; in TE buffer to protect DNA. Groups: carboxyl, amino

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 53

The interior of a cell is also kept close to neutrality by the presence of buffers: weak acids and bases that can release or take up protons near pH 7, keeping the environment of the cell relatively constant under a variety of conditions.

Alberts 7e, p. 52

Pure water has a pH of 7.0 and is said to be neutral; that is, neither acidic (pH < 7) nor basic (pH > 7).

Panel 2–2: Water and Its Influence on the Behavior of Biological Molecules, pH (Alberts 7e, p. 97)

Questions

Why is TRIS useful, and roughly what pH does it buffer?

Its amino group gains and loses H⁺, so it resists pH change. It buffers around pH 8.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Mo.html:
Signalling molecules

Biological Chemistry › Molecules of Life

Source: Molecules of Life gallery (drawn for these notes)

Neurotransmitters and hormones, several made from amino acids, and some made by gut bacteria.

Dopamine: a neurotransmitter. Groups: hydroxyl, amino

Adrenaline: the fight-or-flight hormone. Groups: hydroxyl, amino

Serotonin: made from tryptophan; mostly made in the gut. Groups: hydroxyl, amino

Histamine: made by removing CO₂ from histidine. Groups: amino

GABA: the main calming neurotransmitter. Groups: carboxyl, amino

Equol: made from soy isoflavones by gut bacteria. Groups: hydroxyl

Questions

Which neurotransmitters are made from amino acids?

Serotonin from tryptophan, dopamine and adrenaline from tyrosine, histamine from histidine, GABA from glutamate.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Recap: electron configurations

Biological Chemistry › How Atoms Form Molecules

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 2: How atoms form molecules, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

  • Carbon, atomic number 6, has 6 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p²
  • Sodium, atomic number 11, has 11 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹
  • An isotope of an element has the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons, for example ¹⁴N and ¹⁵N in the Meselson-Stahl experiment

Questions

Write the electron configurations of carbon and sodium.

Carbon (6): 1s² 2s² 2p². Sodium (11): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹.

What is the difference between two isotopes of an element?

The same number of protons but a different number of neutrons.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Why atoms form molecules

Biological Chemistry › How Atoms Form Molecules

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 2: How atoms form molecules, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

A molecule is two or more atoms bonded together. Lone atoms are rare; how they bond depends on their electron configuration.

The most stable state for an atom is a full outer shell, the valence shell. That is why the noble gas group (group 8, also called group 0 or 18) is so unreactive. Atoms bond to gain that stability.

Questions

Why do atoms form bonds?

To reach the most stable state, a full outer (valence) shell. Noble gases already have one, so they are unreactive.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Electron configuration exceptions

Biological Chemistry › How Atoms Form Molecules

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 2: How atoms form molecules, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

  • Exactly half-filled sets of orbitals are more stable than unevenly filled ones
  • 4s and 3d are so close in energy they are almost degenerate (equivalent)
  • So chromium is [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵, not 4s² 3d⁴: an electron moves from 4s to 3d to half-fill the d orbitals

Extra beyond the slides: copper does the same to fill its d orbitals completely: [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰.

Questions

Why is chromium [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ rather than 4s² 3d⁴?

Half-filled orbitals are extra stable and 4s and 3d are almost equal in energy, so one 4s electron moves to 3d.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Ionic bonding

Biological Chemistry › How Atoms Form Molecules

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 2: How atoms form molecules, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

  • An ionic bond forms when one atom gives electrons to another, so both become ions
  • Losing electrons gives a positive cation; gaining electrons gives a negative anion
  • Opposite charges attract electrostatically
  • An atom with few valence electrons (a metal such as Na, K or Mg) gives them to an atom needing a few to complete its shell (Cl, O)

Examples: Na⁺Cl⁻, K⁺Cl⁻ and Mg²⁺O²⁻, where Mg gives two electrons to O.

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 51

Electrostatic attractions are strongest when the atoms involved are fully charged, or ionized.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Covalent bonding

Biological Chemistry › How Atoms Form Molecules

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 2: How atoms form molecules, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

In a covalent bond two atoms share a pair of electrons, so both count it towards a full shell.

Bond Shared pairs Example
Single 1 F–F, C–H, O–H
Double 2 O=O, C=O
Triple 3 N≡N, C≡N
Methane: carbon shares one pair with each of four hydrogens

Water: oxygen shares one pair with each hydrogen and keeps two lone pairs

O₂ shares two pairs: a double bond

F₂ shares one pair: a single bond

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 94

A covalent bond forms when two atoms come very close together and share one or more of their outer-shell electrons. Each atom forms a fixed number of covalent bonds in a defined spatial arrangement.

Panel 2–1: Chemical Bonds and Groups Commonly Encountered in Biological Molecules, Covalent bonds (Alberts 7e, p. 94)

Questions

Is the bond in O₂ single, double or triple? And in F₂?

O₂: double (two shared pairs). F₂: single.

props.subject: Biological Chemistry
props.summary: In a dative bond both shared electrons come from the same atom, which donates a lone pair. Once formed it is the same as any other covalent bond.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Dative (coordinate) bonds

Biological Chemistry › How Atoms Form Molecules

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 2: How atoms form molecules, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

In a dative bond both shared electrons come from the same atom, which donates a lone pair. Once formed it is the same as any other covalent bond.

NH₄⁺: ammonia's lone pair bonds to H⁺, and all four N–H bonds then look identical

Extra beyond the slides: the same happens when water picks up H⁺ to make H₃O⁺, and when metal ions such as Fe²⁺ in haemoglobin bind to nitrogen atoms.

Questions

What is a dative bond? Give an example.

A covalent bond where both electrons come from one atom's lone pair, e.g. N–H in NH₄⁺ formed when NH₃ bonds to H⁺.

props.title: Ionic or covalent?
props.subject: Biological Chemistry
props.summary: F₂: two identical non-metal atoms, so the electrons are shared equally: covalent
props.source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 2: How atoms form molecules, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Ionic or covalent?

Biological Chemistry › How Atoms Form Molecules

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 2: How atoms form molecules, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

  • F₂: two identical non-metal atoms, so the electrons are shared equally: covalent
  • KCl: a metal that easily loses an electron and a non-metal that easily gains one: ionic
The bigger the electronegativity difference, the more ionic the bond

Questions

How does an ionic bond differ from a covalent bond?

Ionic: electrons are transferred, forming cations and anions held by electrostatic attraction. Covalent: a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.

Is KCl ionic or covalent, and why?

Ionic: K easily loses an electron and Cl easily gains one, so K⁺ and Cl⁻ form.

props.source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 2: How atoms form molecules, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Electronegativity

Biological Chemistry › How Atoms Form Molecules

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 2: How atoms form molecules, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to pull the electrons of a covalent bond towards itself. It depends on:

  • The number of protons in the nucleus (atomic number)
  • The distance of the outer electrons from the nucleus (number of shells)

It rises across a period and falls down a group, so fluorine is the most electronegative element.

Pauling electronegativities of elements common in biology

Questions

What is electronegativity and what affects it?

An atom's ability to pull electrons in a covalent bond towards itself. It depends on the number of protons and the distance of the outer electrons from the nucleus.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Polar bonds

Biological Chemistry › Molecular Structure

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 3: Molecular Structure, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

  • A very large electronegativity difference: the bond is likely to be ionic
  • A small but significant difference: one atom pulls harder, giving a polar bond with partial charges (δ+ and δ−)
  • Little or no difference: the bond is treated as non-polar
H–Cl: chlorine is more electronegative, so Cl is δ− and H is δ+

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 50

In a water molecule (H₂O), the two H atoms are linked to the O atom by covalent bonds that are highly polar, inasmuch as the O atom attracts electrons more strongly than does the H atom.

Alberts 7e, p. 51

In these molecules, all of the H atoms are covalently linked to C atoms by a largely nonpolar bond; thus, they cannot form effective hydrogen bonds to other molecules (see Panel 2–1, pp. 94–95).

Questions

What happens when atoms with very different electronegativities bond?

A very large difference gives an ionic bond. A smaller but significant difference gives a polar covalent bond with δ+ and δ− ends.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Polar molecules and water

Biological Chemistry › Molecular Structure

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 3: Molecular Structure, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

Polar molecules interact with each other, which changes how they behave. Water is polar: O is δ− and each H is δ+.

Extra beyond the slides: the δ+ hydrogen of one water molecule is attracted to a lone pair on the oxygen of another, forming a hydrogen bond. Hydrogen bonds give water its high boiling point, hold DNA's two strands together, and shape proteins.

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 50

When a positively charged region of one water molecule (that is, one of its H atoms) approaches a negatively charged region (that is, the O atom) of a second water molecule, the electrical attraction between them can result in a hydrogen bond (Figure 2–3A).

Alberts 7e, p. 50

It is only because of these hydrogen bonds that link water molecules together that water is a liquid at room temperature—with a high boiling point and high surface tension—rather than a gas.

Carbon and its electrons

Biological Chemistry › Molecular Structure

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 3: Molecular Structure, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

  • Carbon is the backbone of the key biological molecules and is extremely versatile
  • Carbon has a valency of 4: it needs 4 more electrons for a full shell

  • Yet in methane all four C–H bonds are identical. Hybridisation explains how

First, life depends on chemical reactions that take place in aqueous solution, and it is based overwhelmingly on carbon compounds, the study of which is known as organic chemistry.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Hybridisation

Biological Chemistry › Molecular Structure

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 3: Molecular Structure, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

Hybridisation mixes the s orbital with one, two or three p orbitals before bonding. The new hybrid orbitals point in set directions instead of surrounding the nucleus, are degenerate (equal in energy), and spread as far apart as possible.

Mix Hybrids Left over Angle Example
s + p 2 sp 2 p 180° CO₂, HCN
s + 2p 3 sp² 1 p 120° C=O in methanal
s + 3p 4 sp³ none 109.5° CH₄

Shortcut: lone pairs + atoms bonded to the central atom = the number of orbitals that hybridise. Methanal's carbon: 0 + 3 = 3, so sp². The slides note the details of hybridisation matter less than the shapes they produce.

Questions

What are sp, sp² and sp³ hybridisation, with angles?

sp: 2 hybrids, 180°. sp²: 3 hybrids, 120°. sp³: 4 hybrids, 109.5°.

props.title: Sigma and pi bonds
props.subject: Biological Chemistry
props.summary: Hybrid orbitals overlap head-on to form sigma (σ) bonds; every single bond is one σ bond
props.source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 3: Molecular Structure, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Sigma and pi bonds

Biological Chemistry › Molecular Structure

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 3: Molecular Structure, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

  • Hybrid orbitals overlap head-on to form sigma (σ) bonds; every single bond is one σ bond
  • The leftover unhybridised p orbitals overlap side-on to form pi (π) bonds
  • A double bond is σ + π, and a triple bond is σ + 2π
CO₂: carbon is sp, making two σ bonds to the oxygens plus two π bonds

Extra beyond the slides: π bonds stop rotation around a double bond, which is why cis and trans fatty acids have fixed, different shapes.

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 94

Atoms joined by two or more covalent bonds cannot rotate freely around the bond axis. This restriction has a major influence on the three-dimensional shape of many macromolecules.

Panel 2–1: Chemical Bonds and Groups Commonly Encountered in Biological Molecules, Alternating double bonds (Alberts 7e, p. 94)

Questions

What is the difference between a σ and a π bond?

σ: head-on overlap, present in every bond. π: side-on overlap of unhybridised p orbitals, adding the second and third bonds of a double or triple bond.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Shapes of molecules: VSEPR

Biological Chemistry › Molecular Structure

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 3: Molecular Structure, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

  • VSEPR theory (valence shell electron pair repulsion): bonds repel each other, so they spread evenly around a central atom
  • A lone pair repels more strongly than a bond: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond > bond–bond
  • So the shape depends on the number of bonds plus the number of lone pairs around the central atom
The five shapes, from bonded atoms and lone pairs around the central atom

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 94

The precise spatial arrangement of covalent bonds influences the three-dimensional structure and chemistry of molecules.

Questions

State the VSEPR repulsion order.

Lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond > bond–bond.

props.title: Worked shapes
props.subject: Biological Chemistry
props.summary: C forms 4 bonds, H and Cl form 1 each, so C is central with 4 bonds and no lone pairs: tetrahedral.
props.source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 3: Molecular Structure, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Worked shapes

Biological Chemistry › Molecular Structure

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 3: Molecular Structure, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

Chloroform, CHCl₃

C forms 4 bonds, H and Cl form 1 each, so C is central with 4 bonds and no lone pairs: tetrahedral.

Chloroform is tetrahedral

Methanal, CH₂O

C forms 4 bonds and is central. O forms 2, so it double bonds to C. That is 3 regions and no lone pairs: trigonal planar, sp².

Methanal is trigonal planar

Ammonia, NH₃

N has 5 valence electrons, so it forms 3 bonds and keeps 1 lone pair: 1 + 3 = 4 regions arranged tetrahedrally. Only 3 hold atoms, so the shape is trigonal pyramidal.

Ammonia is trigonal pyramidal

Hydrogen cyanide, HCN

C forms 4 bonds and N needs 3, so H–C≡N. Two regions around C: linear, sp.

HCN is linear

Water, H₂O

O has 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs: 4 regions, 2 holding atoms. The lone pairs squeeze the angle to about 104.5°: bent (angular).

Questions

What shape is chloroform, CHCl₃?

Tetrahedral: C has 4 bonds and no lone pairs.

What shape is ammonia, and why isn't it tetrahedral?

Trigonal pyramidal: 4 electron regions arranged tetrahedrally, but one is a lone pair, so only 3 positions hold atoms.

What shapes are CH₂O and HCN?

CH₂O: trigonal planar (C=O double bond, sp²). HCN: linear (C≡N triple bond, sp).

props.title: Oxygen makes molecules polar
props.subject: Biological Chemistry
props.summary: C and H have very similar electronegativities, so C–H bonds count as non-polar. Oxygen is highly electronegative, so groups containing oxygen (hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl) make molecules polar and usually more water-soluble.
props.source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 4: Functional Groups in Biology, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Oxygen makes molecules polar

Biological Chemistry › Functional Groups in Biology

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 4: Functional Groups in Biology, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

C and H have very similar electronegativities, so C–H bonds count as non-polar. Oxygen is highly electronegative, so groups containing oxygen (hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl) make molecules polar and usually more water-soluble.

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 51

Molecules, such as alcohols, that contain polar bonds and that can form hydrogen bonds with water dissolve readily in water.

Alberts 7e, p. 51

Such molecules are termed hydrophilic, meaning that they are water-loving.

Questions

Why do oxygen-containing groups make molecules polar?

Oxygen is much more electronegative than C and H, so C–O and O–H bonds are polar. C–H bonds are not.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Carbohydrates and glycosidic bonds

Biological Chemistry › Functional Groups in Biology

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 4: Functional Groups in Biology, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

  • A monosaccharide is a single sugar, such as glucose, fructose or galactose
  • A disaccharide is two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond
Maltose: two glucoses joined by a glycosidic bond (purple)

Extra beyond the slides: the glycosidic bond forms in a condensation reaction, releasing water. Breaking it with water is hydrolysis, which is what β-galactosidase does to lactose in the lac operon.

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 55

Each polymer grows by the addition of a monomer onto the end of a growing chain in a condensation reaction, in which one molecule of water is lost with each subunit added (Figure 2–9).

Figure 2–9: Condensation and hydrolysis as opposite reactions. (Alberts 7e, p. 55)

A glycosidic bond, formed by condensation, releasing water.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Peptide bonds

Biological Chemistry › Functional Groups in Biology

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 4: Functional Groups in Biology, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

  • Amino acids join into polypeptides
  • The carboxyl group of one amino acid bonds to the amino group of the next, releasing water: a peptide bond
  • Polypeptides fold into proteins, and the different R groups interact to give each protein its shape and properties
Glycylalanine: the peptide bond (green) joins glycine to alanine

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 116

This covalent bond forms when the carbon atom of the carboxyl group of one amino acid (such as glycine) shares electrons with the nitrogen atom from the amino group of a second amino acid (such as alanine).

Alberts 7e, p. 116

The two ends of a polypeptide chain are chemically different: the end carrying the free amino group (NH2, which takes up a proton at neutral pH to become NH3+) is the amino terminus, or N-terminus, and the end carrying the free carboxyl group (COOH, which loses a proton at neutral pH to become COO–) is the carboxyl terminus, or C-terminus.

Alberts 7e, p. 117

Because it has a partial double-bond character, the peptide bond is planar (gray shading) and does not permit free rotation.

Figure 3–1: The components of a protein. (Alberts 7e, p. 116)

Questions

How does a peptide bond form?

The carboxyl group of one amino acid joins the amino group of the next, releasing water.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Thiols and disulfide bridges

Biological Chemistry › Functional Groups in Biology

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 4: Functional Groups in Biology, Dr Becky Lewis (ebook)

  • Thiol group: –SH, found in the amino acid cysteine
  • In a folding protein, two thiols can join to form a disulfide bridge (S–S)
  • Disulfide bridges hold different parts of a protein together and help fix its final shape
Cystine: two cysteines linked by a disulfide bridge

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 134

Disulfide bonds do not change the conformation of a protein but instead act as atomic staples to reinforce its most favored conformation.

Alberts 7e, p. 134

Disulfide bonds generally fail to form in the cytosol, where a high concen tration of reducing agents converts S–S bonds back to cysteine –SH groups.

Figure 3–25: Disulfide bonds. (Alberts 7e, p. 134)

Panel 2–1: Chemical Bonds and Groups Commonly Encountered in Biological Molecules, Sulfhydryl group (Alberts 7e, p. 95)

Questions

What is a disulfide bridge and why does it matter?

An S–S bond between two cysteine thiol groups that holds parts of a folded protein together.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Chemical reactions and stoichiometry

Biological Chemistry › Chemical Reactions in Biology

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 5: Common Types of Reactions in Biology, Dr Maria Vardakou (PDF)

  • A chemical reaction is either a chemical change within one compound, or an interaction between two or more reactants that forms one or more products different from the starting compounds
  • A reaction scheme shows it as an equation: A + 2B → C + 3D
  • Example: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃

Stoichiometry

  • Stoichiometry is the relative quantities of reactants and products
  • A + 2B → C + 3D has a ratio of 1 : 2 → 1 : 3
  • N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ has a ratio of 1 : 3 → 2
  • The numbers in front (coefficients) count molecules or moles. The small subscripts belong to the formula and never change when balancing

Atoms are conserved

The number of each type of atom in the reactants must equal the number in the products.

Reactants (N₂ + 3H₂) Products (2NH₃)
N 2 2
H 3 × 2 = 6 2 × 3 = 6

Questions

What is the stoichiometry of N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃?

1 : 3 → 2. One N₂ reacts with three H₂ to give two NH₃.

Why can't H₂O be balanced by changing it to H₂O₂?

Subscripts are part of the formula, so changing them makes a different substance. Only the coefficients in front change.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Balancing equations: the oxidation of glucose

Biological Chemistry › Chemical Reactions in Biology

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 5: Common Types of Reactions in Biology, Dr Maria Vardakou (PDF)

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O

Atom Reactants Products
C 6 6
H 12 6 × 2 = 12
O 6 + (6 × 2) = 18 (6 × 2) + 6 = 18
  • Balancing order that works here: C first (6CO₂), then H (6H₂O), then O last, because O appears in both products
  • Ratio: 1 : 6 → 6 : 6
The overall scheme for glucose oxidation

Same scheme, different routes

  • Burning glucose (like a lit match) releases the energy at once, mostly as heat
  • In cells the same overall change takes more than 20 reactions across glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, so the energy is captured as chemical energy (ATP)
  • The scheme looks identical either way. Only the mechanism differs: see Reaction scheme vs reaction mechanism
Glucose is oxidised in many steps in cells

bc5_glucose_pathway.jpg

The slide draws CO₂ leaving glycolysis. Glycolysis itself releases no CO₂: it comes from the link reaction (pyruvate to acetyl CoA) and the citric acid cycle. O₂ is only used at the very end, in oxidative phosphorylation, where it becomes H₂O.

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 63

Cells use enzymes to catalyze the oxidation of organic molecules in small steps, through a sequence of reactions that allows useful energy to be harvested.

Questions

Balance C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O.

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. Check: C 6 = 6, H 12 = 12, O 18 = 18.

Why do cells oxidise glucose in over 20 steps instead of one?

Small steps let the energy be captured as chemical energy (ATP) instead of being lost all at once as heat.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Reaction scheme vs reaction mechanism

Biological Chemistry › Chemical Reactions in Biology

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 5: Common Types of Reactions in Biology, Dr Maria Vardakou (PDF)

Reaction scheme

  • Gives only a glance of the process: the overall chemical change from reactants to products
  • Shows the identity of the reactants and products and their relative quantities (stoichiometry)
  • Says nothing about how the change happens

Reaction mechanism

  • Reactions break bonds in the reactants and form new bonds in the products. The reaction mechanism describes this rearrangement
  • It shows the steps involved. Most biological reactions take more than one step
  • Different mechanisms have different patterns of bond breaking and forming
  • Every reaction redistributes valence electrons, in one of two ways:
    1. An electron pair moves together, staying a pair: heterolytic
    2. An electron pair splits and the electrons move singly: homolytic

Curly arrows

  • A double-headed curly arrow shows a pair of electrons moving
  • A single-headed (fish-hook) arrow shows one electron moving, as in free radical reactions
  • Arrows start at the electrons (a lone pair or a bond) and point to where they end up

Questions

What does a reaction mechanism show that a scheme does not?

Which bonds break and form, the order they do it in, and how many steps the reaction takes.

What are the two ways valence electrons can redistribute in a reaction?

As a pair moving together (heterolytic) or split, moving singly (homolytic).

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Homolytic and heterolytic bond breaking

Biological Chemistry › Chemical Reactions in Biology

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 5: Common Types of Reactions in Biology, Dr Maria Vardakou (PDF)

  • Homolytic: the bonding pair splits, and each atom keeps one electron. X–Y → X• + •Y. The electrons are split the same way between the two atoms, giving two free radicals
  • Heterolytic: one atom keeps both electrons and the other gets none. X–Y → X:⁻ + Y⁺. The electrons are split differently between the two atoms, giving ions
  • In heterolytic breaking, the more electronegative atom usually takes the pair
Homolytic vs heterolytic bond breaking

bc5_homo_hetero.jpg

Heterolytic reactions in general

  • An electron pair moves as a unit from a nucleophile (A = Nu⁻, the electron pair source) to an electrophile (X = E⁺, the electron pair acceptor)
  • At the start the pair is shared between X and Y. The pair moves to be shared between A and X, so a new A–X bond forms, and the X–Y pair ends up held by Y alone, so X–Y breaks
A nucleophile (A) donates a pair to X while the X–Y pair moves onto Y

bc5_heterolytic.jpg

Questions

What does homolytic fission of Cl–Cl produce?

Two chlorine free radicals, Cl•, each with one electron from the bond.

In heterolytic fission of H–Br, which atom keeps the electron pair and why?

Bromine, because it is more electronegative. This gives H⁺ and Br⁻.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/.html:
Free radical reactions

Biological Chemistry › Chemical Reactions in Biology

Source: Biological Chemistry, Lecture 5: Common Types of Reactions in Biology, Dr Maria Vardakou (PDF)

  • A free radical is a species with an unpaired electron, shown by a dot: Cl•, •CH₃
  • Homolytic reactions form free radicals. Example: chlorination of methane

1. Initiation

Free radicals are first formed. This is triggered by high energy radiation such as UV light: Cl₂ → 2Cl•

Sunlight splits Cl₂ homolytically into two radicals

bc5_radical_initiation.jpg

2. Propagation

  • Free radicals are highly reactive and unstable. They take or give electrons from nearby atoms, which forms even more free radicals
  • Step 1: CH₄ + Cl• → •CH₃ + HCl
  • Step 2: •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•
  • Each step uses one radical and makes another, so the chain keeps going
One radical in, one radical out

bc5_radical_propagation.jpg

Both propagation steps

bc5_radical_propagation_slide.jpg

3. Termination

Two free radicals collide and combine into a stable molecule, ending the chain:

  • Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂
  • •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl
  • •CH₃ + •CH₃ → CH₃CH₃ (ethane)
Termination: two radicals pair their electrons

bc5_radical_termination.jpg

Adding the two propagation steps gives the overall scheme CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.

Questions

Name the three stages of a free radical reaction and what happens in each.

Initiation: UV light splits a molecule into radicals. Propagation: a radical reacts to make a product and a new radical. Termination: two radicals combine into a stable molecule.

Why does one chlorine radical lead to many chloromethane molecules?

Each propagation step regenerates a radical (Cl• is remade in step 2), so the chain continues until termination.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Questions.title: Functional Groups in Biology questions
01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Questions.html:
Functional Groups in Biology: questions

Biological Chemistry › Functional Groups in Biology

13 questions

Organic compounds and R groups

What does 'R' mean in R–OH?

The rest of the molecule: any carbon chain carrying the group.

Alkanes

What makes an alkane saturated?

Only single bonds, so every carbon has its maximum number of bonded hydrogens.

Alkyl and aryl groups

What is an alkyl group?

An alkane with one hydrogen removed so it can attach to another molecule, e.g. methyl –CH₃.

How does the slide's definition of an aryl group differ from most textbooks?

The slide says a group from a cyclic alkane. Textbooks mean an aromatic ring such as phenyl; a ring alkane gives a cycloalkyl group.

Alkenes

What is the difference between an alkane and an alkene?

An alkene has a C=C double bond (two fewer H), so it is unsaturated.

Hydroxyl and carboxyl groups

Name the groups: –OH, –COOH, C=O, –NH₂, –SH.

Hydroxyl, carboxyl, carbonyl, amino, thiol.

Aldehydes and ketones

How do aldehydes and ketones differ?

Both have a carbonyl group: at the end of the chain in an aldehyde, in the middle in a ketone.

Oxygen makes molecules polar

Why do oxygen-containing groups make molecules polar?

Oxygen is much more electronegative than C and H, so C–O and O–H bonds are polar. C–H bonds are not.

Carbohydrates and glycosidic bonds

What bond joins two monosaccharides, and what is released?

A glycosidic bond, formed by condensation, releasing water.

Esters

How does an ester form? Where are they found in biology?

A carboxyl group reacts with a hydroxyl group, releasing water. Ester links join fatty acids to glycerol in fats.

Amino groups and amines

What are primary, secondary and tertiary amines?

N bonded to 1, 2 or 3 carbons, e.g. methylamine, dimethylamine, trimethylamine.

Peptide bonds

How does a peptide bond form?

The carboxyl group of one amino acid joins the amino group of the next, releasing water.

Thiols and disulfide bridges

What is a disulfide bridge and why does it matter?

An S–S bond between two cysteine thiol groups that holds parts of a folded protein together.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Questions.path: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Questions/How Atoms Form Molecules questions.md
01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Questions.title: How Atoms Form Molecules questions
01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Questions.html:
How Atoms Form Molecules: questions

Biological Chemistry › How Atoms Form Molecules

9 questions

Recap: electron configurations

Write the electron configurations of carbon and sodium.

Carbon (6): 1s² 2s² 2p². Sodium (11): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹.

What is the difference between two isotopes of an element?

The same number of protons but a different number of neutrons.

Why atoms form molecules

Why do atoms form bonds?

To reach the most stable state, a full outer (valence) shell. Noble gases already have one, so they are unreactive.

Electron configuration exceptions

Why is chromium [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ rather than 4s² 3d⁴?

Half-filled orbitals are extra stable and 4s and 3d are almost equal in energy, so one 4s electron moves to 3d.

Covalent bonding

Is the bond in O₂ single, double or triple? And in F₂?

O₂: double (two shared pairs). F₂: single.

Dative (coordinate) bonds

What is a dative bond? Give an example.

A covalent bond where both electrons come from one atom's lone pair, e.g. N–H in NH₄⁺ formed when NH₃ bonds to H⁺.

Ionic or covalent?

How does an ionic bond differ from a covalent bond?

Ionic: electrons are transferred, forming cations and anions held by electrostatic attraction. Covalent: a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.

Is KCl ionic or covalent, and why?

Ionic: K easily loses an electron and Cl easily gains one, so K⁺ and Cl⁻ form.

Electronegativity

What is electronegativity and what affects it?

An atom's ability to pull electrons in a covalent bond towards itself. It depends on the number of protons and the distance of the outer electrons from the nucleus.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Questions.title: Molecular Structure questions
01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Questions.html:
Molecular Structure: questions

Biological Chemistry › Molecular Structure

9 questions

Polar bonds

What happens when atoms with very different electronegativities bond?

A very large difference gives an ionic bond. A smaller but significant difference gives a polar covalent bond with δ+ and δ− ends.

Polar molecules and water

Why is water polar, and what does that allow?

O is much more electronegative than H, so O is δ− and the H atoms δ+. Water molecules attract each other through hydrogen bonds.

Carbon and its electrons

How can carbon make four identical bonds if its 2s and 2p electrons differ?

Hybridisation: the 2s and three 2p orbitals mix into four identical sp³ orbitals pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron.

Hybridisation

What are sp, sp² and sp³ hybridisation, with angles?

sp: 2 hybrids, 180°. sp²: 3 hybrids, 120°. sp³: 4 hybrids, 109.5°.

Sigma and pi bonds

What is the difference between a σ and a π bond?

σ: head-on overlap, present in every bond. π: side-on overlap of unhybridised p orbitals, adding the second and third bonds of a double or triple bond.

Shapes of molecules: VSEPR

State the VSEPR repulsion order.

Lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond > bond–bond.

Worked shapes

What shape is chloroform, CHCl₃?

Tetrahedral: C has 4 bonds and no lone pairs.

What shape is ammonia, and why isn't it tetrahedral?

Trigonal pyramidal: 4 electron regions arranged tetrahedrally, but one is a lone pair, so only 3 positions hold atoms.

What shapes are CH₂O and HCN?

CH₂O: trigonal planar (C=O double bond, sp²). HCN: linear (C≡N triple bond, sp).

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Questions.title: Molecules of Life questions
01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Questions.html:
Molecules of Life: questions

Biological Chemistry › Molecules of Life

8 questions

Carbohydrates

How do ribose and deoxyribose differ?

Deoxyribose lacks the OH on carbon 2, so it has one fewer hydroxyl. DNA uses deoxyribose and RNA uses ribose.

What is allolactose and how is IPTG used?

Allolactose is the natural inducer of the lac operon. IPTG mimics it but can't be broken down, so it keeps the operon on in the lab.

Amino acids

Which functional groups are in serine?

Amino, carboxyl and a hydroxyl in the R group.

How do amino acids exist at pH 7?

As zwitterions: the amino group is NH₃⁺ and the carboxyl is COO⁻.

Lipids

What does the cis double bond in oleic acid do?

It puts a kink in the chain, so the chains pack less tightly and the fat stays liquid.

Nucleotides and energy carriers

How do ATP and cAMP differ?

ATP has three phosphates in a chain on carbon 5 of ribose. In cAMP a single phosphate bridges carbons 3 and 5, making a ring.

Buffers and lab reagents

Why is TRIS useful, and roughly what pH does it buffer?

Its amino group gains and loses H⁺, so it resists pH change. It buffers around pH 8.

Signalling molecules

Which neurotransmitters are made from amino acids?

Serotonin from tryptophan, dopamine and adrenaline from tyrosine, histamine from histidine, GABA from glutamate.

01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Questions.text: Molecules of Life: questions Biological Chemistry › Molecules of Life 8 questions Carbohydrates How do ribose and deoxyribose differ? Deoxyribose lacks the OH on carbon 2, so it has one fewer hydroxyl. DNA uses deoxyribose and RNA uses ribose. What is allolactose and how is IPTG used? Allolactose is the natural inducer of the lac operon. IPTG mimics it but can't be broken down, so it keeps the operon on in the lab. Amino acids Which functional groups are in serine? Amino, carboxyl and a hydroxyl in the R group. How do amino acids exist at pH 7? As zwitterions: the amino group is NH₃⁺ and the carboxyl is COO⁻. Lipids What does the cis double bond in oleic acid do? It puts a kink in the chain, so the chains pack less tightly and the fat stays liquid. Nucleotides and energy carriers How do ATP and cAMP differ? ATP has three phosphates in a chain on carbon 5 of ribose. In cAMP a single phosphate bridges carbons 3 and 5, making a ring. Buffers and lab reagents Why is TRIS useful, and roughly what pH does it buffer? Its amino group gains and loses H⁺, so it resists pH change. It buffers around pH 8. Signalling molecules Which neurotransmitters are made from amino acids? Serotonin from tryptophan, dopamine and adrenaline from tyrosine, histamine from histidine, GABA from glutamate.

01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Le.html:
What Biomedicine actually is

Introduction to Biomedicine › Introductory Lecture

Source: BIO-4012Y Introductory Lecture, 2026-27 (open)

Biomedicine: the study of the molecular and cellular basis of human disease, and how this knowledge is translated into diagnosis, monitoring, treatment and prevention. The essential aim is understanding what processes go wrong in disease, in order to diagnose it more accurately, treat it more effectively, and prevent its recurrence.

  • Progress happens at multiple levels of biological organisation: gene, cell, and tissue/organ
  • Disease susceptibility is ultimately determined by genes, which is why so much biomedical research focuses at the molecular level
  • Remarkable advances already achieved: protective vaccines, antibiotic treatments, organ transplantation, childhood leukaemia treatment, IVF
  • Challenges still ahead: better cancer treatment, preventing age-related and cardiovascular disease, curing single-gene disorders, better bacterial infection treatment, preventing HIV/malaria/tropical diseases

Test

How does Biomedicine define its own field?

The study of the molecular and cellular basis of human disease, and how that knowledge becomes diagnosis, monitoring, treatment and prevention.

What does Biomedicine translate its knowledge into?

Diagnosis, monitoring, treatment and prevention of human disease.

How the year is structured

Introduction to Biomedicine › Introductory Lecture

Source: BIO-4012Y Introductory Lecture, 2026-27 (open)

This is the year-long, 40-credit flagship module for Biomedicine's first year. After an induction covering the learning environment and good study practice, a series of introductory lectures covers the Grand Challenges (The Grand Challenges in Biomedicine), running in parallel with a seminar series and lab-technique lectures. Spring semester shifts to hands-on practicals, the drug development pipeline, and clinical diagnosis lectures. The module closes with a Biomedicine symposium, where students present their favourite aspect of biomedicine from the first year.

It is a year-long, 40-credit module. It closes with a Biomedicine symposium where students present their favourite aspect of biomedicine from the first year.

01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Le.html:
What an infectious disease actually is

Introduction to Biomedicine › Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations

Source: 1_What is an infectious disease and how do they spread (pre-session, 4 min) (open)

  • Infectious disease: caused by pathogenic microorganisms, such as bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites (e.g. tetanus, influenza, measles)
  • Communicable disease: an infectious disease spread from person to person (e.g. influenza, measles)
  • Zoonotic disease: an infectious disease of animals that can cause disease when transmitted to humans (e.g. avian influenza, COVID-19)

Test

What's the difference between an infectious, a communicable, and a zoonotic disease?

Infectious: caused by a pathogenic microorganism. Communicable: an infectious disease spread person to person. Zoonotic: an animal infectious disease that can transmit to humans.

Which four groups of microorganism can cause infectious disease?

Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites.

Related

  • How infectious diseases spread
  • Infectious disease terms: endemic to pandemic

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 1313

Infectious diseases currently cause about one-quarter of all human deaths worldwide, more than all forms of cancer combined and second only to cardiovascular diseases.

Alberts 7e, p. 1313

Since the mid-1800s, physicians and scientists have struggled to identify the microbes—collectively called pathogens—that are capable of causing infectious diseases.

Alberts 7e, p. 1314

Primary pathogens can cause overt disease in most healthy, nonimmune people.

Alberts 7e, p. 1314

Opportunistic pathogens do not cause disease in healthy people but can cause illness in individuals suffering from other conditions.

headings.text: What an infectious disease actually is

01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Le.text: What an infectious disease actually is Introduction to Biomedicine › Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations Source: 1_What is an infectious disease and how do they spread (pre-session, 4 min) ( open ) Infectious disease : caused by pathogenic microorganisms, such as bacteria , viruses , fungi or parasites (e.g. tetanus, influenza, measles) Communicable disease : an infectious disease spread from person to person (e.g. influenza, measles) Zoonotic disease : an infectious disease of animals that can cause disease when transmitted to humans (e.g. avian influenza, COVID-19) Test What's the difference between an infectious, a communicable, and a zoonotic disease? Infectious: caused by a pathogenic microorganism. Communicable: an infectious disease spread person to person. Zoonotic: an animal infectious disease that can transmit to humans. Which four groups of microorganism can cause infectious disease? Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. Related How infectious diseases spread Infectious disease terms: endemic to pandemic From the textbook (Alberts 7e) Alberts 7e, p. 1313 Infectious diseases currently cause about one-quarter of all human deaths worldwide, more than all forms of cancer combined and second only to cardiovascular diseases. Alberts 7e, p. 1313 Since the mid-1800s, physicians and scientists have struggled to identify the microbes—collectively called pathogens—that are capable of causing infectious diseases. Alberts 7e, p. 1314 Primary pathogens can cause overt disease in most healthy, nonimmune people. Alberts 7e, p. 1314 Opportunistic pathogens do not cause disease in healthy people but can cause illness in individuals suffering from other conditions.

01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Le.html:
Infectious disease terms: endemic to pandemic

Introduction to Biomedicine › Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations

Source: 1_What is an infectious disease and how do they spread (pre-session, 4 min) (open)

  • Endemic: the amount of a particular disease that's usually present in a community
  • Outbreak: a sudden increase in the number of cases of a disease above what's normally expected in that population and area
  • Epidemic: the same as an outbreak, an increase (often sudden) in cases above what's normally expected in that population and area
  • Pandemic: an epidemic spread over multiple countries or continents, usually affecting a large number of people

Test

What's the difference between an outbreak/epidemic and a pandemic?

An outbreak/epidemic is a sudden increase in cases above what's normally expected in one population and area. A pandemic is an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents.

What does 'endemic' mean?

The amount of a particular disease that is usually present in a community, i.e. its baseline level, not a sudden increase.

Related

  • What an infectious disease actually is

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 1313

Newer infectious diseases continually emerge, including the current pandemic (worldwide epidemic) of COVID-19 (coronavirus disease 2019), which was first clinically observed in 2019 and has since infected hundreds of millions of people and caused millions of deaths worldwide.

01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Le.html:
How infectious diseases spread

Introduction to Biomedicine › Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations

Source: 1_What is an infectious disease and how do they spread (pre-session, 4 min) (open)

Person to person

  • Airborne (water droplets): influenza, common cold, meningitis, tuberculosis
  • Direct contact, faecal-oral route: diarrhoeal diseases, e.g. rotavirus, norovirus
  • Exposure to bodily fluids: hepatitis B, Ebola
  • Sexually transmitted: HIV/AIDS
  • Mother to child: HIV, hepatitis

Other routes

  • Food or water: Salmonellosis and Listeriosis (food), cholera (water)
  • Soil: tetanus, anthrax
  • Arthropods: malaria and yellow fever (mosquitoes), Lyme disease (ticks)
  • Animals: rabies

Test

Give an example of a disease spread by each route: airborne, bodily fluids, arthropods and soil.

Airborne: influenza or tuberculosis. Bodily fluids: hepatitis B or Ebola. Arthropods: malaria (mosquitoes) or Lyme disease (ticks). Soil: tetanus or anthrax.

By which routes can HIV spread?

Sexual transmission, and from mother to child.

Name a disease spread through food and one spread through water.

Food: salmonellosis or listeriosis. Water: cholera.

Related

  • What an infectious disease actually is

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 1314

These long spiral-shaped bacteria live in deer ticks and can be transmitted to humans during a tick’s blood meal.

Alberts 7e, p. 1321

It is caused by four species of Plasmodium, which are transmitted to humans by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito.

01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Le.html:
Why this is a Grand Challenge

Introduction to Biomedicine › Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations

Source: The Grand Challenges: Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations (Laura Wagstaff) (open)

Infectious diseases feature in the top 10 global causes of death (roughly 12 million deaths). Three of the ten are infectious: COVID-19, lower respiratory infections, and tuberculosis (WHO, Aug 2024 data).

WHO global causes of death, 2000/2019/2021. COVID-19, lower respiratory infections and tuberculosis (highlighted) are the infectious diseases in the top 10

People in low-income countries are far more likely to die of a communicable disease than a non-communicable one: 6 of the leading causes of death there are communicable, versus only 2 in high-income countries.

Top 10 causes of death, low-income vs high-income countries. Malaria, HIV/AIDS, diarrhoeal diseases, preterm birth complications and birth asphyxia all appear for low-income countries but not high-income ones

The 'big three' infectious diseases

Disease Scale (most recent data)
TB (2019) 10 million people fell ill worldwide; 1.4 million died. WHO runs an 'End TB Strategy'
HIV (2020) 37.6 million living with HIV/AIDS worldwide; 690,000 died of HIV-related illness; 1.5 million newly infected
Malaria (2019) 229 million cases worldwide; 409,000 deaths

Test

What are the 'big three' infectious diseases, and roughly how many people do they affect?

TB (~10 million ill, 1.4 million deaths in 2019), HIV (37.6 million living with it in 2020), Malaria (229 million cases, 409,000 deaths in 2019).

Why do infectious diseases hit low-income countries harder?

6 of the leading causes of death in low-income countries are communicable diseases, versus only 2 in high-income countries.

Which 3 infectious diseases appear in the WHO's top 10 global causes of death (as opposed to the 'big three')?

COVID-19, lower respiratory infections, and tuberculosis. Note this is a different list from the 'big three' (TB, HIV, Malaria), which are the three biggest infectious disease burdens specifically, not the overall top 10 causes of death.

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 1313

There is a continuing heavy burden of ancient diseases such as tuberculosis and malaria, and these are increasingly difficult to treat because of rising drug resistance.

Alberts 7e, p. 1314

Bacteria cause illnesses ranging from tuberculosis, which causes roughly 1.4 million deaths per year, to pneumonia, as well as diarrheal and sexually transmitted diseases.

Alberts 7e, p. 1321

Malaria is the most devastating protozoal disease, infecting more than 200 million people every year and killing upward of 400,000.

01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Le.html:
Microorganisms: bacteria

Introduction to Biomedicine › Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations

Source: 2_Microorganisms and infectious disease (pre-session, 9 min) (open)

  • Bacteria are single-celled microbes (prokaryotes): simple cell structure, no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles
  • Genetic information sits in a single loop of DNA in the cytoplasm, called the nucleoid. Some bacteria also carry an extra circle of DNA called a plasmid
  • Found in every habitat on Earth, including soil, rock, oceans and arctic snow. Most bacteria aren't harmful; relatively few are pathogens

Harmful vs helpful

  • Harmful: food spoilage, crop damage, infectious disease
  • Helpful: nutrient cycling, fermented foods (yoghurt, soy sauce), source of antibiotics (e.g. tetracycline), part of the human microbiome (skin, gut, saliva)

Cell shape

Shape helps distinguish bacterial cells, but it's a poor predictor of their actual biology (plenty of rod-shaped microbes aren't bacteria at all).

a. Bacillus (rods), b. Coccus (spherical), c. Filamentous, d. Spirillum (loose spiral), e. Spirochete (tightly coiled/corkscrew)

Cell wall and the Gram stain

  • Cell walls protect against osmotic lysis and give the cell its rigidity and shape. The main component is peptidoglycan
  • Gram positive cells have several layers of peptidoglycan and retain the crystal violet stain, appearing purple
  • Gram negative cells have a thinner peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane (lipopolysaccharide), lose the crystal violet stain, and appear pink when counterstained with safranin
  • Cell wall structure informs antibiotic sensitivity and transmission routes
Gram-positive (thick peptidoglycan, no outer membrane) vs Gram-negative (thin peptidoglycan plus an outer membrane and periplasmic space)

The Gram stain procedure: crystal violet, then iodine (mordant), then an alcohol wash (decolorization), then safranin (counterstain)

Test

Name the 5 main bacterial cell shapes.

Bacillus (rods), Coccus (spherical), Filamentous, Spirillum (loose spiral), Spirochete (tightly coiled/corkscrew).

What's the key structural difference between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria?

Gram-positive cells have several thick layers of peptidoglycan and retain crystal violet stain (purple). Gram-negative cells have a thinner peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane, lose the stain, and appear pink when counterstained with safranin.

Related

  • Case study: pneumonia

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 1314

Much larger and more complex than viruses, bacteria are prokaryotic cells that perform most of their basic metabolic functions themselves, relying on the host primarily for nutrition (Figure 23–2B).

Alberts 7e, p. 1316

Gram-positive bacteria have a thick layer of peptidoglycan cell wall outside their inner (plasma) membrane (Figure 23–3B), whereas Gram-negative bacteria have a thinner peptidoglycan cell wall.

Alberts 7e, p. 1316

In both cases, the cell wall protects against lysis by osmotic swelling, and it is a target of host antibacterial proteins such as lysozyme and antibiotics such as penicillin.

Alberts 7e, p. 1316

Gram-negative bacteria are also covered outside the cell wall by an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Figure 23–3C).

Alberts 7e, p. 1316

They are called Gram positive because they retain the violet dye used in the Gram-staining procedure.

Figure 23–3: Bacterial shapes and cell-surface structures. (Alberts 7e, p. 1316)

props.summary: A virus is "an infectious nucleic acid (RNA or DNA) surrounded by protein".

01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Le.html:
Microorganisms: viruses

Introduction to Biomedicine › Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations

Source: 2_Microorganisms and infectious disease (pre-session, 9 min) (open)

A virus is "an infectious nucleic acid (RNA or DNA) surrounded by protein". Viruses can only replicate inside a suitable host cell (they're obligate intracellular parasites), and aren't considered to be alive: they rely on the host cell for energy, metabolic intermediates and protein synthesis.

  • Genetic information: DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded. Viruses are classified by their genetic information and the hosts they infect
  • Virion: the extracellular form of a virus, letting it travel between host cells, protecting the genome, with surface proteins that aid attachment
Naked virus (capsid only, mainly infects bacteria) vs enveloped virus (capsid plus a phospholipid envelope, mainly infects animals)

What happens once a virus gets inside a host cell

  • Lytic infection: the virus replicates and destroys the host cell, releasing new virus
  • Persistent infection: the virus replicates and is released by budding, without destroying the host cell
  • Latent infection: viral DNA exists in the host cell but doesn't replicate
  • Transformation: the virus converts the host cell into a tumour cell

Test

Why are viruses not considered to be alive?

They're obligate intracellular parasites: they can only replicate inside a host cell, relying on it for energy, metabolic intermediates and protein synthesis.

What's the difference between a naked virus and an enveloped virus?

A naked virus has just a protein capsid (mainly infects bacteria). An enveloped virus has a capsid plus an outer phospholipid envelope derived from the host cell (mainly infects animals).

Name the four outcomes a virus can have once inside a host cell.

Lytic infection (replicates and destroys the host cell), persistent infection (replicates and buds out without destroying the cell), latent infection (viral DNA present but not replicating), and transformation (converts the host cell into a tumour cell).

Related

  • Case study: HIV/AIDS

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 1314

Viruses are essentially fragments of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) that generally encode a relatively small number of gene products and are wrapped in a protective shell of proteins (Figure 23–2A) and (in some cases) an outer membrane envelope.

Alberts 7e, p. 1324

Viral genomes are packaged in a protein coat, called a capsid, which in some viruses is further enclosed by a lipid bilayer membrane, or envelope.

Alberts 7e, p. 1323

A single virus particle (a virion) that infects a single host cell can produce thousands of progeny.

Alberts 7e, p. 1325

The nucleocapsids of nonenveloped viruses usually leave an infected cell by lysing it.

Alberts 7e, p. 1325

For enveloped viruses, by contrast, the nucleocapsid is enclosed within a lipid bilayer membrane that the virus acquires in the process of budding from the host-cell plasma membrane, which it does without disrupting the membrane or killing the cell (Figure 23–12).

Figure 23–11: Examples of viral morphology. (Alberts 7e, p. 1324)

01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Le.html:
Microorganisms: fungi and parasites

Introduction to Biomedicine › Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations

Source: 2_Microorganisms and infectious disease (pre-session, 9 min) (open)

Fungi

  • A very diverse group, found in almost any habitat but mostly living in soil or on plant material. Includes moulds, mushrooms and yeasts
  • Most fungi are harmless to humans, and only a small number cause disease (e.g. athlete's foot, ringworm). Fungal infections can become serious in immune-compromised people (HIV/AIDS, cancer treatment)
  • Many fungi benefit humans directly: fermentation (yeast, for bread and beer) and antibiotics (e.g. penicillin)

Parasites

  • Parasitism: a symbiotic relationship between a host and a parasite, where the parasite derives essential nutrients from the host. Usually causes disease in the host
  • Gastrointestinal parasitic disease (vomiting/diarrhoea): e.g. toxoplasmosis, from cats
  • Infection of blood and internal tissues: e.g. malaria, from the female mosquito

Test

Are most fungi harmful to humans? Who is most at risk from fungal infections?

No. Most are harmless and only a few cause disease (for example athlete's foot and ringworm). Fungal infections can become serious in immune-compromised people, such as with HIV/AIDS or during cancer treatment.

Give two ways fungi benefit humans.

Fermentation (yeast for bread and beer) and antibiotics such as penicillin.

What is parasitism, and what is an example of a parasitic disease?

A symbiotic relationship in which the parasite gets essential nutrients from the host, usually causing disease. Examples: malaria (from the female mosquito) and toxoplasmosis (from cats).

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 1321

Fungi include both unicellular yeasts (such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe, which are used to bake bread and brew beer, and as model organisms for cell biology research) and filamentous, multicellular molds (like those found on moldy fruit or bread; see Figure 23–2D).

Alberts 7e, p. 1321

Because antifungal and antiparasitic drugs often target core molecules that are similar between parasite and host, they can be less effective and more toxic to the host than are antibiotics that target bacteria.

Alberts 7e, p. 1321

Protozoan parasites are single-celled eukaryotes with more elaborate life cycles than fungi, and they frequently require more than one host.

Figure 23–9: The complex life cycle of malaria parasites. (Alberts 7e, p. 1322)

Case study: pneumonia

Introduction to Biomedicine › Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations

Source: 3_Infectious disease case studies (pre-session, 11 min) (open)

  • Lower respiratory infections remain in the top 10 global causes of death, over 2 million deaths worldwide in 2021
  • Pneumonia is the single largest infectious cause of death in children worldwide: 15% of all deaths in under-5s (808,694 child deaths in 2017)
  • WHO/UNICEF's Global Action Plan for Pneumonia and Diarrhoea (GAPPD) aims to end preventable child deaths from pneumonia and diarrhoea by 2025

Cause and transmission

  • Can be caused by viruses, bacteria, or fungi; the most common cause is the bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • These bacteria live in the nose and throat of many healthy people without causing problems; they can infect young children and those with weakened immune systems if inhaled
  • Not very infectious. Spreads through coughs/sneezes, or direct contact with an infected person, sheets or tissues
  • Risk factors: babies, young children, the elderly, those with pre-existing illness/treatment (HIV/AIDS, flu, asthma, chemotherapy), and parental smoking/smokers

Symptoms, treatment and prevention

The air sacs (alveoli) in one or both lungs become inflamed and fill with fluid, making it difficult to breathe. Common symptoms: cough (dry or producing thick yellow/green/brown/blood-stained mucus), difficulty breathing, chest pain, rapid heartbeat, high temperature, sweating and shivering, loss of appetite.

  • Treatment: most people recover at home (rest, fluids, antibiotics); severe cases need hospital treatment (IV fluids, antibiotics, oxygen)
  • Prevention: vaccination against Streptococcus pneumoniae and against flu (a risk factor for pneumonia), plus improved nutrition, housing and hygiene

Test

What's the single most common cause of pneumonia, and who is most at risk from it?

The bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae. Most at risk: babies and young children, the elderly, and those with weakened immune systems or pre-existing illness.

What happens in the lungs in pneumonia?

The air sacs (alveoli) in one or both lungs become inflamed and fill with fluid, making it difficult to breathe.

How big a cause of child deaths is pneumonia?

It is the single largest infectious cause of death in children worldwide: 15% of all deaths in under-5s (808,694 child deaths in 2017).

How is pneumonia prevented?

Vaccination against Streptococcus pneumoniae and against flu (a risk factor for pneumonia), plus improved nutrition, housing and hygiene.

01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Le.title: 09 Case study, HIV and AIDS
01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Le.html:
Case study: HIV/AIDS

Introduction to Biomedicine › Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations

Source: 3_Infectious disease case studies (pre-session, 11 min) (open)

  • Approximately 40.8 million people living with HIV/AIDS worldwide at the end of 2024 (1.4 million of them children aged 0 to 14)
  • New infections have fallen 40% since 2010; an estimated 1.3 million people were newly infected in 2024
  • AIDS-related deaths have fallen 54% since the 2004 peak; 630,000 people died from AIDS-related illness in 2024
  • AIDS is caused by the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), with HIV-1 the main focus of research

Transmission and disease pathogenesis

  • Transmitted via body fluids (semen, vaginal secretions, blood, breast milk) and mother-to-child. Not transmitted through ordinary contact like kissing, hugging or shaking hands
  • Risk factors: unprotected sex, sharing contaminated needles/syringes, unsafe injections/transfusions/medical procedures
  • HIV infects host immune cells displaying the CD4 surface receptor, most commonly T-cells, macrophages and monocytes. CD4 and CXCR4 form the docking site where the virus fuses with the host membrane, then the viral RNA enters the cell
  • Infected T-cells stop replicating and eventually die, causing immune deficiency

Disease progression

HIV progression without treatment: CD4 cells (protective) decline while HIV particles (destructive) increase, from acute infection through chronic infection to AIDS

  • Acute infection: flu-like symptoms, high viral load, destruction of CD4+ T-cells
  • Chronic infection: HIV multiplies at low levels, asymptomatic, until the immune system is eventually overwhelmed (HIV levels rise, CD4+ T-cells fall)
  • AIDS: the most advanced stage, taking 2 to 15 years to develop without treatment. The immune system can no longer fight off opportunistic infections. Typical survival time without treatment: about 3 years. Most common opportunistic disease: pneumonia. Most common cancer: Kaposi's sarcoma

Treatment and prevention

  • No cure exists. Without treatment, it's rare for an HIV-positive person to live more than 10 years
  • HAART (highly active anti-retroviral therapy): 3 or more antiretroviral (ARV) drugs, aiming to reduce viral load to undetectable levels. Doesn't cure HIV, but suppresses it and lets the immune system recover
  • No licensed vaccine exists yet: the virus mutates quickly, has huge subtype variability, and surface proteins help it hide from the immune system. The 2009 RV144 trial showed a modest ~30% reduction in infection risk
  • Preventative ARV use: an HIV-positive person on effective treatment with no detectable virus won't pass HIV to sexual partners; daily ARV use by HIV-negative people in high-risk groups can block acquisition; ARV within 72 hours of exposure can prevent infection; ARV treatments can prevent mother-to-child transmission

Test

Which immune cell surface receptor does HIV target, and what cell types display it?

The CD4 receptor, found on T-cells, macrophages, and monocytes.

What are the stages of HIV disease progression without treatment?

Acute infection (flu-like symptoms, high viral load) then chronic infection (low-level multiplication, asymptomatic, immune system eventually overwhelmed) then AIDS (immune system can no longer fight opportunistic infections; typical survival without treatment is about 3 years).

What is HAART, and what does it actually do?

Highly active anti-retroviral therapy: 3 or more antiretroviral drugs aiming to reduce HIV viral load to undetectable levels. It doesn't cure HIV, but suppresses it and lets the immune system recover.

Related

  • Microorganisms: viruses

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 1329

An important example is HIV, which requires two types of receptors to enter a host cell.

Alberts 7e, p. 1329

Its primary receptor is CD4, a cell-surface protein on helper T cells and macrophages that is involved in immune recognition (discussed in Chapter 24).

Alberts 7e, p. 1330

The viruses that are found within the first few months after HIV infection almost invariably use CCR5, which explains why individuals that carry an altered CCR5 gene are less suscep tible to HIV infection.

Alberts 7e, p. 1343

Retroviral genomes, for example, acquire on average one point mutation every replication cycle, because the viral reverse transcriptase (see Figure 5–61) needed to produce DNA from the viral RNA genome lacks the proofreading activity of DNA polymerases.

Alberts 7e, p. 1343

This extraordinary genomic plasticity greatly complicates attempts to develop vaccines against HIV.

Figure 23–18: Receptor and co-receptors for HIV. (Alberts 7e, p. 1330)

01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Le.html:
Vaccination: approaches

Introduction to Biomedicine › Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations

Source: 4_An introduction to vaccinations (pre-session, audio, 5 min) (open)

Vaccination: deliberate exposure to a preparation from an infectious agent, to induce immunity.

  • Whole microbe approach: live-attenuated (weakened), inactivated (killed), or recombinant vector (a live replicating virus engineered to carry extra genes from a pathogen)
  • Subunit approach: uses just part of the microorganism (protein, sugar, capsid), including subunit/recombinant/polysaccharide/conjugate vaccines and inactivated toxins (toxoids)
  • Genetic approach: DNA and mRNA vaccines. A single viral gene gets injected directly, and the host's own cells produce the immunogenic protein

Effective vaccines exist against roughly 25 diseases (cholera, COVID-19, diphtheria, measles, tetanus and more among them); the lecture is explicit that the full list isn't something to memorise. Globally, vaccination saves 2 to 3 million lives every year, while over 1.5 million children still die annually from vaccine-preventable disease.

Test

What does vaccination actually do, and what's its estimated global impact?

Deliberate exposure to a preparation from an infectious agent to induce immunity. Saves an estimated 2 to 3 million lives globally each year.

What are the three general approaches to vaccine design?

Whole microbe approach (live-attenuated, inactivated, or recombinant vector), subunit approach (using part of the microorganism, e.g. protein or sugar), and genetic approach (DNA or mRNA, where host cells produce the immunogenic protein themselves).

Related

  • Vaccination: success stories

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 1364

One can trick the adaptive immune system into responding to a harmless foreign molecule, such as a foreign protein, by co-injecting a molecule (often of microbial origin) called an adjuvant, which activates PRRs. This trick is called immunization, and it can be exploited in vaccination (discussed later).

Alberts 7e, p. 1367

This arrangement, called clonal selection, provides an explanation for immunological memory, whereby we develop long-lasting immunity to many common infectious diseases after our initial exposure to the pathogen—either through natural infection or vaccination.

Alberts 7e, p. 1367

If, after some weeks, months, or even years have elapsed, the animal is immunized again with antigen A, it will usually produce a secondary immune response that differs from the primary response: the lag period is shorter, because there are now many more preexisting B or T cells (or both) with specificity for antigen A, and the response is greater and more efficient.

Figure 24–16: Immunological memory: primary and secondary antibody responses. (Alberts 7e, p. 1368)

01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Le.html:
Vaccination: success stories

Introduction to Biomedicine › Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations

Source: 4_An introduction to vaccinations (pre-session, audio, 5 min) (open)

  • Eradication: complete, permanent, worldwide reduction to zero new cases through deliberate effort, with no further control measures needed. Example: smallpox
  • Elimination: reduction to zero (or a very low target rate) of new cases within a defined geographical area through deliberate effort, but continued measures are still needed to prevent transmission re-establishing. Example: measles

Test

What's the difference between disease eradication and disease elimination? Give an example of each.

Eradication is a complete, permanent, worldwide reduction to zero new cases, with no further control measures needed (e.g. smallpox). Elimination is reduction to zero or a very low rate within a defined area, but continued measures are still needed to prevent it re-establishing (e.g. measles).

Related

  • Vaccination: approaches

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 1325

The most effective strategy for containing viral diseases is through vaccination of potential hosts.

Alberts 7e, p. 1325

For example, a highly successful vaccination program eradicated smallpox infection from the planet by 1980.

Alberts 7e, p. 1325

Vaccines effective against poliovirus, which causes poliomyelitis and paralysis, have existed since the 1950s, and a more recent global vaccination initiative, begun in 1988, seeks to completely eradicate poliovirus infection.

Figure 23–13: Effective control of a viral disease through vaccination. (Alberts 7e, p. 1325)
