Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations: quiz

Introduction to Biomedicine › Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations
How to use this

Read a question and answer it out loud or on paper first. Then click the question to reveal the answer. Questions are grouped by topic, in lecture order, and the same questions sit at the bottom of each topic note.

28 questions

What an infectious disease actually is

What's the difference between an infectious, a communicable, and a zoonotic disease?

Infectious: caused by a pathogenic microorganism. Communicable: an infectious disease spread person to person. Zoonotic: an animal infectious disease that can transmit to humans.

Which four groups of microorganism can cause infectious disease?

Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites.

Infectious disease terms: endemic to pandemic

What's the difference between an outbreak/epidemic and a pandemic?

An outbreak/epidemic is a sudden increase in cases above what's normally expected in one population and area. A pandemic is an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents.

What does 'endemic' mean?

The amount of a particular disease that is usually present in a community, i.e. its baseline level, not a sudden increase.

How infectious diseases spread

Give an example of a disease spread by each route: airborne, bodily fluids, arthropods and soil.

Airborne: influenza or tuberculosis. Bodily fluids: hepatitis B or Ebola. Arthropods: malaria (mosquitoes) or Lyme disease (ticks). Soil: tetanus or anthrax.

By which routes can HIV spread?

Sexual transmission, and from mother to child.

Name a disease spread through food and one spread through water.

Food: salmonellosis or listeriosis. Water: cholera.

Why this is a Grand Challenge

What are the 'big three' infectious diseases, and roughly how many people do they affect?

TB (~10 million ill, 1.4 million deaths in 2019), HIV (37.6 million living with it in 2020), Malaria (229 million cases, 409,000 deaths in 2019).

Why do infectious diseases hit low-income countries harder?

6 of the leading causes of death in low-income countries are communicable diseases, versus only 2 in high-income countries.

Which 3 infectious diseases appear in the WHO's top 10 global causes of death (as opposed to the 'big three')?

COVID-19, lower respiratory infections, and tuberculosis. Note this is a different list from the 'big three' (TB, HIV, Malaria), which are the three biggest infectious disease burdens specifically, not the overall top 10 causes of death.

Microorganisms: bacteria

Name the 5 main bacterial cell shapes.

Bacillus (rods), Coccus (spherical), Filamentous, Spirillum (loose spiral), Spirochete (tightly coiled/corkscrew).

What's the key structural difference between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria?

Gram-positive cells have several thick layers of peptidoglycan and retain crystal violet stain (purple). Gram-negative cells have a thinner peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane, lose the stain, and appear pink when counterstained with safranin.

Microorganisms: viruses

Why are viruses not considered to be alive?

They're obligate intracellular parasites: they can only replicate inside a host cell, relying on it for energy, metabolic intermediates and protein synthesis.

What's the difference between a naked virus and an enveloped virus?

A naked virus has just a protein capsid (mainly infects bacteria). An enveloped virus has a capsid plus an outer phospholipid envelope derived from the host cell (mainly infects animals).

Name the four outcomes a virus can have once inside a host cell.

Lytic infection (replicates and destroys the host cell), persistent infection (replicates and buds out without destroying the cell), latent infection (viral DNA present but not replicating), and transformation (converts the host cell into a tumour cell).

Microorganisms: fungi and parasites

Are most fungi harmful to humans? Who is most at risk from fungal infections?

No. Most are harmless and only a few cause disease (for example athlete's foot and ringworm). Fungal infections can become serious in immune-compromised people, such as with HIV/AIDS or during cancer treatment.

Give two ways fungi benefit humans.

Fermentation (yeast for bread and beer) and antibiotics such as penicillin.

What is parasitism, and what is an example of a parasitic disease?

A symbiotic relationship in which the parasite gets essential nutrients from the host, usually causing disease. Examples: malaria (from the female mosquito) and toxoplasmosis (from cats).

Case study: pneumonia

What's the single most common cause of pneumonia, and who is most at risk from it?

The bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae. Most at risk: babies and young children, the elderly, and those with weakened immune systems or pre-existing illness.

What happens in the lungs in pneumonia?

The air sacs (alveoli) in one or both lungs become inflamed and fill with fluid, making it difficult to breathe.

How big a cause of child deaths is pneumonia?

It is the single largest infectious cause of death in children worldwide: 15% of all deaths in under-5s (808,694 child deaths in 2017).

How is pneumonia prevented?

Vaccination against Streptococcus pneumoniae and against flu (a risk factor for pneumonia), plus improved nutrition, housing and hygiene.

Case study: HIV/AIDS

Which immune cell surface receptor does HIV target, and what cell types display it?

The CD4 receptor, found on T-cells, macrophages, and monocytes.

What are the stages of HIV disease progression without treatment?

Acute infection (flu-like symptoms, high viral load) then chronic infection (low-level multiplication, asymptomatic, immune system eventually overwhelmed) then AIDS (immune system can no longer fight opportunistic infections; typical survival without treatment is about 3 years).

What is HAART, and what does it actually do?

Highly active anti-retroviral therapy: 3 or more antiretroviral drugs aiming to reduce HIV viral load to undetectable levels. It doesn't cure HIV, but suppresses it and lets the immune system recover.

Vaccination: approaches

What does vaccination actually do, and what's its estimated global impact?

Deliberate exposure to a preparation from an infectious agent to induce immunity. Saves an estimated 2 to 3 million lives globally each year.

What are the three general approaches to vaccine design?

Whole microbe approach (live-attenuated, inactivated, or recombinant vector), subunit approach (using part of the microorganism, e.g. protein or sugar), and genetic approach (DNA or mRNA, where host cells produce the immunogenic protein themselves).

Vaccination: success stories

What's the difference between disease eradication and disease elimination? Give an example of each.

Eradication is a complete, permanent, worldwide reduction to zero new cases, with no further control measures needed (e.g. smallpox). Elimination is reduction to zero or a very low rate within a defined area, but continued measures are still needed to prevent it re-establishing (e.g. measles).

Introductory Lecture: quiz

Introduction to Biomedicine › Introductory Lecture
How to use this

Read a question and answer it out loud or on paper first. Then click the question to reveal the answer. Questions are grouped by topic, in lecture order, and the same questions sit at the bottom of each topic note.

15 questions

What Biomedicine actually is

How does Biomedicine define its own field?

The study of the molecular and cellular basis of human disease, and how that knowledge becomes diagnosis, monitoring, treatment and prevention.

What does Biomedicine translate its knowledge into?

Diagnosis, monitoring, treatment and prevention of human disease.

The Grand Challenges in Biomedicine

What are the nine Grand Challenge themes?

Infectious diseases and vaccinations; antibiotic resistance; microbiome and host disease risk; stem cells and biomedical engineering; curing cancer; ageing; nutrition, diet and health; obesity and eating disorders; and exploiting the human genome for personalised medicine.

How the year is structured

What happens in the autumn semester of this module?

Grand Challenges lectures, a disease pathogenesis and treatment seminar series, and lectures on techniques for biomedical research.

How big is the Introduction to Biomedicine module, and how does it end?

It is a year-long, 40-credit module. It closes with a Biomedicine symposium where students present their favourite aspect of biomedicine from the first year.

Autumn semester: the two lecture series

What are the two lecture series in the autumn semester?

Grand Challenges in Biomedicine, and Techniques for Biomedical Research and Biomedical Science.

Which Grand Challenge lectures fall in weeks 2 and 3, and what is week 6?

Week 2 is infectious diseases and vaccinations and week 3 is antibiotic resistance. Week 6 is an independent learning week.

The seminar series: disease pathogenesis and treatment

How big are the seminar groups and who leads them?

6 to 8 students, with a faculty seminar leader who is an expert in that biomedical field.

What is week 8 of the seminar series for?

A dedicated troubleshooting and de-brief workshop.

Spring semester: three more lecture series, plus practicals

What happens in the spring semester of this module?

Practical classes in biomedical research techniques, the drug development pipeline, and clinical diagnosis lectures from NNUH biomedical scientists.

Who gives the laboratory medicine lectures in the spring semester?

Biomedical scientists from the Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital.

What are the spring practical classes for?

Hands-on experience of the techniques described in the autumn semester, applied to a biomedical research problem.

Seminar topics

How many seminar topics are offered, and how do you choose one?

Eleven. Students email their top 3 choices to the module organiser.

Name four of the eleven seminar topics.

For example: stem cells for tendon regeneration, biomedical application of stem cells, skin in health and disease, pharmacology of glaucoma, congenital diseases, personalized medicine, will we ever cure cancer, why does menopause exist, the placenta in pregnancy complications, Alzheimer's disease, and experimental models in Cystic Fibrosis drug development.

General

How is BIO-4012Y assessed overall?

Exam 50% (25% autumn sitting + 25% summer sitting), Seminar Essay 25%, Clinical Case Study 25%.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Genetics: from Mendel to chromosomes

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Heredity and DNA

Heredity is the passing of physical or mental characteristics from one generation to the next. It's the basic observation the whole lecture builds from. Genetics is the study of heredity and the variation of inherited characteristics.

  • Mendel's pea experiment: Le (dominant, tall) and le (recessive, dwarf); F2 ratio tall:dwarf ≈ 3:1
  • Gene sits on pea Chromosome 3 (pea has 7 chromosomes total)
  • Sutton and Boveri (1902) proposed the chromosome theory of inheritance: chromosome behaviour during meiosis explains inheritance patterns

Why segregation actually happens (the mechanism, not just the ratio)

Chromosome replication → Meiosis I splits the homologous pair → Meiosis II splits the chromatids → 4 gametes

  • Start: one homologous pair, where one chromosome carries Le and the other carries le
  • Replication: each becomes an X-shaped pair of sister chromatids (Le-Le, le-le)
  • Meiosis I: the whole homologous pair is pulled apart, Le-Le to one cell and le-le to the other. This is the actual moment of segregation
  • Meiosis II: each daughter splits its own chromatids, producing 4 gametes total: 2 carrying Le, 2 carrying le
  • Cross two Le/le heterozygotes → 1/4 Le/Le, 2/4 Le/le, 1/4 le/le → since Le is dominant, 3 look tall and 1 looks dwarf → matches Mendel's 3:1 exactly

Test

What does 'heredity' mean?

The passing on of physical or mental characteristics from one generation to the next.

What ratio did Mendel observe in the F2 pea generation for tall:dwarf?

Approximately 3:1 (tall:dwarf).

Which chromosome carries the pea height gene (Le/le)?

Chromosome 3 (pea has 7 chromosomes total).

What ratio did Mendel observe for tall:dwarf pea plants in the F2 generation?
  • A. 1:1
  • B. 1:3
  • C. 3:1
  • D. 9:3:3:1

Answer: C. 3:1

From the lecture slides

Mendel's cross: tall × dwarf gives all-tall F1, then about 3 : 1 tall : dwarf in F2 (Lecture 1, slide 7)

The Le/le cross as genotypes, gametes and an F2 Punnett square (Lecture 1, slide 8)

Cytogenetics: chromosomes seen at prometaphase and anaphase (Lecture 1, slide 9)

The F2 Punnett square drawn with chromosomes carrying Le and le (Lecture 1, slide 11)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 183

This hereditary information is passed on from a cell to its daughter cells at cell division and from one generation of an organism to the next through the organism’s reproductive cells.

Alberts 7e, p. 523

Alternative forms of the same gene are known as alleles.

Alberts 7e, p. 523

A recessive mutation is one that is no longer able to cause the mutant phenotype in the presence of a single wild-type copy of the gene.

Alberts 7e, p. 523

In the majority of cases, recessive mutations are loss of function and dominant mutations are gain of function—although cases have been described in which a loss-of-function mutation is dominant or a gain-of-function mutation is recessive.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Proving DNA is the hereditary material

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Heredity and DNA

Griffith's experiment (1928)

Live IIR + heat-killed IIIS together → mouse dies, living IIIS recovered from tissue

  • Live IIIS (virulent) → mouse dies. Live IIR (avirulent) → mouse lives. Heat-killed IIIS alone → mouse lives
  • Live IIR + heat-killed IIIS together → mouse dies, and living IIIS bacteria are recovered from its tissue
  • Something from the dead virulent bacteria converted the harmless ones to virulent. Griffith called this the transforming principle (unidentified at this point)

Dawson reproduced this same effect in vitro (a test tube, no mouse needed), ruling out any mouse-specific explanation.

Avery, MacLeod and McCarty: identifying the transforming principle

Only the DNase-treated batch failed to transform: proof by elimination that DNA is the active factor

  • IIIS filtrate split into batches, each treated with one enzyme, then mixed with live IIR cells
  • DNase-treated → NO transformation → active factor is DNA
  • RNase-treated → transformation still occurs → not RNA
  • Protease-treated → transformation still occurs → not protein
  • Only destroying DNA stopped transformation: DNA is the transforming principle, by elimination

From Klug, Cummings, Spencer and Palladino, Concepts of Genetics (Ch. 10, 10th–12th ed.)

The Hershey-Chase experiment (1952): a third, independent confirmation

Used the T2 bacteriophage (a virus with just a protein coat and a DNA core) and a chemical quirk: DNA contains phosphorus but no sulfur; protein contains sulfur (in some amino acids) but no phosphorus.

  • Batch 1 phages grown with radioactive ³²P (labels DNA only). Batch 2 grown with radioactive ³⁵S (labels protein only). Each batch infects separate, unlabelled E. coli
  • Blending: infected mixtures agitated to shear the empty phage coats off the outside of the bacteria, without bursting the bacteria
  • Centrifugation separates by density: heavy bacteria form a pellet, lighter empty coats stay in the supernatant
  • Result: ³²P (DNA) found in the PELLET, inside the bacteria. ³⁵S (protein) found in the SUPERNATANT, outside with the discarded coats
  • Conclusion: the molecule that actually enters the cell, and therefore must direct new phage production, is DNA, not protein

Two conceptual questions worth knowing. Why ³²P and ³⁵S specifically: they selectively tag DNA and protein via each molecule's unique element. Does this distinguish DNA from RNA: no, both contain phosphorus, so the experiment only distinguishes nucleic acids as a group from protein, and it works here because T2 phage contains DNA and no RNA.

Test

What did Griffith's experiment show?

Live IIR plus heat-killed IIIS together kills the mouse and produces living IIIS bacteria. Something from the dead bacteria transformed the harmless ones. He called it the transforming principle.

How did Avery, MacLeod and McCarty identify the transforming principle as DNA?

Only the DNase-treated batch of IIIS filtrate failed to transform IIR cells. RNase and protease treatment didn't stop transformation. By elimination, DNA is the active factor.

What isotopes did Hershey and Chase use, and why?

³²P labels DNA (phosphorus is in the DNA backbone, not protein); ³⁵S labels protein (sulfur is in some amino acids, not DNA).

What did Griffith's 1928 experiment demonstrate?
  • A. DNA is the genetic material
  • B. Something from dead bacteria could transform living bacteria
  • C. RNA carries hereditary information
  • D. Bacteria can exchange plasmids directly

Answer: B. Something from dead bacteria could transform living bacteria

In the Hershey-Chase experiment, which isotope was used to label bacteriophage protein?
  • A. ³²P
  • B. ¹⁴C
  • C. ³⁵S
  • D. ¹⁵N

Answer: C. ³⁵S

Which enzyme treatment abolished the transforming activity in Avery, MacLeod and McCarty's experiment?
  • A. Protease
  • B. RNase
  • C. DNase
  • D. Lipase

Answer: C. DNase

Related

  • The Meselson-Stahl experiment

Dawson's in vitro transformation: heat-killed smooth cells turn rough cells smooth in a test tube (Lecture 1, slide 16)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 184

For many decades, the DNA was thought to be merely a structural element.

Alberts 7e, p. 184

However, the other crucial advance made in the 1940s was the identification of DNA as the likely carrier of hereditary information. This breakthrough in our understanding of cells came from studies of inheritance in bacteria (Figure 4–2).

Figure 4–2: The first experimental demonstration that DNA is the genetic material. (Alberts 7e, p. 184)

props.summary: Recombinant DNA is DNA artificially combined from two different sources: a bacterial plasmid backbone plus a gene from a completely different organism.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Transformation in the lab

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Heredity and DNA

Recombinant DNA is DNA artificially combined from two different sources: a bacterial plasmid backbone plus a gene from a completely different organism.

Making E. coli competent, and why it actually works

CaCl₂ neutralises charge repulsion; heat shock briefly opens the membrane to let plasmid DNA in

  • Problem: both the cell membrane and DNA's phosphate backbone are negatively charged, so they repel each other
  • CaCl₂ treatment: positive calcium ions shield that negative charge, letting DNA sit close to the membrane. This makes the cell 'competent'
  • Heat shock (42°C): briefly destabilises the membrane so nearby DNA gets pulled inside
  • Plate on ampicillin: the selection step, where only cells that took up a plasmid carrying AmpR survive
pBR322, a 4,361 bp cloning vector: AmpR and TcR resistance genes as selectable markers, plus an ori for self-replication

pGLO: recombinant DNA in action

E. coli transformed with pGLO glow green under UV, visible proof the foreign gene (GFP, from jellyfish) was taken up and expressed

Synthetic genome (Gibson et al., 2010): a 1.08 Mb Mycoplasma mycoides genome was built entirely from scratch and transplanted into a recipient cell. The resulting cells were controlled entirely by the synthetic chromosome and self-replicated continuously.

Test

Why does CaCl₂ make E. coli 'competent'?

It provides positive ions that neutralise the negative charge on both the cell membrane and DNA's phosphate backbone, reducing repulsion so DNA can approach the cell.

What does the pGLO experiment demonstrate?

That foreign DNA (a jellyfish GFP gene) was taken up by E. coli and actively expressed. The bacteria glow green under UV.

What does CaCl2 do in making E. coli cells competent?
  • A. Breaks down the cell wall
  • B. Neutralises negative charges to reduce repulsion between DNA and the membrane
  • C. Provides nutrients for growth
  • D. Activates restriction enzymes

Answer: B. Neutralises negative charges to reduce repulsion between DNA and the membrane

Related

  • Aim and background (Transformation)
  • Transforming the cells
  • Aim and background (Restriction Mapping)
  • Natural transformation

From the lecture slides

A chemically synthesised Mycoplasma mycoides genome (JCVI-syn1.0) running a recipient cell, next to wild type (Lecture 1, slide 24)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 502

One of the simplest involves inserting a particular fragment of DNA into the purified DNA of a self-replicating genetic element—usually a plasmid.

Alberts 7e, p. 502

The plasmid vectors most widely used for gene cloning are small, circular molecules of double-stranded DNA derived from plasmids that occur naturally in bacterial cells.

Alberts 7e, p. 502

For use as cloning vectors, the purified plasmid DNA circles are first cut with a restriction nuclease to create linear DNA molecules.

Alberts 7e, p. 502

The DNA to be cloned is added to the cut plasmid and then covalently joined using the enzyme DNA ligase (Figure 8–26 and Figure 8–27).

Alberts 7e, p. 503

The resulting recombinant plasmid DNA is then introduced into a bacterium, where it is replicated many millions of times as the bacterium multiplies.

Figure 8–26: The insertion of a DNA fragment into a bacterial plasmid with the enzyme DNA ligase. (Alberts 7e, p. 502)

Figure 8–28: A DNA fragment can be replicated inside a bacterial cell. (Alberts 7e, p. 503)

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Natural transformation

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Heredity and DNA

In the lab, scientists deliberately force DNA into a cell (Transformation in the lab). Agrobacterium does the same basic thing naturally, with no lab involved.

Ti plasmid: T-DNA is the cargo that gets transferred; vir genes are the transfer machinery

  • Agrobacterium tumefaciens causes crown gall disease by inserting its own DNA into a plant's genome
  1. Detects wound-site signals on a plant.
  2. Attaches.
  3. vir genes cut out T-DNA and inject it into the plant cell, which incorporates it into its own genome.
  4. Hijacked growth control builds a gall (tumour) that feeds the bacteria
  • Real GM-crop science hijacks this exact mechanism, replacing Agrobacterium's own disease genes in the T-DNA with whatever gene scientists want inserted into a crop

Test

What is T-DNA, and what does Agrobacterium do with it?

T-DNA is the segment of the Ti plasmid that gets physically transferred into a plant cell's genome during infection, hijacking its growth to form a gall.

What is the function of T-DNA in Agrobacterium-mediated transformation?
  • A. It degrades plant cell walls
  • B. It gets physically transferred into the plant genome
  • C. It produces the Ti plasmid
  • D. It encodes antibiotic resistance only

Answer: B. It gets physically transferred into the plant genome

Related

  • Transformation in the lab

From the lecture slides

Agrobacterium tumefaciens causes crown gall disease (Lecture 1, slide 27)

Infection: T-DNA is transferred into the host plant cells, which then grow into a gall (Lecture 1, slide 29)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 1317

Pathogenic bacteria are thought to emerge when groups of virulence genes are transferred together into a previously avirulent bacterium by a process called horizontal gene transfer (to distinguish it from vertical gene transfer from parent to offspring).

Alberts 7e, p. 1317

This can occur by three mechanisms: natural transformation, in which naked DNA is taken in by competent bacteria; transduction, in which bacterial viruses (bacteriophages) transfer DNA from one bacterium (in the example shown, a pathogen) into another; and conjugation, during which plasmid DNA, and even chromosomal DNA, is transferred from a donor to a recipient bacterium.

Alberts 7e, p. 1317

Sequencing the genomes of pathogenic and nonpathogenic bacteria has revealed that horizontal gene transfer has made important contributions to bacterial evolution, enabling species to inhabit new ecological and nutritional niches and to cause disease.

Alberts 7e, p. 541

A disc is cut out of a leaf and incubated in a culture of Agrobacterium that carries a recombinant plasmid with both a selectable marker and a desired genetically engineered gene.

Figure 23–4: Genetic differences between pathogenic and nonpathogenic bacteria. (Alberts 7e, p. 1317)

Figure 8–71: Transgenic plants can be made using recombinant DNA techniques optimized for plants. (Alberts 7e, p. 541)

props.title: Physical and chemical properties of DNA and RNA

props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Physical and chemical properties of DNA and RNA

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Heredity and DNA

From Klug, Cummings, Spencer and Palladino, Concepts of Genetics (Ch. 10, 10th–12th ed.)

The physical and chemical side of DNA underpins a lot of real lab technique, from checking DNA purity to PCR itself.

  • UV absorption: DNA and RNA absorb UV light maximally at 260 nm (because of the bases). The standard way to measure nucleic acid concentration and purity in a lab
  • Denaturation: separating the two DNA strands by breaking hydrogen bonds (heat or chemicals), without breaking the covalent sugar-phosphate backbone
  • Hyperchromic effect: UV absorbance at 260 nm increases as DNA denatures, because unstacked single-stranded bases absorb more UV than stacked double-stranded ones
  • Melting temperature (Tm): the temperature at which half the DNA sample is denatured. Higher GC content means a higher Tm, since G≡C's 3 hydrogen bonds take more energy to break than A=T's 2
  • Molecular hybridization: complementary single strands from different sources can reanneal and base-pair with each other. The underlying principle behind PCR, probes, and primers

Test

At what wavelength do DNA and RNA absorb UV light most strongly, and what is that used for?

260 nm, because of the bases. It is the standard way to measure nucleic acid concentration and purity.

What is denaturation of DNA, and what does it leave intact?

Separating the two strands by breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases (using heat or chemicals). The covalent sugar-phosphate backbone stays intact.

What is the hyperchromic effect?

UV absorbance at 260 nm increases as DNA denatures, because unstacked single-stranded bases absorb more UV than stacked double-stranded ones.

What is melting temperature (Tm), and why does more G and C raise it?

The temperature at which half the DNA sample is denatured. G≡C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds, which take more energy to break than the 2 in A=T.

What is molecular hybridization?

Complementary single strands from different sources re-annealing and base-pairing with each other. It is the principle behind PCR, probes and primers.

Related

  • Measuring absorbance

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 505

Under normal conditions, the two strands of a DNA double helix are held together by hydrogen bonds between the complementary base pairs (see Figure 4–3).

Alberts 7e, p. 505

Such DNA denaturation releases the two strands from each other but does not break the covalent bonds that link together the nucleotides within each strand.

Alberts 7e, p. 505

The simplest way to achieve this separation is to heat the DNA to around 90°C.

Alberts 7e, p. 505

When the conditions are reversed—by slowly lowering the temperature—the complementary strands will readily come back together to re-form a double helix.

Alberts 7e, p. 505

This hybridization, or DNA renaturation, is driven by the re-formation of the hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs (Figure 8-31).

Alberts 7e, p. 273

We saw in Figure 4–5A that an A-T base pair is held together by fewer hydrogen bonds than is a G-C base pair.

Figure 8–31: A molecule of DNA can undergo denaturation and renaturation (hybridization). (Alberts 7e, p. 505)

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.title: 06 Perspectives, where inheritance gets stranger
01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Perspectives: where inheritance gets stranger

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Heredity and DNA

What a tsRNA actually is (built from scratch)

  • tRNA normally translates mRNA's code into amino acids during protein synthesis; its job usually ends there
  • A tsRNA is a tRNA-derived small RNA: a chopped-up fragment of a tRNA molecule, found specifically in sperm
  • Experiment: tsRNAs from high-fat-diet (HFD) male mice injected into normal zygotes caused metabolic disorders (glucose and insulin intolerance) in the offspring, despite the zygote's DNA being completely normal
  • This means a father's diet can affect offspring health via RNA fragments in sperm: inheritance that has nothing to do with DNA sequence

The Le gene: the exact mutation, finally revealed

  • Le encodes gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase, an enzyme that helps produce gibberellin, the plant hormone that promotes cell elongation (stem growth)
  • Mutant le: one A→G DNA letter change leads to one amino acid swap (ala229→thr, 'A229T'), the enzyme barely works, very little hormone is made, and the plant stays dwarf
  • Closes the whole lecture's loop: Mendel's ratio, the chromosome mechanism, and finally the exact single DNA letter responsible for the height difference

Test

What is a tsRNA?

A tRNA-derived small RNA: a fragment chopped from a full tRNA molecule, found in sperm, which can carry non-DNA hereditary information to a zygote.

What enzyme does the Le gene encode, and what happens in the dwarf mutant?

Gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase. The mutant (le) has an A→G DNA change causing an ala229→thr amino acid swap, crippling the enzyme and reducing the height-promoting hormone.

What is a tsRNA, as discussed in the lecture on inheritance beyond DNA sequence?
  • A. A type of ribosomal RNA
  • B. A tRNA-derived small RNA fragment found in sperm
  • C. A transfer RNA synthase
  • D. A bacterial transformation vector

Answer: B. A tRNA-derived small RNA fragment found in sperm

From the lecture slides

Sperm tsRNAs from high-fat-diet fathers pass a metabolic disorder to offspring (Lecture 1, slide 33)

Le encodes gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase (GA20 → active GA1); the le mutation is A229T (Lecture 1, slide 34)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 444

The ability of a daughter cell to retain a memory of the gene expression patterns that were present in the parent cell is an example of epigenetic inheritance, which we define as a heritable alteration in a cell or organism’s phenotype that does not result from changes in the nucleotide sequence of DNA.

Alberts 7e, p. 445

DNA methylation underlies the phenomenon in mammals of genomic imprinting, in which the expression of a gene depends on whether that gene was inherited from the mother or the father.

The Le gene: the exact mutation, finally revealed

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.text: Perspectives: where inheritance gets stranger Molecular Biology and Genetics › Heredity and DNA What a tsRNA actually is (built from scratch) tRNA normally translates mRNA's code into amino acids during protein synthesis; its job usually ends there A tsRNA is a tRNA-derived small RNA: a chopped-up fragment of a tRNA molecule, found specifically in sperm Experiment: tsRNAs from high-fat-diet (HFD) male mice injected into normal zygotes caused metabolic disorders (glucose and insulin intolerance) in the offspring, despite the zygote's DNA being completely normal This means a father's diet can affect offspring health via RNA fragments in sperm: inheritance that has nothing to do with DNA sequence The Le gene: the exact mutation, finally revealed Le encodes gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase , an enzyme that helps produce gibberellin, the plant hormone that promotes cell elongation (stem growth) Mutant le: one A→G DNA letter change leads to one amino acid swap (ala229→thr, 'A229T'), the enzyme barely works, very little hormone is made, and the plant stays dwarf Closes the whole lecture's loop: Mendel's ratio, the chromosome mechanism, and finally the exact single DNA letter responsible for the height difference Test What is a tsRNA? A tRNA-derived small RNA: a fragment chopped from a full tRNA molecule, found in sperm, which can carry non-DNA hereditary information to a zygote. What enzyme does the Le gene encode, and what happens in the dwarf mutant? Gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase. The mutant (le) has an A→G DNA change causing an ala229→thr amino acid swap, crippling the enzyme and reducing the height-promoting hormone. What is a tsRNA, as discussed in the lecture on inheritance beyond DNA sequence? A. A type of ribosomal RNA B. A tRNA-derived small RNA fragment found in sperm C. A transfer RNA synthase D. A bacterial transformation vector Answer: B. Alberts 7e, p. 445 DNA methylation underlies the phenomenon in mammals of genomic imprinting, in which the expression of a gene depends on whether that gene was inherited from the mother or the father.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
The nucleotide: DNA and RNA's shared building block

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Structure of DNA and RNA

A nucleotide has three parts: a 5-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base. Chain these together and you get DNA or RNA. Everything else in this lecture elaborates on this one building block.

General nucleotide structure, carbons numbered 1′ to 5′, base attached at the 1′ position

  • RNA uses ribose; DNA uses deoxyribose. The only difference is a 2′-OH (ribose) vs 2′-H (deoxyribose)
  • That single -OH is why RNA is less chemically stable than DNA, part of why DNA, not RNA, is the long-term storage molecule
  • Sugar carbons are numbered 1′ through 5′. This defines a strand's 5′ end and 3′ end
Purines (bottom, 2 fused rings) are visibly bigger than pyrimidines (top, 1 ring)

  • Purines (2 rings, 4 N): Adenine, Guanine
  • Pyrimidines (1 ring, 2 N): Cytosine, Thymine (DNA only), Uracil (RNA only)
  • Naming pattern: base alone + sugar = nucleoside (e.g. Adenosine). Nucleoside + phosphate = nucleotide (e.g. AMP). Same pattern across all 4 bases
  • Nucleotides aren't always monophosphate: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the same base unit, used as the cell's energy currency

Test

What three parts make up a nucleotide?

A 5-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base.

What's the chemical difference between ribose and deoxyribose?

Ribose has an -OH group on its 2′ carbon; deoxyribose has just -H there instead.

Name the two purines and three pyrimidines.

Purines: Adenine, Guanine. Pyrimidines: Cytosine, Thymine (DNA only), Uracil (RNA only).

What distinguishes ribose from deoxyribose?
  • A. Ribose has a phosphate group, deoxyribose doesn't
  • B. Ribose has an -OH at the 2' carbon, deoxyribose has -H
  • C. Deoxyribose is found only in RNA
  • D. Ribose lacks a nitrogenous base

Answer: B. Ribose has an -OH at the 2' carbon, deoxyribose has -H

Related

  • Linking nucleotides: the phosphodiester bond

From the lecture slides

Ribose (RNA) has a 2′-OH; 2-deoxyribose (DNA) has only H at C2′ (Lecture 2, slide 4)

Base + sugar = nucleoside; base + sugar + phosphate = nucleotide (adenosine 5′-monophosphate) (Lecture 2, slide 8)

Nucleotides can carry one, two or three phosphates (dTDP and ATP shown) (Lecture 2, slide 10)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 185

As we saw in Chapter 2 (Panel 2–6, pp. 104–105), a nucleotide is composed of a five-carbon sugar to which a phosphate group and a nitrogen-containing base are attached. In the case of the nucleotides in DNA, the sugar is deoxyribose attached to a phosphate group (hence the name deoxyribonucleic acid), and the base may be either adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G), or thymine (T).

Alberts 7e, p. 186

In each case, a bulkier two-ring base (a purine; see Panel 2–6, pp. 104–105) is paired with a single-ring base (a pyrimidine): A always pairs with T, and G with C (Figure 4–5A).

Figure 4–3: DNA and its four nucleotide building blocks. (Alberts 7e, p. 186)

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Linking nucleotides: the phosphodiester bond

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Structure of DNA and RNA
A 3′→5′ phosphodiester bond links two nucleotides, repeated all the way along a strand

  • Nucleotides link via a phosphodiester bond, between the 5′ carbon of one sugar and the 3′ carbon of the next
  • 2 linked = dinucleotide, 3 = trinucleotide, a full chain = a polynucleotide (what DNA and RNA actually are)
  • This gives every strand directionality: a free 5′ end (phosphate) and a free 3′ end (hydroxyl)

Why 5′→3′ matters: it governs everything downstream

  • Sequences are always written 5′ to 3′ by convention
  • DNA and RNA are only ever synthesised 5′→3′
  • Genes are transcribed 5′→3′
  • RNA is translated into protein reading 5′→3′
  • One directionality rule governs replication, transcription, and translation

Test

What bond links nucleotides together, and between which carbons?

A phosphodiester bond, between the 5′ carbon of one sugar and the 3′ carbon of the next.

What direction is DNA/RNA always synthesised, transcribed, and translated in?

5′ to 3′, in all three processes.

What type of bond links adjacent nucleotides in a DNA strand?
  • A. Hydrogen bond
  • B. Glycosidic bond
  • C. Phosphodiester bond
  • D. Peptide bond

Answer: C. Phosphodiester bond

Related

  • How new nucleotides get added
  • Replication forks: leading and lagging strands
  • The nucleotide: DNA and RNA's shared building block

From the lecture slides

Nucleotides join by 3′ to 5′ phosphodiester bonds, giving a strand with a 5′ and a 3′ end (Lecture 2, slide 11)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 185

The nucleotides are covalently linked together in a chain through the sugars and phosphates, which thus form a “backbone” of alternating sugar–phosphate–sugar–phosphate (Figure 4–4).

Alberts 7e, p. 185

The way in which the nucleotides are linked together gives a DNA strand a chemical polarity.

Figure 4–4: The nucleotide subunits within a DNA strand are held together by a phosphodiester bond. (Alberts 7e, p. 186)

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Discovering the structure: Franklin, Chargaff, Watson and Crick

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Structure of DNA and RNA

X-ray diffraction: a DNA crystal in an X-ray beam produces a regular pattern of reflections. Rotating the crystal and recording every spot's intensity reveals the actual positions of atoms in the molecule. Rosalind Franklin produced the key diffraction photographs, distinguishing A-form from B-form DNA and concluding the molecule was probably helical. Watson and Crick used this data, shared via Franklin's colleague Maurice Wilkins, to build the double-helix model in 1953.

DNA source A T G C
Human 30.9 29.4 19.9 19.8
Sea urchin 32.8 32.1 26.0 25.7
E. coli 24.7 23.6 26.0 25.7
Sarcina 13.4 12.4 37.1 37.1

Chargaff's rule: %A ≈ %T and %G ≈ %C, always, regardless of species, even though the overall A+T vs G+C ratio varies wildly between species. This was the direct clue toward complementary base pairing, before anyone had seen the double helix itself.

Test

What did Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction photographs show?

They distinguished A-form from B-form DNA and suggested the molecule was probably helical. Watson and Crick used this data, shared via Maurice Wilkins, to build the double-helix model in 1953.

What is Chargaff's rule, and why was it an important clue?

%A is roughly equal to %T and %G roughly equal to %C in every species, even though the overall A+T versus G+C ratio varies widely. It was a direct clue toward complementary base pairing.

Sarcina DNA is about 13% A and 37% G. What does that show about Chargaff's rule?

A is still roughly equal to T (13.4 and 12.4) and G equal to C (37.1 and 37.1), even though the balance of A+T to G+C is very different from other species.

Which experimental technique did Rosalind Franklin use that was central to solving DNA's structure?
  • A. Mass spectrometry
  • B. X-ray diffraction
  • C. Electron microscopy
  • D. Gel electrophoresis

Answer: B. X-ray diffraction

From the lecture slides

Chargaff's base composition data: G ≈ C and A ≈ T in every species (Lecture 2, slide 13)

X-ray crystallography workflow and Rosalind Franklin's diffraction photograph of DNA (Lecture 2, slide 14)

Watson and Crick with their model, and Rosalind Franklin (Lecture 2, slide 16)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 185

In the early 1950s, DNA was examined by x-ray diffraction analysis, a technique for determining the three-dimensional atomic structure of a molecule (discussed in Chapter 8). The x-ray diffraction results indicated that DNA was composed of two strands of the polymer wound into a helix. The observation that DNA was double-stranded provided one of the major clues that led to the Watson–Crick model for DNA structure that, as soon as it was proposed in 1953, made DNA’s potential for replication and information storage immediately apparent.

Alberts 7e, p. 184

The puzzle was suddenly solved in 1953, when James Watson and Francis Crick derived the answers from their model for the structure of a DNA molecule.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
The double helix: full structure

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Structure of DNA and RNA
A=T (2 H-bonds) vs G≡C (3 H-bonds); note the antiparallel 5′/3′ labels on each strand

  • DNA is double-stranded; the two strands are antiparallel (one 5′→3′, the other 3′→5′)
  • Held together by hydrogen bonds: A=T (2 bonds), G≡C (3 bonds); this is complementary base pairing
  • G≡C's extra bond means GC-rich DNA has a higher melting temperature (Tm) than AT-rich DNA

Why salt helps DNA strands bind

  • The sugar-phosphate backbone is negatively charged, so two negative strands naturally repel each other
  • Salt (e.g. NaCl) provides positive ions that neutralise this charge, letting strands bind more strongly
  • In real cells, positively-charged proteins do this same job. It's the exact same principle behind why CaCl₂ makes E. coli 'competent' in Lecture 1
Full picture: 2 nm diameter, 0.34 nm rise per bp, major (22 Å) and minor (12 Å) grooves

  • Diameter: 2 nm. Rise: 0.34 nm per base pair. 10 bp per turn (10.4, precisely)
  • B-DNA is the predominant form in cells; A-DNA and Z-DNA also occur, with different helical structures
  • The major groove exposes more of each base pair's distinguishing chemical detail. This is where sequence-reading proteins (like transcription factors) actually bind. The minor groove is less useful for sequence-specific recognition
  • 23 human chromosome pairs = 3 billion base pairs total ≈ 1 metre of DNA, packed into a nucleus a few micrometres across

From Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed. (Ch. 4, pp. 225–227, “The Structure and Function of DNA”)

A sharper mental model for why a DNA strand has consistent directionality: picture each sugar as a block with a knob on one side (the 5′ phosphate) and a hole on the other (the 3′ hydroxyl). A complete strand is built by interlocking knobs into holes all the way along, which is exactly why every subunit faces the same direction, and why the two ends of a strand are chemically different.

Why the grooves exist geometrically: the two sugar-phosphate backbones don't attach to each base pair symmetrically opposite each other; they attach at an angle. Coiling the two backbones around each other this way creates one wide gap (major groove) and one narrow gap (minor groove), rather than two identical grooves.

The replication preview: because each strand's sequence is exactly complementary to its partner, either strand alone can act as a template to build a new matching partner strand. This is the conceptual basis for how DNA replication actually works, covered in more procedural detail in Extra depth: semiconservative replication.

Test

How many hydrogen bonds hold A=T together, vs G≡C?

A=T: 2 hydrogen bonds. G≡C: 3 hydrogen bonds.

What does 'antiparallel' mean for the two DNA strands?

One strand runs 5′→3′, the other runs 3′→5′: opposite directions.

What are the double helix's key dimensions?

2 nm diameter, 0.34 nm rise per base pair, ~10 (precisely 10.4) base pairs per turn.

Why does the major groove matter more than the minor groove for protein binding?

The major groove exposes more of each base pair's distinguishing chemical detail, making it the site where sequence-reading proteins (e.g. transcription factors) typically bind.

How many hydrogen bonds hold a G-C base pair together?
  • A. 1
  • B. 2
  • C. 3
  • D. 4

Answer: C. 3

What is the approximate diameter of the DNA double helix?
  • A. 0.34 nm
  • B. 1 nm
  • C. 2 nm
  • D. 3.4 nm

Answer: C. 2 nm

Why do most sequence-reading proteins bind in the major groove rather than the minor groove?
  • A. The major groove is narrower
  • B. The major groove exposes more distinguishing chemical detail of each base pair
  • C. The minor groove is inaccessible
  • D. The minor groove only forms in RNA

Answer: B. The major groove exposes more distinguishing chemical detail of each base pair

Related

  • The semiconservative model

From the lecture slides

The negatively charged phosphate backbone is neutralised by cations and positive proteins (Lecture 2, slide 18)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 185

The two strands run antiparallel to each other, and hydrogen bonds between the base portions of the nucleotides hold the two strands together (Figure 4–3).

Alberts 7e, p. 186

Because the DNA strands are held together by hydrogen-bonding between the bases on the two different strands, all the bases are on the inside of the double helix, and the sugar–phosphate backbones are on the outside (see Figure 4–3).

Alberts 7e, p. 186

To maximize the efficiency of base-pair packing, the two sugar–phosphate backbones wind around each other to form a right-handed double helix, with one complete turn every 10.4 base pairs (Figure 4–5B and Figure 4–6).

Alberts 7e, p. 187

The coiling of the two strands around each other creates two grooves in the double helix: the wider groove is called the major groove, and the narrower groove is called the minor groove, as indicated.

Figure 4–5: How the two strands of the DNA double helix are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs. (Alberts 7e, p. 187)

Figure 4–6: A space-filling model of the DNA double helix. (Alberts 7e, p. 187)

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
RNA: structure and the three main types

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Structure of DNA and RNA
  • RNA composition: ribose sugar + phosphate + base (A, G, C, or U)
  • All RNA is copied from DNA sequences; its main job is expressing that information (protein synthesis)

mRNA (Messenger)

Single-stranded copies of DNA sequences that get translated into protein: the molecule literally carrying the genetic message.

tRNA (Transfer)

Synthesised single-stranded, but folds back on itself into double-stranded regions via complementary base pairing within the same molecule. Carries amino acids to ribosomes during protein synthesis.

rRNA (Ribosomal)

A core structural and functional component of the ribosome itself, not just a passing messenger.

Test

What are the three main types of RNA and their roles?

mRNA carries the genetic message, tRNA delivers amino acids to ribosomes, rRNA is a structural and functional component of ribosomes.

tRNA is made single-stranded. Why does it still contain double-stranded regions?

It folds back on itself, and complementary base pairing within the same molecule forms the double-stranded regions.

Which RNA type carries amino acids to the ribosome during translation?
  • A. mRNA
  • B. rRNA
  • C. tRNA
  • D. snRNA

Answer: C. tRNA

Related

  • The central dogma

From the lecture slides

RNA: ribose, phosphate and the bases A, G, C and U (Lecture 2, slide 21)

mRNA carries the DNA sequence out of the nucleus to the ribosomes (Lecture 2, slide 23)

tRNA folds into a cloverleaf through base pairing within the strand; the anticodon reads the mRNA codon (Lecture 2, slide 24)

rRNA in prokaryotic (70S) and eukaryotic (80S) ribosomes (Lecture 2, slide 25)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 324

It differs from DNA chemically in two respects: (1) the nucleotides in RNA are ribonucleotides—that is, they contain the sugar ribose (hence the name ribo nucleic acid) rather than deoxyribose; (2) although, like DNA, RNA contains the bases adenine (A), guanine (G), and cytosine (C), it contains the base uracil (U) instead of the thymine (T) in DNA (Figure 6–5).

Alberts 7e, p. 324

Whereas DNA always occurs in cells as a double-strand helix, RNA is single-stranded.

Alberts 7e, p. 324

An RNA chain can therefore fold up into a particular shape, just as a polypeptide chain folds up to form the final shape of a protein (Figure 6–7).

Alberts 7e, p. 327

The majority of genes carried in a cell’s DNA specify the amino acid sequence of proteins, and the RNAs that are copied from these genes (which ultimately direct the synthesis of proteins) are called messenger RNA (mRNA) molecules.

Alberts 7e, p. 327

We shall see in this chapter that ribosomal RNA (rRNA) molecules form the core of ribosomes, that transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules serve as the adaptors that select amino acids and hold them in place on a ribosome for incorporation into protein, and that small nuclear RNA (snRNA) molecules direct the splicing of pre-mRNA to form mRNA.

Figure 6–5: The chemical structure of RNA. (Alberts 7e, p. 324)

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
The central dogma

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Structure of DNA and RNA

Francis Crick, 1970: information flows one way, DNA → RNA → protein. Sequential information can pass between nucleic acids and from nucleic acid to protein, but never back from protein to nucleic acid or protein. This is the conceptual skeleton the whole module hangs on.

Test

State the central dogma of molecular biology.

Information flows one-way: DNA → RNA → protein. It cannot flow back from protein to nucleic acid.

What does the central dogma say can never happen?

Information can pass between nucleic acids and from nucleic acid to protein, but never back from protein to nucleic acid or to another protein (Crick, 1970).

Related

  • RNA: structure and the three main types

From the lecture slides

From chromatin to protein: every stage where expression can be regulated (Lecture 2, slide 26)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 321

When the cell needs a particular protein, the nucleotide sequence of the appropriate portion of the DNA molecule in a chromosome is first copied into RNA (a process called transcription). These RNA copies of segments of the DNA sequence are then used to direct the synthesis of the protein (a process called translation).

Alberts 7e, p. 321

All cells, from bacteria to humans, express their genetic information in this way—a principle so fundamental that it is termed the central dogma of molecular biology (Figure 6–1).

Figure 6–1: Genetic information directs the synthesis of proteins. (Alberts 7e, p. 321)

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Extra depth: semiconservative replication

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Structure of DNA and RNA

Not covered directly in this lecture, but it sets up the DNA Replication lecture (The semiconservative model): when DNA replicates, each daughter molecule keeps exactly one original strand plus one newly-made strand. This is called semiconservative replication.

From Genetics in Medicine (Ch. 1.1, “Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid (DNA)”)

The history, in brief

  • Watson and Crick published the double-helix model in Nature, 1953 (vol 171, p.737), built heavily on X-ray diffraction data from Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling, published in the same issue directly afterward (p.740)
  • Franklin's data was shared with Watson and Crick by her King's College colleague Maurice Wilkins, before her own paper was published: the crux of the ongoing debate over Franklin's contribution
  • Erwin Chargaff's 1950 finding (roughly equal A/T and roughly equal C/G across species) is the same data behind the Chargaff table in Discovering the structure: Franklin, Chargaff, Watson and Crick, a direct precursor clue Watson and Crick built on

Semiconservative replication

  • Two structural facts explain how DNA is copied accurately: it's a double helix of two strands, and one strand's sequence is exactly complementary to the other
  • When DNA replicates, each daughter molecule contains one original (old) strand plus one newly-made strand: semiconservative replication
  • Replication happens during the S (synthesis) phase of both mitosis and meiosis

The replication fork and the three enzyme roles

  • Replication fork: the Y-shaped point where the helix is actively unwound and copied
  • Leading strand, synthesised continuously. Lagging strand, synthesised backwards in short Okazaki fragments, because DNA polymerase only builds 5′→3′
  • Helicase and topoisomerase: unwind the strands and prevent tangling
  • DNA polymerase: adds nucleotides and proofreads, pausing to fix an incorrect base if one gets inserted
  • DNA ligase: joins the separate Okazaki fragments into one continuous strand
  • Fidelity: roughly 1 error per 100 million (10⁸) base pairs copied, thanks to that proofreading, based on studies comparing parent/child genome trios

Mitochondrial DNA: a genuinely separate genome

  • A small amount of DNA exists outside the nucleus, in mitochondria: approximately 17,000 base pairs, double-stranded and circular, organisationally closer to a bacterial genome than a nuclear chromosome
  • Multiple copies exist per mitochondrion, and mitochondria-per-cell varies by cell type, so mitochondrial DNA copy number isn't fixed the way nuclear chromosome number is
  • Nuclear genome for comparison: 23 chromosome pairs, ~3 billion base pairs per haploid copy

Test

What is semiconservative replication?

DNA replication where each daughter molecule contains one original (old) strand and one newly synthesised strand.

Why is the lagging strand synthesised in fragments (Okazaki fragments)?

DNA polymerase only builds in the 5′→3′ direction, so the strand running the wrong way relative to the replication fork has to be copied backwards in short pieces.

What are the three enzyme roles in DNA replication?

Helicase and topoisomerase unwind strands and prevent tangling, DNA polymerase adds nucleotides and proofreads, DNA ligase joins Okazaki fragments.

Related

  • The semiconservative model

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 187

The answer to the second question came from the double-stranded nature of the structure: because each strand of DNA contains a sequence of nucleotides that is exactly complementary to the nucleotide sequence of its partner strand, each strand can act as a template, or mold, for the synthesis of a new complementary strand. In other words, if we designate the two DNA strands as S and S′, strand S can serve as a template for making a new strand S′, while strand S′ can serve as a template for making a new strand S (Figure 4–7).

Alberts 7e, p. 257

DNA replication is semiconservative because each daughter DNA double helix is composed of one conserved (old) strand and one newly synthesized strand.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Three theoretical ways DNA could replicate

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Replication

Source: Lecture 3: DNA Replication (PowerPoint)

Even though DNA is organised differently in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, replication is essentially similar in both, suggesting the process has been conserved through evolution. Before it was known which model was correct, three were theoretically possible:

Conservative (both parental strands stay together, an entirely new molecule forms), Semiconservative (each daughter has one parental and one new strand), Dispersive (parental and new DNA are mixed throughout each strand)

Test

What are the three theoretical models for how DNA could replicate, and which one is correct?

Conservative (both parental strands stay together), semiconservative (each daughter has one parental and one new strand), and dispersive (parental and new DNA mixed throughout). Semiconservative is correct.

How do the conservative and dispersive models differ?

Conservative: both parental strands stay together and an entirely new molecule forms. Dispersive: parental and new DNA are mixed throughout each strand.

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 256

Because each of the two daughters of a dividing cell inherits a new DNA double helix containing one original and one new strand (Figure 5–5), the DNA double helix is said to be replicated semiconservatively.

Figure 5–5: In each round of DNA replication, each of the two strands of DNA is used as a template for the formation of a new, complementary strand. (Alberts 7e, p. 257)

props.title: The Meselson-Stahl experiment
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: Meselson and Stahl designed an experiment to distinguish between the three possible models of replication (Three theoretical ways DNA could replicate).
props.source: Meselson, M. and Stahl, F.W. (1958) Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 44(7): 671-682

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
The Meselson-Stahl experiment

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Replication

Source: Meselson, M. and Stahl, F.W. (1958) Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 44(7): 671-682

Meselson and Stahl designed an experiment to distinguish between the three possible models of replication (Three theoretical ways DNA could replicate). The principle: grow E. coli on medium where the nitrogen source switches from the heavier isotope ¹⁵N to the lighter ¹⁴N, then use centrifugation to separate DNA fragments by weight.

E. coli DNA gets uniformly labelled with ¹⁵N, then switched to ¹⁴N medium. After each generation, DNA is extracted and centrifuged in a density gradient

The results predicted for the semiconservative model were exactly what was observed: Generation 0 gave a single heavy (¹⁵N/¹⁵N) band, Generation I gave a single intermediate (¹⁵N/¹⁴N) band, and Generation II gave two bands, one intermediate and one light (¹⁴N/¹⁴N).

The actual 1958 published data: density gradient photographs (a) and densitometer traces (b) across successive generations. A single band splits into two as replication proceeds, exactly as the semiconservative model predicts

Test#

How did Meselson and Stahl's experiment distinguish between the three replication models?

They grew E. coli in heavy (¹⁵N) nitrogen medium, switched them to light (¹⁴N) medium, then used density gradient centrifugation to separate DNA by weight across successive generations.

What banding pattern did Meselson and Stahl actually observe, and why did it confirm semiconservative replication?

Generation 0 gave one heavy band; Generation I gave one intermediate band; Generation II gave one intermediate and one light band. This matches semiconservative replication exactly, since each new duplex should contain one old (heavy) and one new (light) strand.

Which model of DNA replication was confirmed by the Meselson-Stahl experiment?
  • A. Conservative
  • B. Semiconservative
  • C. Dispersive
  • D. Discontinuous

Answer: B. Semiconservative

In the Meselson-Stahl experiment, what banding pattern appeared after one round of replication in light medium?
  • A. One heavy band
  • B. One light band
  • C. One intermediate band
  • D. Two bands, heavy and light

Answer: C. One intermediate band

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.title: 03 The semiconservative model
01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
The semiconservative model

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Replication

Source: Lecture 3: DNA Replication (PowerPoint)

  • Parental strands act as templates that determine the sequence of the daughter strands
  • The parental strands are antiparallel, but DNA is only ever synthesised in the 5′ to 3′ direction. This is the same directionality rule from DNA structure (Linking nucleotides: the phosphodiester bond), now applied to the actual copying process

Test

What role do the parental strands play in DNA replication?

They act as templates that determine the sequence of the daughter strands.

In which direction is new DNA always synthesised, and where else have you met this rule?

5′ to 3′. It is the same directionality rule as in DNA structure, where the two strands are antiparallel, now applied to copying.

Related

  • Extra depth: semiconservative replication
  • The double helix: full structure

From the lecture slides

Each parental strand templates a new daughter strand, always synthesised 5′ to 3′ (Lecture 3, slide 9)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 256

During DNA replication inside a cell, each of the two original DNA strands serves as a template for the formation of an entire new strand.

Alberts 7e, p. 257

DNA replication is semiconservative because each daughter DNA double helix is composed of one conserved (old) strand and one newly synthesized strand.

Alberts 7e, p. 187

The answer to the second question came from the double-stranded nature of the structure: because each strand of DNA contains a sequence of nucleotides that is exactly complementary to the nucleotide sequence of its partner strand, each strand can act as a template, or mold, for the synthesis of a new complementary strand. In other words, if we designate the two DNA strands as S and S′, strand S can serve as a template for making a new strand S′, while strand S′ can serve as a template for making a new strand S (Figure 4–7).

Figure 4–7: DNA as a template for its own duplication. (Alberts 7e, p. 188)

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
How new nucleotides get added

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Replication

Source: Lecture 3: DNA Replication (PowerPoint)

In E. coli, DNA synthesis is carried out primarily by DNA polymerase III, and to a lesser extent by DNA polymerase I. The parental strand acts as the template: it determines which base gets incorporated opposite it into the new strand.

A new nucleotide (as a dNTP, carrying three phosphates) attaches its 5′ end to the free 3′-OH end of the growing chain, releasing a pyrophosphate (two linked phosphates) in the process

Test

Which enzyme does most of the DNA synthesis in E. coli?

DNA polymerase III, with DNA polymerase I playing a lesser role.

What decides which base is added opposite a base on the parental strand?

The parental strand is the template: it determines which base is incorporated opposite it into the new strand.

How does a new nucleotide join the growing DNA chain?

The incoming nucleotide (a dNTP, carrying three phosphates) attaches its 5′ end to the free 3′-OH end of the growing chain, releasing a pyrophosphate.

Related

  • Linking nucleotides: the phosphodiester bond

From the lecture slides

DNA polymerase adds nucleotides complementary to the template strand (Lecture 3, slide 13)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 256

The free nucleotides that serve as substrates for this enzyme were found to be deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates, and their polymerization into DNA required a single-strand DNA template.

Alberts 7e, p. 257

It is then covalently attached to the free 3′-hydroxyl (3′-OH) end of the growing DNA strand.

Alberts 7e, p. 257

The new DNA strand is therefore synthesized in the 5′-to-3′ direction.

Alberts 7e, p. 259

In this way, DNA polymerase functions as a “self-correcting” enzyme that removes its own polymerization errors as it moves along the DNA (Figure 5–8 and Figure 5–9).

Figure 5–4: How DNA polymerase adds a deoxyribonucleotide to the end of a growing DNA strand. (Alberts 7e, p. 257)

Figure 5–8: During DNA synthesis, DNA polymerase proofreads its own work. (Alberts 7e, p. 259)

props.title: Starting a new strand: primers

props.summary: DNA polymerases can only add nucleotides to an existing chain, they can't start one from scratch.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Starting a new strand: primers

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Replication

Source: Lecture 3: DNA Replication (PowerPoint)

DNA polymerases can only add nucleotides to an existing chain, they can't start one from scratch. So an RNA polymerase called primase first makes a short RNA primer to give DNA polymerase a free 3′ end to extend.

  • Primer length: 10 to 12 nucleotides in E. coli, 7 to 14 nucleotides in humans

Test

Why can't DNA polymerase start building a new strand from scratch?

It can only add nucleotides onto an existing free 3′ end. Primase first makes a short RNA primer to provide that starting point.

What is the role of primase in DNA replication?
  • A. It unwinds the double helix
  • B. It synthesises a short RNA primer
  • C. It joins Okazaki fragments
  • D. It removes supercoiling

Answer: B. It synthesises a short RNA primer

Related

  • The enzymes of replication

From the lecture slides

Primase lays down a short RNA primer (red) that DNA polymerase then extends (Lecture 3, slide 12)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 259

Because the self-correcting properties of DNA polymerase depend on its requirement for a perfectly base-paired primer terminus, it is apparently not possible for such an enzyme to start DNA synthesis de novo without an existing primer.

Alberts 7e, p. 260

This requires an enzyme called DNA primase that uses ribonucleoside triphosphates to synthesize short RNA primers on the lagging strand (Figure 5–10).

Alberts 7e, p. 261

In eukaryotes, RNA primers are made at intervals of about 200 nucleotides on the lagging strand, and each RNA primer is approximately 10 nucleotides long.

Alberts 7e, p. 261

It therefore seems likely that the use of RNA rather than DNA for priming brings a powerful advantage to the cell: the ribonucleotides in the primer automatically mark these sequences as “suspect copy” to be efficiently removed and replaced by DNA produced by a highly accurate DNA polymerase.

Figure 5–10: RNA primers are synthesized by an RNA polymerase called DNA primase, which uses a DNA strand as a template. (Alberts 7e, p. 260)

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Visualising replication: the growing bubble

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Replication

Source: Lecture 3: DNA Replication (PowerPoint)

Electron microscope images of DNA isolated from replicating E. coli cells showed that the 'replication bubble' increases in size as replication proceeds, direct physical evidence that replication spreads outward from a starting point.

Real electron micrographs (left) alongside the schematic (right): a circular viral chromosome cut once by EcoRI, showing the replication bubble growing progressively larger over time

Test

What did electron microscope images of replicating E. coli DNA show?

The replication bubble gets bigger as replication proceeds. It is direct physical evidence that replication spreads outward from a starting point.

Alberts 7e, p. 272

The positions at which the DNA helix is first opened are called replication origins (Figure 5–24).

Alberts 7e, p. 272

In the last step, two replication forks move away from each other, separated by an expanding replication bubble.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Replication forks: leading and lagging strands

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Replication

Source: Lecture 3: DNA Replication (PowerPoint)

New DNA strands are always synthesised 5′ to 3′. Since the two template strands run in opposite directions, one new strand can be built continuously in the same direction the fork moves (the leading strand), while the other has to be built discontinuously, in short pieces running against the direction of fork movement (the lagging strand, made of Okazaki fragments).

The leading strand is synthesised continuously toward the fork; the lagging strand is built backwards in Okazaki fragments

  • Okazaki fragment length: roughly 1,000 to 2,000 nucleotides in bacteria, roughly 150 to 200 nucleotides in eukaryotes
  • Two molecules of DNA polymerase III work at each fork: one uses the leading strand as template, the other uses the lagging strand as template

Test

What's the difference between the leading strand and the lagging strand?

The leading strand is synthesised continuously in the same direction the replication fork moves. The lagging strand is synthesised discontinuously, in short Okazaki fragments, running in the opposite direction to fork movement.

Why is the lagging strand synthesised as Okazaki fragments?
  • A. DNA polymerase can only synthesise 5' to 3', so the strand running the other way must be copied in short pieces
  • B. The lagging strand has a different chemical composition
  • C. Ligase requires fragmented DNA to function
  • D. The leading strand is synthesised in the opposite direction

Answer: A. DNA polymerase can only synthesise 5' to 3', so the strand running the other way must be copied in short pieces

Related

  • Linking nucleotides: the phosphodiester bond

From the lecture slides

Two DNA polymerase III molecules at the fork: one on the leading strand, one on the lagging strand (Lecture 3, slide 17)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 257

But because of the antiparallel orientation of the two DNA strands in the DNA double helix (see Figure 5–2), this mechanism would require one daughter strand to polymerize in the 5′-to-3′ direction and the other in the 3′-to-5′ direction.

Alberts 7e, p. 257

However, as attractive as this model might seem, the DNA polymerases at replication forks can synthesize only in the 5′-to-3′ direction.

Alberts 7e, p. 258

The DNA daughter strand that is synthesized continuously is known as the leading strand.

Alberts 7e, p. 258

Its synthesis slightly precedes the synthesis of the daughter strand that is synthesized discontinuously, known as the lagging strand.

Alberts 7e, p. 258

The Okazaki fragments were shown to be synthesized only in the 5′-to-3′ chain direction and to be joined together after their synthesis to create long DNA chains.

Figure 5–7: At each replication fork, the lagging DNA strand is synthesized in pieces. (Alberts 7e, p. 258)

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
The enzymes of replication

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Replication

Source: Lecture 3: DNA Replication (PowerPoint)

  • Helicase (DnaB): unwinds the DNA double helix
  • Primase: 'primes' DNA synthesis by making a short RNA primer
  • DNA polymerase III: synthesises new DNA, does most of the actual copying
  • DNA polymerase I: removes the RNA primers and replaces them with DNA
  • Ligase: seals the phosphodiester bond joining Okazaki fragments together
  • DNA gyrase (a topoisomerase): removes supercoiling caused by unwinding the helix ahead of the fork
All six players at once: helicase and DNA gyrase unwinding ahead of the fork, single-stranded binding proteins holding strands apart, RNA primers, the polymerase III dimer with its sliding clamp, and Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand

Test

Name the six key enzymes/proteins in E. coli DNA replication and what each one does.

Helicase (DnaB): unwinds the helix. Primase: makes the RNA primer. DNA polymerase III: does most of the actual DNA synthesis. DNA polymerase I: removes RNA primers and replaces them with DNA. Ligase: joins Okazaki fragments together. DNA gyrase: removes supercoiling ahead of the fork.

Which enzyme removes the RNA primers, and which seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments?

DNA polymerase I removes the primers and replaces them with DNA. DNA ligase seals the phosphodiester bonds joining the Okazaki fragments.

What does DNA gyrase do?

It is a topoisomerase that removes the supercoiling caused by unwinding the helix ahead of the fork.

Related

  • Starting a new strand: primers

From the lecture slides

Replication enzymes and their jobs (Lecture 3, slide 18)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 272

DNA replication requires the cooperation of many proteins. These include (1) DNA polymerases and DNA primases to catalyze nucleoside triphosphate polymerization; (2) DNA helicases and single-strand DNA-binding (SSB) proteins to help in opening up the DNA helix so that it can be copied; (3) clamps and clamp loaders to enable DNA polymerases to copy longer stretches of DNA; (4) DNA ligases and enzymes that degrade RNA primers to seal together the discontinuously synthesized lagging-strand DNA fragments; and (5) DNA topoisomerases to help to relieve helical winding and DNA tangling problems.

Alberts 7e, p. 264

At the front of the replication fork, DNA helicase opens the DNA helix.

Alberts 7e, p. 262

Single-strand DNA-binding (SSB) proteins bind tightly and cooperatively to the single-stranded DNA that is produced by helicases.

Alberts 7e, p. 262

However, an accessory protein (called PCNA in eukaryotes) forms a sliding clamp that keeps the polymerase firmly on the DNA when it is moving but releases the polymerase as soon as it runs into a double-strand region of DNA.

Alberts 7e, p. 261

The completed DNA fragments are finally joined together by an enzyme called DNA ligase, which catalyzes the formation of a phosphodiester bond between the 3′-hydroxyl end of one fragment and the 5′-phosphate end of the next, thus linking up the sugar–phosphate backbones.

Alberts 7e, p. 269

This overwinding is continually relieved by enzymes known as DNA topoisomerases.

Figure 5–18: A bacterial replication fork. (Alberts 7e, p. 265)

Figure 5–19: Schematic diagram of a eukaryotic replication fork. (Alberts 7e, p. 266)

props.title: Origins of replication: oriC
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: The E. coli replication origin, oriC, is 245 bp long and contains well-conserved sequence elements: three repeats of a 13 bp sequence, and four repeats of a 9 bp sequence.
props.source: Nelson & Cox, Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry, 4th ed., p. 959

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Origins of replication: oriC

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Replication

Source: Nelson & Cox, Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry, 4th ed., p. 959

The E. coli replication origin, oriC, is 245 bp long and contains well-conserved sequence elements: three repeats of a 13 bp sequence, and four repeats of a 9 bp sequence.

Initiation at oriC: (a) around 20 DnaA proteins (each bound to ATP) bind the four 9 bp repeats, wrapping the DNA around the complex. (b) The three 13 bp repeats get denatured (unwound) in sequence. (c) DnaB helicase hexamers bind each strand, helped by DnaC, and begin unwinding DNA ready for priming and synthesis

Test

What is oriC, and what does it consist of?

The E. coli chromosomal origin of replication: 245 bp, containing three repeats of a 13 bp sequence and four repeats of a 9 bp sequence.

Describe the three stages of initiation at oriC.

(a) Around 20 DnaA proteins, each bound to ATP, bind the four 9 bp repeats and wrap the DNA around the complex. (b) The three 13 bp repeats are denatured in sequence. (c) DnaB helicase hexamers, helped by DnaC, bind each strand and start unwinding, ready for priming and synthesis.

Related

  • Termination of replication

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 273

Therefore, DNA rich in A-T base pairs is relatively easy to pull apart, and regions of DNA enriched in A-T base pairs are typically found at replication origins.

Alberts 7e, p. 273

DNA replication begins at a single origin of replication, and the two replication forks assembled there proceed (at approximately 1000 nucleotides per second) in opposite directions until they meet up roughly halfway around the chromosome (Figure 5–25).

Alberts 7e, p. 273

The process begins when specialized initiator proteins (in their ATP-bound state) bind in multiple copies to specific DNA sites located at the replication origin, wrapping the DNA around the proteins to form a large protein–DNA filament that introduces torsional stress on the DNA double helix (Figure 5–26).

Alberts 7e, p. 274

DNA methylation occurs at GATC sequences, 11 of which are found in the origin of replication (spanning approximately 250 nucleotide pairs).

Figure 5–26: The proteins that initiate DNA replication in bacteria. (Alberts 7e, p. 274)

props.title: Termination of replication
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: On circular bacterial DNA, the two replication forks (moving in opposite directions from the single origin) eventually meet at a terminus region, which traps them.
props.source: Nelson & Cox, Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry, 4th ed., p. 964

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Termination of replication

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Replication

Source: Nelson & Cox, Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry, 4th ed., p. 964

On circular bacterial DNA, the two replication forks (moving in opposite directions from the single origin) eventually meet at a terminus region, which traps them. In E. coli this region contains multiple copies of a 20 bp sequence called Ter.

Ter sequences are arranged as a 'fork trap': each Ter site only blocks a fork moving in one particular direction, so a fork can pass through some Ter sites but gets stopped once it reaches one facing the right way

Ter sequences function as binding sites for the Tus (terminus utilisation sequence) protein. Tus-Ter complexes only arrest a fork approaching from one direction, which is why they're arranged in opposite orientations around the chromosome.

Test

How does replication terminate in E. coli?

The two replication forks, moving in opposite directions from the single origin, meet at a terminus region containing Ter sequences. These are bound by the Tus protein, which arrests a fork approaching from one particular direction only (a 'fork trap').

What does the Tus protein do at Ter sites during replication termination?
  • A. It initiates a new round of replication
  • B. It arrests a replication fork approaching from one particular direction
  • C. It synthesises the final Okazaki fragment
  • D. It removes RNA primers

Answer: B. It arrests a replication fork approaching from one particular direction

Related

  • Origins of replication: oriC

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 280

We saw earlier in this chapter that E. coli DNA replication begins at a single origin, and two replication forks proceed bidirectionally around the circular genome, meeting at a spot opposite to the origin of replication.

Alberts 7e, p. 275

A replication fork is thought to stop only when it encounters a replication fork moving in the opposite direction or when it reaches the end of the chromosome; in this way, all the DNA is eventually replicated.

Figure 5–25: DNA replication of a bacterial genome. (Alberts 7e, p. 273)
