props.title: Eukaryotic replication: multiple origins
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: Eukaryotic genomes are linear, and replicate via 'eye-form' replication: many separate bubbles opening up at once, rather than the single origin bacteria use.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Eukaryotic replication: multiple origins

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Replication

Source: Lecture 3: DNA Replication (PowerPoint)

Eukaryotic genomes are linear, and replicate via 'eye-form' replication: many separate bubbles opening up at once, rather than the single origin bacteria use.

  • Individual replicons (the stretch of DNA replicated from one origin) are 40 to 100 kbp
  • Replication starts from multiple origins simultaneously
  • Individual replicons get activated at specific times during S-phase, and neighbouring replicons tend to activate around the same time as each other
Two separate origins each open their own replication bubble; as both expand, they eventually meet and fuse into one continuous replicated region

Test

How does eukaryotic DNA replication differ from bacterial replication in terms of origins?

Eukaryotes replicate from many origins at once (replicons of roughly 40 to 100 kbp each), rather than the single origin bacterial chromosomes use, since eukaryotic chromosomes are far larger.

What is a replicon, and how big are eukaryotic ones?

The stretch of DNA replicated from one origin. In eukaryotes they are 40 to 100 kbp, and replication starts from many origins at once.

Related

  • Replication of chromosome ends: telomeres

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 275

Experiments of this type have shown the following: (1) Approximately 30,000– 50,000 origins of replication are used each time a human cell divides.

Alberts 7e, p. 275

(3) Origins of replication do not all “fire” simultaneously; rather, they often are activated in a prescribed order in a given cell type.

Alberts 7e, p. 276

Although different origins of replication fire at different times, all DNA replication is begun and completed during S phase.

Alberts 7e, p. 276

These DNA sequences that can serve as an origin of replication are found to contain (1) a binding site for a large, multisubunit initiator protein called ORC, for origin recognition complex; (2) a stretch of DNA that is rich in A’s and T’s and therefore easy to pull apart; and (3) at least one binding site for proteins that facilitate ORC binding, probably by adjusting the local chromatin structure.

props.title: Replication of chromosome ends: telomeres
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: The ends of eukaryotic chromosomes contain many short repeated sequences.
props.source: Nelson & Cox, Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry, 4th ed., p. 1026

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Replication of chromosome ends: telomeres

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Replication

Source: Nelson & Cox, Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry, 4th ed., p. 1026

The ends of eukaryotic chromosomes contain many short repeated sequences. Because of how lagging-strand synthesis works, a chromosome would otherwise lose a little DNA from its ends with every round of replication. Telomerase synthesises new repeats to prevent this loss.

Organism Telomere repeat
Vertebrates TTAGGG
Tetrahymena TTGGGG
Arabidopsis TTTAGGG
Telomerase carries its own internal template RNA, which it uses to extend the DNA 3′ end (a), before translocating along and repeating the process (b, c) to build up repeat after repeat

Test

What problem does telomerase solve, and how?

Because of how lagging-strand synthesis works, a linear chromosome would lose a little DNA from its ends with every round of replication. Telomerase solves this by adding new repeat sequences onto the chromosome ends, using its own internal RNA template.

What problem does telomerase solve in eukaryotic cells?
  • A. It prevents mutations during replication
  • B. It compensates for DNA lost from chromosome ends each replication cycle
  • C. It speeds up the replication fork
  • D. It joins multiple origins of replication together

Answer: B. It compensates for DNA lost from chromosome ends each replication cycle

Related

  • Eukaryotic replication: multiple origins

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 281

The final RNA primer synthesized on the lagging-strand template cannot be replaced by DNA because there is no primer ahead of it to provide a 3′-OH end for the repair polymerase.

Alberts 7e, p. 281

Bacteria avoid this “end-replication” problem by having circular DNA molecules as chromosomes, as we have seen.

Alberts 7e, p. 281

Telomerase recognizes the tip of an existing telomere DNA repeat sequence and elongates it in the 5′-to-3′ direction, using an RNA template that is a component of the enzyme itself to synthesize new DNA copies of the repeat (Figure 5–33).

Alberts 7e, p. 282

Such cells lose 100–200 nucleotides from each telomere every time they divide.

Alberts 7e, p. 283

Also consistent with these ideas is the observation that, in approximately 90% of cancer cells, the telomerase gene has become reactivated, thereby circumventing the normal safety mechanism

Figure 5–34: Telomere replication. (Alberts 7e, p. 281)

Summary

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Replication

Source: Lecture 3: DNA Replication (PowerPoint)

  • DNA replication is semiconservative. Parental strands act as templates that determine the sequence of daughter strands
  • Replication of double-stranded DNA is semi-discontinuous: one strand synthesised continuously, one discontinuously as Okazaki fragments
  • Key enzymes: helicase, primase, DNA polymerases, and DNA ligase
  • Replication begins at origins (bacteria have one, eukaryotes have many) and proceeds bidirectionally
  • In bacteria, replication stops at terminator (Ter) sites
  • In eukaryotes, chromosome ends (telomeres) get synthesised by telomerase

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Information flow: DNA to mRNA to protein

Molecular Biology and Genetics › The Genetic Code

Source: Lecture 5: The Genetic Code (PowerPoint)

The central dogma of molecular biology describes how information flows from DNA to RNA to protein. Francis Crick (1970) defined it as the residue-by-residue transfer of sequential information, and stated that such information cannot be transferred back from protein to either protein or nucleic acid. It is often put more simply as "DNA makes RNA and RNA makes protein".

DNA is transcribed into mRNA, rRNA and tRNA; all three come together at the ribosome for translation into protein

For a protein-coding gene the flow is DNA → mRNA → protein:

  • Transcription: the DNA sequence is copied into messenger RNA (mRNA)
  • The mRNA is read in groups of three ribonucleotides called codons. Each codon specifies one of 20 amino acids, or a stop signal
  • Translation: the order of codons in the mRNA sets the order of amino acids in the protein, which is assembled on the ribosome
The DNA template strand is transcribed into mRNA, which is read as triplet code words (codons) on ribosomes to give a chain of amino acids

The full flow of information in a eukaryotic cell, from chromatin to modified protein, with the points where each step is regulated

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 358

The nucleotide sequence of a gene, through the intermediary of mRNA, is instead translated into the amino acid sequence of a protein by rules that are known as the genetic code.

Alberts 7e, p. 358

This code was deciphered in the early 1960s.

Questions

What is the central dogma of molecular biology?

Information flows DNA → RNA → protein (Crick, 1970). Sequence information cannot be transferred back from protein to protein or nucleic acid. Often put as 'DNA makes RNA and RNA makes protein'.

What happens in transcription and in translation?

Transcription copies the DNA sequence into mRNA. Translation reads the mRNA codons on ribosomes, and the order of codons sets the order of amino acids in the protein.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Why the code must be a triplet

Molecular Biology and Genetics › The Genetic Code

Source: Lecture 5: The Genetic Code (PowerPoint)

In the 1960s Sydney Brenner predicted that the genetic code must be a triplet code, using simple arithmetic:

  • Proteins determine the physical and metabolic features of cells, and a protein's properties are set by the sequence of its 20 amino acids
  • DNA has only 4 bases: A, G, C and T
  • Read one base at a time, DNA could specify only 4 amino acids
  • Read in pairs, it could specify 4 × 4 = 16 codons, so only 16 amino acids
  • Read in triplets, it could specify 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons: enough for 20 amino acids, with room to spare

Triplets are the smallest unit that gives enough combinations, and the spare combinations mean several codons can share an amino acid.

From the lecture slides

Brenner's argument: 4 bases read in threes give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons, enough for 20 amino acids (Lecture 5, slide 9)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 358

Moreover, because there are only 4 different nucleotides in mRNA and 20 different types of amino acids in a protein, this translation cannot be accounted for by a direct one-to-one correspondence between a nucleotide in RNA and an amino acid in protein.

Alberts 7e, p. 359

RNA is a linear polymer of four different nucleotides, so there are 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 possible combinations of three nucleotides: the triplets AAA, AUA, AUG, and so on.

Alberts 7e, p. 359

Either some nucleotide triplets are never used or the code is redundant and some amino acids are specified by more than one triplet.

Questions

Why must the genetic code be read in triplets?

DNA has 4 bases. Singles give 4 combinations and pairs give 16, too few for 20 amino acids. Triplets give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons, enough with redundancy (Brenner).

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Proving the triplet code: frameshift mutations

Molecular Biology and Genetics › The Genetic Code

Source: Lecture 5: The Genetic Code (PowerPoint)

Crick and colleagues tested the idea using **frameshift mutation**s in the rII gene of bacteriophage T4 (a virus that infects bacteria):

  • Inserting or deleting one or two nucleotides abolished gene function
  • Inserting or deleting three nucleotides often did not abolish gene function

Adding one base shifts the reading frame, so every codon after it is misread. Adding three bases puts the reading frame back in step after a short stretch, so most of the protein is still made correctly. That only makes sense if the code is read three bases at a time.

(a) Inserting a single C throws every following codon out of frame. (b) Inserting three bases (CAG) gives a short out-of-frame stretch, then the frame is restored. GAG is a codon for glutamic acid

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 359

In principle, an RNA sequence can be translated in any one of three different reading frames, depending on where the decoding process begins (Figure 6–53).

Alberts 7e, p. 359

However, only one of the three possible reading frames in an mRNA encodes the required protein.

Figure 6–53: The three possible reading frames in protein synthesis. (Alberts 7e, p. 359)

Questions

What did Crick's frameshift experiments in phage T4 rII show?

Inserting or deleting 1 or 2 nucleotides abolished gene function, but 3 often did not, because three restores the reading frame. So the code is read in triplets.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Cracking the code: Nirenberg and Matthaei

Molecular Biology and Genetics › The Genetic Code

Source: Lecture 5: The Genetic Code (PowerPoint)

Researchers predicted an intermediate messenger molecule must carry DNA sequence information to be turned into amino acid sequence, although mRNA had not yet been identified. Marshall Nirenberg, Har Gobind Khorana and Robert W. Holley shared the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for deciphering the genetic code.

Making synthetic RNA

Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei made RNA polymers using polynucleotide phosphorylase, an enzyme that joins ribonucleoside diphosphates into RNA without needing a DNA template. They made poly-U, poly-A and poly-C (for example 5′-UUUUUUUU…-3′) and tested whether each could direct protein synthesis.

Polynucleotide phosphorylase links ribonucleoside diphosphates into RNA, releasing inorganic phosphate; the reaction is reversible

The method

They used a cell-free system containing:

  • An RNA polymer, for example poly-U
  • Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules, each coupled to a single radioactive amino acid
  • Ribosomes
  • An energy source (GTP)

Acetone was added to precipitate the protein polymers (but not the tRNA-amino acid molecules), and the radioactivity in the precipitate was measured. Radioactivity in the precipitate meant that amino acid had been built into protein.

The result

Only poly-U drove incorporation of radioactive phenylalanine into protein, so UUU codes for phenylalanine:

Artificial mRNA Radioactivity (counts/min)
None 44
Poly-U 39,800
Poly-A 50
Poly-C 38

Repeating the experiment with other radioactive amino acids gave AAA = lysine (lys, K) and CCC = proline (pro, P). They then extended the work to RNAs containing mixtures of bases (heteropolymers).

From the lecture slides

Nirenberg, Khorana and Holley shared the 1968 Nobel Prize for deciphering the code (Lecture 5, slide 11)

The cell-free system: synthetic mRNA, tRNAs with radioactive amino acids, ribosomes and GTP (Lecture 5, slide 13)

Poly-U gives radioactive polyphenylalanine, so UUU codes for Phe (Lecture 5, slide 14)

Questions

What was in Nirenberg and Matthaei's cell-free system?

An RNA polymer (e.g. poly-U), tRNAs each coupled to a radioactive amino acid, ribosomes, and an energy source (GTP). Protein was precipitated with acetone and its radioactivity measured.

What did the poly-U experiment show, and how was the RNA made?

Poly-U gave about 39,800 counts/min of phenylalanine in protein versus about 40 to 50 for poly-A, poly-C or none, so UUU = phenylalanine. The RNA was made with polynucleotide phosphorylase, which needs no DNA template.

Who shared the 1968 Nobel Prize for deciphering the genetic code?

Marshall Nirenberg, Har Gobind Khorana and Robert W. Holley.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.text: Cracking the code: Nirenberg and Matthaei Molecular Biology and Genetics › The Genetic Code Source: Lecture 5: The Genetic Code (PowerPoint) Researchers predicted an intermediate messenger molecule must carry DNA sequence information to be turned into amino acid sequence, although mRNA had not yet been identified. Marshall Nirenberg, Har Gobind Khorana and Robert W. Holley shared the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for deciphering the genetic code. Making synthetic RNA Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei made RNA polymers using polynucleotide phosphorylase , an enzyme that joins ribonucleoside diphosphates into RNA without needing a DNA template . They made poly-U, poly-A and poly-C (for example 5′-UUUUUUUU…-3′) and tested whether each could direct protein synthesis. Polynucleotide phosphorylase links ribonucleoside diphosphates into RNA, releasing inorganic phosphate; the reaction is reversible The method They used a cell-free system containing: An RNA polymer, for example poly-U Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules, each coupled to a single radioactive amino acid Ribosomes An energy source (GTP) Acetone was added to precipitate the protein polymers (but not the tRNA-amino acid molecules), and the radioactivity in the precipitate was measured. Radioactivity in the precipitate meant that amino acid had been built into protein. 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Repeating copolymers: Khorana

Molecular Biology and Genetics › The Genetic Code

Source: Lecture 5: The Genetic Code (PowerPoint)

Har Gobind Khorana synthesised RNA molecules with simple repeating sequences (a repeating copolymer) and used them to prime protein synthesis in a cell-free system. A repeat can be read in different frames, giving a predictable set of codons:

A dinucleotide repeat (UG) gives alternating UGU and GUG codons; a trinucleotide repeat (UUG) gives UUG, UGU or GUU depending on the starting point; a tetranucleotide repeat (UAUC) gives UAU, CUA, UCU and AUC

Repeating copolymer Codons Amino acids in the polypeptides
UC UCU, CUC Leu, Ser
UUC UUC, UCU, CUU Phe, Ser, Leu
UAUC UAU, CUA, UCU, AUC Tyr, Leu, Ser, Ile
UG UGU, GUG Cys, Val
AC ACA, CAC Thr, His
AUC AUC, UCA, CAU Ile, Ser, His

Not every codon codes for an amino acid

RNAs made of repeating GUA, GAU, AUAG or GUAA did not prime synthesis of a polypeptide product. Each of them contains a codon that ends translation:

Repeating copolymer Codons Result
GUA GUA, UAG, AGU Val, STOP, Ser
GAU GAU, AUG, UGA Asp, Met, STOP
GUAA GUA, UAA, AAG, AGU Val, STOP, Lys, Ser

This identified UAA, UAG and UGA as translation termination codons.

From the lecture slides

Khorana's repeating copolymers and the amino acids they produced (Lecture 5, slide 16)

GUA, GAU and GUAA repeats contain stop codons, revealing UAA, UAG and UGA (Lecture 5, slide 17)

Questions

How did Khorana's repeating copolymers assign codons? Give an example.

A repeat read in different frames gives a known set of codons. Repeating UC gives UCU and CUC, and the product contained leucine and serine.

Which codons did Khorana's GUA, GAU and GUAA repeats reveal?

The stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA: these repeats did not prime synthesis of a polypeptide product.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
The code is redundant

Molecular Biology and Genetics › The Genetic Code

Source: Lecture 5: The Genetic Code (PowerPoint)

The genetic code shows redundancy:

  • There are 64 possible codons
  • Rare exceptions apart, 61 codons encode amino acids, and these encode 20 amino acids
  • Several amino acids are encoded by more than one codon
  • Three codons (UAA, UAG and UGA) do not usually encode amino acids and specify chain termination: these are the **stop codon**s
The genetic code: find the first base on the left, the second along the top and the third on the right. AUG (initiation) and the three stop codons are highlighted

A pattern to the redundancy

Codons for the same amino acid tend to be similar, usually differing only in the third base:

  • Valine: GUU, GUC, GUA, GUG
  • Leucine: UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, CUG

Amino acid abbreviations

Amino acid 3-letter 1-letter
Alanine Ala A
Cysteine Cys C
Aspartic acid Asp D
Glutamic acid Glu E
Phenylalanine Phe F
Glycine Gly G
Histidine His H
Isoleucine Ile I
Lysine Lys K
Leucine Leu L
Methionine Met M
Asparagine Asn N
Proline Pro P
Glutamine Gln Q
Arginine Arg R
Serine Ser S
Threonine Thr T
Valine Val V
Tryptophan Trp W
Tyrosine Tyr Y
Selenocysteine (some species only) Sec U
Pyrrolysine (some species only) Pyl O

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 359

Note that most amino acids are represented by more than one codon, and that there are some regularities in the set of codons that specifies each amino acid: codons for the same amino acid tend to contain the same nucleotides at the first and second positions, and vary at the third position.

Alberts 7e, p. 359

We saw above that the genetic code is redundant; that is, several different codons can specify a single amino acid.

Figure 6–52: The genetic code. (Alberts 7e, p. 359)

Questions

What does it mean that the genetic code is redundant?

64 codons: 61 encode the 20 amino acids and 3 are stops, so most amino acids have several codons, which usually differ at the third base (e.g. valine: GUU, GUC, GUA, GUG).

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
The wobble hypothesis

Molecular Biology and Genetics › The Genetic Code

Source: Lecture 5: The Genetic Code (PowerPoint)

The pattern of redundancy led Crick to propose the wobble hypothesis:

  • The first two nucleotides of a codon are the most critical for binding the correct tRNA
  • Hydrogen bonding at the third position is less constrained
  • Pairing at the third position does not always follow the standard base-pairing rules
  • So one tRNA can bind to more than one codon

This explains why synonymous codons mostly differ at the third base, as in the valine codons GUU, GUC, GUA and GUG.

From the lecture slides

Wobble: the codon's third base pairs loosely, so one tRNA can read several codons (Lecture 5, slide 24)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 360

This wobble base-pairing explains why so many of the alternative codons for an amino acid differ only in their third nucleotide (see Figure 6–52).

Alberts 7e, p. 360

Codon–anticodon base-pairing is more stringent at positions 1 and 2 of the codon, where only conventional base pairs are permitted.

Alberts 7e, p. 361

Some of the modified nucleotides lie within the anticodon—most notably inosine, produced by the deamination of adenosine—and affect the base-pairing of the anticodon, thereby facilitating the recognition of the appropriate mRNA codon by the tRNA molecule (see Figure 6–55).

Figure 6–55: Wobble base-pairing between codons and anticodons. (Alberts 7e, p. 360)

Questions

What is the wobble hypothesis?

Crick's proposal that the first two codon bases pair strictly with the tRNA, but pairing at the third base is less constrained and can break standard rules, so one tRNA can read more than one codon.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Start and stop: AUG and the stop codons

Molecular Biology and Genetics › The Genetic Code

Source: Lecture 5: The Genetic Code (PowerPoint)

  • AUG is the start codon: it signals the ribosome to start translation
  • AUG encodes methionine, so proteins start with methionine
  • In bacteria the first amino acid of a polypeptide chain is a modified form of methionine, N-formylmethionine (fMet)
  • Translation continues codon by codon until a stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA) is reached

Worked example

mRNA: 5′-UCGGGUGUCGAUACGCUGGUGUCAAAUAUGCUUUUGCCAAUU-3′

Reading from the AUG in groups of three gives AUG CUU UUG CCA AUU, so the peptide starts met-leu-leu-pro-ile. Everything before the AUG is not translated.

From the lecture slides

AUG starts translation and codes for methionine (N-formylmethionine in bacteria) (Lecture 5, slide 25)

Reading from the first AUG: met-arg-ser-val-gly (Lecture 5, slide 29)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 373

The translation of an mRNA usually begins with the codon AUG, and a special tRNA is required to start translation.

Alberts 7e, p. 373

This initiator tRNA always carries the amino acid methionine (in bacteria, a modified form of methionine—formylmethionine—is used), with the result that all newly made proteins have methionine as the first amino acid at their N-terminus, the end of a protein that is synthesized first.

Alberts 7e, p. 373

In about 90% of mRNAs, translation begins at the first AUG encountered by the small subunit.

Alberts 7e, p. 374

The end of the protein-coding message is signaled by the presence of one of three stop codons (UAA, UAG, or UGA) (see Figure 6–52).

Alberts 7e, p. 374

Proteins known as release factors bind to any ribosome with a stop codon positioned in the A site, forcing the peptidyl transferase in the ribosome to catalyze the addition of a water molecule instead of an amino acid to the peptidyl-tRNA (Figure 6–76).

Questions

What is the start codon, and what is the first amino acid in bacteria?

AUG, which encodes methionine. In bacteria the first amino acid is the modified form N-formylmethionine (fMet).

mRNA 5′-UGAUUCCUAGGAGGUUUGACCUAUGCGAUCUGUUGGU-3′ has one start codon. What are the first five amino acids?

Met, Arg, Ser, Val, Gly: reading from AUG gives AUG CGA UCU GUU GGU.

Which peptide starts at the AUG in 5′-UCGGGUGUCGAUACGCUGGUGUCAAAUAUGCUUUUGCCAAUU-3′?

Met, Leu, Leu, Pro, Ile: AUG CUU UUG CCA AUU.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.title: 09 Non-overlapping and commaless
01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Non-overlapping and commaless

Molecular Biology and Genetics › The Genetic Code

Source: Lecture 5: The Genetic Code (PowerPoint)

  • The code is a non-overlapping code: each nucleotide belongs to only one codon
  • The code is commaless: codons are read one after the other, with no breaks or spacer bases between them

So once the reading frame is set by the start codon, every following base falls into exactly one codon, which is why a single inserted or deleted base wrecks everything downstream.

Worked example

mRNA: 5′-UGAUUCCUAGGAGGUUUGACCUAUGCGAUCUGUUGGU-3′ contains a single initiation codon. Reading from it gives AUG CGA UCU GUU GGU: met, arg, ser, val, gly.

From the lecture slides

Codons are read one after another with no gaps and no overlap (Lecture 5, slide 27)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 359

Each group of three consecutive nucleotides in mRNA is called a codon, and each codon specifies either one amino acid or a stop to the translation process.

Questions

What do 'non-overlapping' and 'commaless' mean for the genetic code?

Non-overlapping: each nucleotide is part of only one codon. Commaless: codons are read one after the other with no gaps between them.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
A (nearly) universal code: selenocysteine and pyrrolysine

Molecular Biology and Genetics › The Genetic Code

Source: Lecture 5: The Genetic Code (PowerPoint)

The same genetic code is used by almost all organisms, a near-universal code. Two rare exceptions mean it is not quite universal:

Selenocysteine (Sec, U)

  • In some proteins in some species, UGA (normally a stop codon) encodes selenocysteine
  • It is like cysteine but has a selenium (Se) atom in place of the sulphur
  • Found in all three domains of life (Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya) but not in all species; found in fewer than 100 human proteins

Pyrrolysine (Pyl, O)

  • In some proteins in some species, UAG (normally a stop codon) encodes pyrrolysine
  • Its side chain is similar to lysine's but contains an additional pyrroline group
  • Found in methanogenic archaea and in the Gram-positive bacterium Desulfitobacterium hafniense
Structures of selenocysteine, pyrrolysine and lysine

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 375

As discussed in Chapter 1, the genetic code (shown in Figure 6–52) applies to all three major branches of life, providing important evidence for the common ancestry of all life on Earth.

Alberts 7e, p. 375

Although rare, there are exceptions to this code.

Alberts 7e, p. 375

For example, Candida albicans, the most prevalent fungal pathogen of humans, translates the codon CUG as serine, whereas nearly all other organisms translate it as leucine.

Alberts 7e, p. 376

For example, in mammalian mitochondria AUA is translated as methionine, whereas in the cytosol of the cell it is translated as isoleucine (see Table 14–4, p. 864).

Alberts 7e, p. 376

Selenocysteine, which contains a selenium atom in place of the sulfur atom of cysteine, is essential for the efficient function of a variety of enzymes.

Alberts 7e, p. 376

It is enzymatically produced from a serine attached to a special tRNA molecule that base-pairs with the UGA codon, a codon normally used to signal a translation stop.

Figure 6–78: Incorporation of selenocysteine into a growing polypeptide chain. (Alberts 7e, p. 376)

Questions

Why is the genetic code only 'nearly' universal?

In some proteins in some species, UGA encodes selenocysteine (cysteine with selenium for sulphur) and UAG encodes pyrrolysine (lysine plus a pyrroline group).

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.text: A (nearly) universal code: selenocysteine and pyrrolysine Molecular Biology and Genetics › The Genetic Code Source: Lecture 5: The Genetic Code (PowerPoint) The same genetic code is used by almost all organisms, a near- universal code . Two rare exceptions mean it is not quite universal: Selenocysteine (Sec, U) In some proteins in some species, UGA (normally a stop codon ) encodes selenocysteine It is like cysteine but has a selenium (Se) atom in place of the sulphur Found in all three domains of life (Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya) but not in all species; found in fewer than 100 human proteins Pyrrolysine (Pyl, O) In some proteins in some species, UAG (normally a stop codon) encodes pyrrolysine Its side chain is similar to lysine's but contains an additional pyrroline group Found in methanogenic archaea and in the Gram-positive bacterium Desulfitobacterium hafniense Structures of selenocysteine, pyrrolysine and lysine From the textbook (Alberts 7e) Alberts 7e, p. 375 As discussed in Chapter 1, the genetic code (shown in Figure 6–52) applies to all three major branches of life, providing important evidence for the common ancestry of all life on Earth. Alberts 7e, p. 375 Although rare, there are exceptions to this code. Alberts 7e, p. 375 For example, Candida albicans, the most prevalent fungal pathogen of humans, translates the codon CUG as serine, whereas nearly all other organisms translate it as leucine. Alberts 7e, p. 376 For example, in mammalian mitochondria AUA is translated as methionine, whereas in the cytosol of the cell it is translated as isoleucine (see Table 14–4, p. 864). Alberts 7e, p. 376 Selenocysteine, which contains a selenium atom in place of the sulfur atom of cysteine, is essential for the efficient function of a variety of enzymes. Alberts 7e, p. 376 It is enzymatically produced from a serine attached to a special tRNA molecule that base-pairs with the UGA codon, a codon normally used to signal a translation stop. Figure 6–78: Incorporation of selenocysteine into a growing polypeptide chain. (Alberts 7e, p. 376) Questions Why is the genetic code only 'nearly' universal? In some proteins in some species, UGA encodes selenocysteine (cysteine with selenium for sulphur) and UAG encodes pyrrolysine (lysine plus a pyrroline group).

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Summary

Molecular Biology and Genetics › The Genetic Code

Source: Lecture 5: The Genetic Code (PowerPoint)

  • Information flow in protein synthesis: DNA → mRNA → protein
  • The genetic code is a triplet code, and each triplet is a codon
  • The code is redundant: 64 codons encode 20 amino acids
  • Three codons (UAA, UAG and UGA) do not encode amino acids and specify chain termination (stop codons)
  • One codon (AUG) is the start codon
  • The code is commaless and non-overlapping
  • The code is nearly universal: selenocysteine and pyrrolysine are rare exceptions

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Transcription: making an RNA copy of DNA

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

mRNA is made by RNA polymerase, which makes an RNA copy of DNA. This is transcription, the first step of the central dogma (DNA → mRNA → protein).

  • RNA polymerase reads the template strand and builds the mRNA from 5′ to 3′
  • The mRNA is complementary to the template strand
  • So the mRNA has the same sequence as the other DNA strand, the coding strand, with U in place of T
The coding strand ATGCTTTTGCCAATT… is copied via the template strand into mRNA AUGCUUUUGCCAAUU…, translated as Met-Leu-Leu-Pro-Ile

Worked example: coding strand 5′-ATGCTTTTGCCAATT-3′ gives mRNA 5′-AUGCUUUUGCCAAUU-3′, read as AUG CUU UUG CCA AUU = Met, Leu, Leu, Pro, Ile.

From the lecture slides

The template strand is copied into mRNA, which carries the same sequence as the coding strand (U for T) (Lecture 6, slide 6)

RNA polymerase reads the template strand 3′→5′ and grows the mRNA 5′→3′ (Lecture 6, slide 7)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 325

Unlike a newly formed DNA strand, the RNA strand does not remain hydrogen-bonded to the DNA template strand.

Alberts 7e, p. 326

The almost immediate separation of the RNA strand from the DNA as it is synthesized means that many RNA copies can be made from the same gene in a relatively short time, with the synthesis of additional RNA molecules being started before the previous RNA molecules are completed (Figure 6–10).

Alberts 7e, p. 326

Second, unlike the DNA polymerases involved in DNA replication (see pp. 259–260), RNA polymerases can start an RNA chain without a primer.

Alberts 7e, p. 326

Finally, unlike DNA polymerases, which make their products in segments that are later stitched together, RNA polymerases are processive; that is, the same RNA polymerase that begins an RNA molecule must finish it without dissociating from the DNA template.

Figure 6–8: DNA transcription produces a single-strand RNA molecule that is complementary to one strand of the DNA double helix. (Alberts 7e, p. 326)

Questions

Which DNA strand does RNA polymerase read, and which strand does the mRNA match?

It reads the template strand. The mRNA is complementary to the template and has the same sequence as the coding strand, with U in place of T.

A coding strand reads 5′-ATGCTTTTGCCAATT-3′. What is the mRNA and the peptide?

mRNA 5′-AUGCUUUUGCCAAUU-3′, read as AUG CUU UUG CCA AUU: Met, Leu, Leu, Pro, Ile.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Gene and mRNA structure

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

  • The promoter sits upstream of the gene and sets where transcription starts
  • Transcription starts before the start codon, so the mRNA begins with an untranslated region (the 5′ UTR)
  • Translation runs from AUG to a stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA): the coding sequence
  • After the stop codon there is a 3′ UTR before transcription ends
A gene: promoter, then the transcribed region (5′ UTR, coding sequence, 3′ UTR). Only the coding sequence is translated

From the lecture slides

A gene: promoter, then the mRNA with 5′ UTR, coding sequence from AUG to the stop codon, and 3′ UTR (Lecture 6, slide 8)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 339

Discovered in 1977, this feature of eukaryotic genes came as a surprise to scientists, who had been, until that time, familiar only with bacterial genes, which consist of a continuous stretch of coding DNA that is directly transcribed into mRNA.

Alberts 7e, p. 328

In bacteria, a set of adjacent genes is often transcribed as a unit; the resulting mRNA molecule therefore carries the information for producing several distinct proteins.

Alberts 7e, p. 338

Both ends of eukaryotic mRNAs are modified: by capping on the 5′ end and by polyadenylation of the 3′ end (Figure 6–22).

Figure 6–22: A comparison of the structures of bacterial and eukaryotic mRNA molecules. (Alberts 7e, p. 338)

Figure 6–25: Structure of two human genes showing the arrangement of exons and introns. (Alberts 7e, p. 340)

Questions

What are the 5′ and 3′ UTRs?

Untranslated regions of the mRNA: the 5′ UTR lies between the start of transcription and AUG, the 3′ UTR between the stop codon and the end of transcription.

props.title: Prokaryotic promoters and RNA polymerase
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: The promoter is a cis-acting sequence: it acts only on the gene it is part of

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Prokaryotic promoters and RNA polymerase

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

  • The promoter is a cis-acting sequence: it acts only on the gene it is part of
  • RNA polymerase is a trans-acting factor: a protein that can act on any matching promoter
  • E. coli RNA polymerase has 2 α, 1 β, 1 β′ and 1 σ (sigma) subunit
  • Molecular weights: β 150,000; β′ 160,000; α 40,000; σ 70,000

The −10 and −35 boxes

A typical E. coli promoter has two short conserved sequences, counted back from the start of transcription (+1):

Element Consensus Position
−35 box TTGACA 15 to 20 bp upstream of the −10 box
−10 box TATAAT 5 to 9 bp upstream of +1

Each is a consensus sequence: the most common base at each position across many promoters. The full consensus shows how often each base appears, e.g. −10: T80 A95 T45 A60 A50 T96 (% of promoters).

An E. coli promoter: −35 box (TTGACA) and −10 box (TATAAT), then the start of transcription at +1

The sigma factor binds the −10 and −35 boxes. Different sigma factors recognise different sets of promoters, so switching sigma factor switches on a different group of genes.

From the lecture slides

RNA polymerase holoenzyme with its σ factor binds the promoter to start transcription (Lecture 6, slide 10)

Core E. coli promoter: TTGACA at −35 and TATAAT at −10, upstream of the +1 start site (Lecture 6, slide 11)

σ helps the polymerase find the promoter, then dissociates as the chain elongates (Lecture 6, slide 12)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 328

An additional subunit called sigma (σ) factor associates with the core enzyme and assists it in reading the signals in the DNA that tell it where to begin transcribing (Figure 6–11).

Alberts 7e, p. 329

However, when the polymerase holoenzyme slides into a special sequence of nucleotides indicating the starting point for RNA synthesis called a promoter, the polymerase binds tightly because its σ factor makes specific contacts with the edges of bases exposed on the outside of the DNA double helix (step 1 in Figure 6–11A).

Alberts 7e, p. 331

As shown in Figure 6–12, promoter sequences are asymmetric, ensuring that RNA polymerase can bind in only one orientation.

Alberts 7e, p. 331

Because the polymerase can synthesize RNA only in the 5′-to-3′ direction, the promoter orientation specifies the strand to be used as a template.

Figure 6–11: The transcription cycle of bacterial RNA polymerase. (Alberts 7e, p. 328)

Figure 6–13: Directions of transcription along a short portion of a bacterial chromosome. (Alberts 7e, p. 331)

Questions

What do 'cis-acting' and 'trans-acting' mean for a promoter and RNA polymerase?

The promoter is cis-acting: a DNA sequence that only controls its own gene. RNA polymerase is trans-acting: a protein that can act on any matching promoter.

What are the subunits of E. coli RNA polymerase?

2 α, 1 β, 1 β′ and 1 σ (sigma) subunit.

What are the −10 and −35 consensus sequences of an E. coli promoter?

−35: TTGACA. −10: TATAAT. They are 15 to 20 bp apart, and the −10 box is 5 to 9 bp before +1.

What does the sigma factor do?

It binds the −10 and −35 boxes so RNA polymerase starts at the right place. Different sigma factors recognise different sets of promoters.

props.title: Termination of transcription

props.summary: Terminator sequences in the RNA signal the end of transcription

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Termination of transcription

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

  • Terminator sequences in the RNA signal the end of transcription
  • Intrinsic terminators: the RNA folds into a hairpin loop, and RNA polymerase and the mRNA are released from the DNA
  • Extrinsic terminators need the rho protein to end transcription

Textbook detail beyond the slides: an intrinsic terminator is a GC-rich hairpin followed by a run of U residues; the weak A-U pairing lets the RNA slip off the template.

From the lecture slides

Intrinsic termination: a GC-rich hairpin followed by a run of U residues releases the polymerase (Lecture 6, slide 13)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 329

For most bacterial genes, a termination signal consists of a string of A-T nucleotide pairs preceded by a twofold symmetric DNA sequence, which, when transcribed into RNA, folds into a “hairpin” structure through Watson–Crick base-pairing (see Figure 6–92).

Alberts 7e, p. 329

As the polymerase transcribes across a terminator, the formation of the hairpin helps release the RNA transcript, which is held in place by relatively weak A-T and U-A base pairs (step 7 in Figure 6–11A).

Alberts 7e, p. 330

Like bacterial promoters, transcription terminators also have a wide range of sequences, with the potential to form a simple hairpin RNA structure being the most important common feature.

Questions

How do intrinsic and extrinsic terminators differ?

Intrinsic: the RNA forms a hairpin loop and polymerase and RNA are released. Extrinsic: the rho protein is needed to end transcription.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Prokaryotic genomes and gene regulation

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

  • E. coli genome: 4,639,221 bp, about 4,300 genes
  • Genes are tightly packed
  • Not all genes are expressed at any one time
  • Gene expression is strictly regulated

Controlling when transcription starts is the main way bacteria regulate gene expression.

From the lecture slides

The E. coli genome: one circular chromosome of 4,639,221 bp holding about 4,300 genes (Lecture 6, slide 15)

Genes are tightly packed and transcribed from both strands, and not all are expressed at once (Lecture 6, slide 16)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 410

These genes are arranged in a cluster on the chromosome and are transcribed from a single promoter as one long mRNA molecule; such coordinately transcribed clusters are called operons (Figure 7–15).

Figure 7–15: A cluster of bacterial genes can be transcribed from a single promoter. (Alberts 7e, p. 410)

How big is the E. coli genome?

4,639,221 bp with about 4,300 tightly packed genes, not all expressed at once.

props.title: The lac operon
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: An operon is a unit of linked genes under the control of a single promoter. The lac operon, worked out by François Jacob and Jacques Monod, lets E. coli use lactose.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
The lac operon

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

An operon is a unit of linked genes under the control of a single promoter. The lac operon, worked out by François Jacob and Jacques Monod, lets E. coli use lactose.

  • Glucose (a monosaccharide) is E. coli's preferred carbon source
  • Lactose is a disaccharide of glucose and galactose, used only when glucose is low
  • lacZ encodes β-galactosidase, which hydrolyses lactose to glucose and galactose
  • lacY encodes a permease, which transports lactose into the cell
  • lacA encodes a transacetylase, which acetylates lactose

The genes are induced when lactose is present and glucose is absent, and repressed when lactose is absent.

From the lecture slides

Lactose is taken up by the LacY permease and split into glucose and galactose by β-galactosidase (Lecture 6, slide 17)

Jacob and Monod, and the parts of the lac operon: lacI, promoter, operator, then lacZ, lacY and lacA (Lecture 6, slide 18)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 412

The Lac operon encodes proteins required to import and digest the disaccharide lactose, a key nutrient in milk.

Alberts 7e, p. 412

The Lac operon in E. coli, for example, is controlled by both the Lac repressor and the CAP activator just discussed.

Alberts 7e, p. 412

This arrangement enables the control region of the Lac operon to integrate two different signals, so that the operon is highly expressed only when two conditions are met: glucose must be absent and lactose must be present (Figure 7–18).

Alberts 7e, p. 413

LacZ, the first gene of the operon, encodes the enzyme β-galactosidase, which breaks down lactose to galactose and glucose.

Figure 7–18: How the Lac operon is controlled by two transcription regulators, causing it to be expressed only when needed. (Alberts 7e, p. 413)

Questions

What is an operon? Name the lac operon genes and their products.

Linked genes under one promoter. lacZ: β-galactosidase (splits lactose). lacY: permease (brings lactose in). lacA: transacetylase.

props.title: Repression and induction
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: No lactose: the repressor (made by the lacI gene) binds the operator, blocking RNA polymerase. The operon is repressed

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Repression and induction

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

  • No lactose: the repressor (made by the lacI gene) binds the operator, blocking RNA polymerase. The operon is repressed
  • Lactose present: lactose binds the repressor, which lets go of the operator. RNA polymerase can transcribe lacZ, lacY and lacA

Textbook detail beyond the slides: strictly, the inducer that binds the repressor is allolactose, an isomer of lactose made by β-galactosidase. In the lab IPTG is used instead, because E. coli cannot break it down.

From the lecture slides

No lactose: the repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription (Lecture 6, slide 19)

Lactose present: it binds the repressor, which leaves the operator, so lacZYA are transcribed (Lecture 6, slide 20)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 413

When lactose is absent, the Lac repressor binds to a cis-regulatory sequence, called the Lac operator, and shuts off expression of the operon.

Alberts 7e, p. 413

Addition of lactose increases the intracellular concentration of a related compound, allolactose; allolactose binds to the Lac repressor, causing it to undergo a conformational change that releases its grip on the operator DNA.

Questions

How does lactose switch on the lac operon?

Without lactose the lacI repressor sits on the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. Lactose (strictly allolactose) binds the repressor so it releases the operator.

props.title: Glucose control: cAMP and CAP
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: No glucose: cAMP (cyclic AMP) levels rise

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Glucose control: cAMP and CAP

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

  • No glucose: cAMP (cyclic AMP) levels rise
  • cAMP binds CAP, which binds the CAP-binding site next to the promoter and strongly activates transcription
  • Glucose present: the cell has plenty of ATP and little cAMP, so CAP binds poorly and activation is low

The slides describe cAMP rising as ATP is used up. Textbook detail beyond the slides: cAMP is made from ATP by the enzyme adenylyl cyclase, which becomes more active when glucose is scarce.

Lactose Glucose Repressor cAMP-CAP lac genes
absent present on operator not bound off
absent absent on operator bound off
present present released not bound low
present absent released bound high
The four combinations: the genes are fully on only with lactose present and glucose absent

From the lecture slides

Glucose absent: cAMP rises, the CAP–cAMP complex binds the CAP site and transcription occurs (Lecture 6, slide 21)

Glucose present: cAMP is low, CAP cannot bind and transcription is diminished (Lecture 6, slide 22)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 412

Like the tryptophan repressor, activator proteins often have to interact with a second molecule to be able to bind DNA. For example, the bacterial activator protein CAP has to bind cyclic AMP (cAMP) before it can bind to DNA. Genes activated by CAP are switched on in response to an increase in intracellular cAMP concentration, which rises when glucose, the bacterium’s preferred carbon source, is no longer available. CAP then drives the production of enzymes that allow the bacterium to digest other sugars.

Alberts 7e, p. 412

In the absence of glucose (the cell’s favorite energy source), the bacterium makes cAMP, which activates CAP to switch-on genes that allow the cell to utilize alternative sources of carbon—including lactose.

Alberts 7e, p. 413

This removes a block to expression of the Lac operon, but the operon can turn on only if the sugar glucose, a preferred carbon source, is absent.

Questions

How does glucose control the lac operon?

No glucose: cAMP rises, binds CAP, and cAMP-CAP binds next to the promoter to strongly activate transcription. With glucose, cAMP is low and activation is weak.

Lactose present, glucose present: what happens to lac gene expression and why?

Low. The repressor is released, but with little cAMP, CAP does not activate, so transcription is weak.

props.title: lac operon mutants
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: Jacob and Monod used mutants to work out how the operon works:

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
lac operon mutants

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

Jacob and Monod used mutants to work out how the operon works:

  • lacI mutants whose repressor cannot bind the operator: constitutive expression (genes always on), because nothing blocks RNA polymerase
  • Operator (Oᶜ) mutants that the repressor cannot bind: also constitutive, for the same reason
  • lacI mutants whose repressor cannot bind lactose: repressed even with lactose present, because the repressor never lets go

From the lecture slides

I⁻: the repressor cannot bind the operator, so the operon is constitutive (Lecture 6, slide 40)

Oᶜ: the operator cannot bind the repressor, so the operon is constitutive (Lecture 6, slide 41)

Iˢ: the repressor cannot bind lactose, so the operon stays repressed even with lactose (Lecture 6, slide 42)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 412

All transcription regulators, whether they are repressors or activators, must be bound to DNA to exert their effects.

Questions

What do lacI mutants that can't bind the operator, and operator Oᶜ mutants, have in common?

Both give constitutive expression: the repressor can't block transcription, so the genes are always on.

What happens with a lacI mutant whose repressor can't bind lactose?

The operon stays repressed even with lactose present, because the repressor never leaves the operator.

props.title: Eukaryotic transcription: an overview
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: Transcription makes the primary transcript, containing exons (which code for protein) and introns (non-coding)

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Eukaryotic transcription: an overview

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

  • Transcription makes the primary transcript, containing exons (which code for protein) and introns (non-coding)
  • Splicing removes the introns to give the mRNA
  • The mature mRNA is made by capping and tailing
  • RNA Pol II transcribes all protein-coding genes and microRNA genes

Textbook detail beyond the slides: eukaryotes have three main RNA polymerases. Pol I makes most rRNA, Pol II makes mRNA and microRNA, and Pol III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA.

From the lecture slides

Eukaryotic genes give a primary transcript of exons and introns, which is spliced, capped and tailed (Lecture 6, slide 26)

Three eukaryotic RNA polymerases: I makes rRNA, II makes mRNA and snRNA, III makes 5S rRNA and tRNA (Lecture 6, slide 27)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 331

In contrast to bacteria, which contain a single type of RNA polymerase, eukaryotic nuclei have three: RNA polymerase I, RNA polymerase II, and RNA polymerase III.

Alberts 7e, p. 331

RNA polymerase II transcribes most genes, including all those that encode proteins, and our subsequent discussion therefore focuses on this enzyme.

Alberts 7e, p. 331
  1. While bacterial RNA polymerase requires only a single transcription-initiation factor (σ) to begin transcription, eukaryotic RNA polymerases require many such factors, collectively called the general transcription factors.
Alberts 7e, p. 331
  1. Eukaryotic transcription initiation must take place on DNA that is packaged into nucleosomes and higher-order forms of chromatin structure (described in Chapter 4), features that are absent from bacterial chromosomes.

Questions

What is in a eukaryotic primary transcript, and which polymerase makes mRNA?

Exons (coding) and introns (non-coding). RNA Pol II makes all protein-coding mRNAs and microRNAs.

props.title: Starting eukaryotic transcription
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: The TATA-binding protein (TBP) binds the TATA box in the promoter

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Starting eukaryotic transcription

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

  • The TATA-binding protein (TBP) binds the TATA box in the promoter
  • TBP-associated factors (TAFs) help RNA Pol II bind, forming the basal transcription complex, which is highly conserved in all eukaryotes
  • A transcription factor binding an enhancer interacts with the basal complex and can increase initiation up to 100 times

Chromatin remodelling

  • Naked DNA binds RNA Pol II and the basal machinery strongly, but chromatin reduces binding and transcription to low levels
  • Chromatin remodelling exposes the promoter. Complexes such as yeast SWI-SNF destabilise chromatin and allow access to promoter sequences
  • SWI-SNF is conserved in eukaryotes and is one of many remodelling complexes

From the lecture slides

TBP binds the TATA box and TAFs help assemble the basal transcription complex (Lecture 6, slide 28)

Transcription factors bound at enhancers raise initiation up to about 100-fold (Lecture 6, slide 29)

Nucleosomes keep promoter binding and transcription low (Lecture 6, slide 30)

Remodelling complexes such as SWI-SNF expose the promoter so basal factors and Pol II can bind (Lecture 6, slide 31)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 332

The assembly process begins when TFIID binds to a short double-helical DNA sequence primarily composed of T and A nucleotides. For this reason, this sequence is known as the TATA sequence, or TATA box, and the subunit of TFIID that recognizes it is called TBP (for TATA-binding protein).

Alberts 7e, p. 332

The TATA box is typically located about 30 nucleotides upstream from the transcription start site.

Alberts 7e, p. 333

TFIIH makes this step possible by hydrolyzing ATP and pulling apart the DNA strands at the start site, thereby exposing the template strand.

Alberts 7e, p. 334

During transcription initiation, the serines located at the fifth position in each repeat sequence (Ser5) are phosphorylated by TFIIH, which contains a protein kinase in one of its subunits.

Alberts 7e, p. 334

First, regulatory proteins known as transcriptional activators must bind to specific sequences in DNA (called enhancers) to help attract the general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II to the start point of transcription (Figure 6–18).

Figure 6–15: Initiation of transcription of a eukaryotic gene by RNA polymerase II. (Alberts 7e, p. 332)

Figure 6–18: Transcription initiation by RNA polymerase II in a eukaryotic cell. (Alberts 7e, p. 334)

Questions

How does transcription start in eukaryotes?

Chromatin remodelling exposes the promoter, TBP binds the TATA box, TAFs help RNA Pol II bind to form the basal transcription complex, and transcription factors on enhancers boost initiation up to 100 times.

props.title: Capping and tailing
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: A capping enzyme adds a G to the 5′ end through a 5′-5′ triphosphate link. This 5′ cap is then methylated

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Capping and tailing

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

  • A capping enzyme adds a G to the 5′ end through a 5′-5′ triphosphate link. This 5′ cap is then methylated
  • The 3′ end is cut downstream of a conserved AAUAAA motif
  • Poly-A polymerase then adds 100 to 200 A residues: the poly-A tail
Primary transcript → capped and tailed → spliced into mature mRNA

Textbook detail beyond the slides: the cap and tail protect the mRNA from breakdown and help it get exported from the nucleus and translated.

From the lecture slides

A G cap is added through a 5′–5′ triphosphate link, then the RNA is cut downstream of AAUAAA and poly-A polymerase adds the tail (Lecture 6, slide 32)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 338

As soon as RNA polymerase II has produced about 20 nucleotides of RNA, the 5′ end of the new RNA molecule is modified by addition of a cap that consists of a modified guanine nucleotide (see Figure 6–22B).

Alberts 7e, p. 339

The 7-methylguanosine cap signifies the 5′ end of eukaryotic mRNAs, and this landmark helps the cell to distinguish mRNAs from the other types of RNA molecules present in the cell.

Alberts 7e, p. 339

In the nucleus, the cap binds a protein complex called CBC (cap-binding complex), which, as we discuss in subsequent sections, helps a future mRNA to be further processed and exported.

Alberts 7e, p. 348

Once the RNA is cleaved, an enzyme called poly-A polymerase (PAP) adds approximately 200 A nucleotides, one at a time, to the 3′ end produced by the cleavage (see Figure 6–37).

Alberts 7e, p. 348

But unlike other RNA polymerases, poly-A polymerase does not require a template; hence, the poly-A tail of eukaryotic mRNAs is not directly encoded in the genome.

Alberts 7e, p. 349

Only when the proteins present on an mRNA molecule collectively signify that processing was successfully completed is the mRNA exported from the nucleus into the cytosol, where it can be translated into protein.

Alberts 7e, p. 349

Indeed, the default fate of RNAs in the nucleus is degradation; only those bearing the proper constellation of proteins are spared.

Figure 6–24: The reactions that cap the 5 ′ end of each RNA molecule synthesized by RNA polymerase II. (Alberts 7e, p. 339)

Figure 6–37: Some of the major steps in generating the 3 ′ end of a eukaryotic mRNA. (Alberts 7e, p. 348)

Questions

How is a eukaryotic mRNA capped and tailed?

A G is added to the 5′ end by a 5′-5′ triphosphate link and methylated. The 3′ end is cut after AAUAAA and poly-A polymerase adds 100 to 200 A.

props.title: Splicing
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: Splicing removes introns and joins adjacent exons

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Splicing

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

  • Splicing removes introns and joins adjacent exons
  • Each intron has three key sequence motifs: the splice donor (5′ end), the branch site, and the splice acceptor (3′ end)
  • Intron removal is catalysed by the spliceosome, a large complex (60S in mammals)
  • The spliceosome contains small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) whose RNA base pairs with intron sequences

The slide lists U1 to U6. Textbook detail beyond the slides: the main spliceosome uses U1, U2, U4, U5 and U6; U3 works in rRNA processing instead.

From the lecture slides

Introns are removed from the capped and tailed pre-mRNA, joining exons E1, E2 and E3 (Lecture 6, slide 33)

Splice donor, branch site and splice acceptor: the three intron motifs the spliceosome reads (Lecture 6, slide 34)

The intron is cut out as a lariat and the exons are ligated (Lecture 6, slide 35)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 340

Each splicing event removes one intron, proceeding through two sequential phosphoryl-transfer reactions known as transesterifications; these join two exons together while removing the intron between them as a “lariat” (Figure 6–26).

Alberts 7e, p. 341

The mechanism of pre-mRNA splicing shown in Figure 6–26 requires that the splicing machinery recognize three portions of the precursor RNA molecule: the 5′ splice site, the 3′ splice site, and the branch point in the intron sequence that forms the base of the excised lariat.

Alberts 7e, p. 341

These RNA molecules are relatively short (less than 200 nucleotides each), and there are five of them, U1, U2, U4, U5, and U6.

Alberts 7e, p. 341

Known as snRNAs (small nuclear RNAs), each is complexed with at least seven protein subunits to form an snRNP (small nuclear ribonucleoprotein).

Alberts 7e, p. 343

Third, as mentioned earlier, the catalytic site of the spliceosome (which catalyzes both steps of the splicing reaction) is formed by RNA molecules (the snRNAs) rather than by proteins (Figure 6–30), with the proteins required to correctly position these RNAs.

Alberts 7e, p. 340

On average, there are 11 introns in each of the approximately 20,000 human protein-coding genes, so the cell devotes considerable resources to this step in gene expression.

Figure 6–26: The pre-mRNA splicing reaction. (Alberts 7e, p. 340)

Figure 6–28: The consensus nucleotide sequences in an RNA molecule that signal the beginning and the end of most introns in humans. (Alberts 7e, p. 341)

Questions

What are the three key intron motifs, and what removes introns?

Splice donor, branch site and splice acceptor. The spliceosome, which contains snRNPs that base pair with the intron, removes them.

props.title: Alternative splicing
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: Alternative splicing joins exons in different combinations, so one gene can make more than one mRNA and protein. This generates protein diversity.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Alternative splicing

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

Alternative splicing joins exons in different combinations, so one gene can make more than one mRNA and protein. This generates protein diversity.

Including or skipping exon 2 gives two different mRNAs, and two proteins, from one gene

From the lecture slides

Choosing a different splice acceptor gives two mRNAs, and two proteins, from one pre-mRNA (Lecture 6, slide 36)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 340

In many organisms, the transcript of a given gene can be spliced in more than one way, and this allows the same gene to produce a set of different but related proteins (Figure 6–27).

Alberts 7e, p. 447

In one extreme case, a single Drosophila gene can, in principle, produce as many as 38,000 different proteins through alternative splicing (Figure 7–60), although only a fraction of these forms have thus far been experimentally observed.

Alberts 7e, p. 447

In many cases, however, alternative RNA splicing is regulated.

Figure 6–27: Alternative splicing of the a -tropomyosin gene from rat. (Alberts 7e, p. 341)

Figure 7–59: Patterns of alternative RNA splicing. (Alberts 7e, p. 447)

Questions

What is alternative splicing and why does it matter?

Joining exons in different combinations, so one gene gives several mRNAs and proteins: it generates protein diversity.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Summary (Transcription)

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

Source: Lecture 6: Transcription (PowerPoint)

  • mRNA is made by RNA polymerase, which makes an RNA copy of DNA
  • The mRNA is complementary to the template strand and has the same sequence as the coding strand
  • In prokaryotes RNA polymerase binds a promoter with conserved −10 and −35 sequences
  • Controlling initiation of transcription is a major way of regulating gene expression
  • Eukaryotic transcription starts after chromatin remodelling and binding of the basal transcription complex to the TATA box
  • In eukaryotes the primary transcript is capped, tailed and spliced
  • Alternative splicing generates protein diversity

props.title: Translation and the central dogma
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: Ribosomes read mRNA codons to build a polypeptide

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Translation and the central dogma

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Translation (Lecture 7)

Source: Lecture 7: Translation (PowerPoint)

  • Information flows DNA → mRNA → protein (the central dogma)
  • DNA is copied into mRNA in transcription
  • The mRNA is read in groups of three ribonucleotides, codons, each specifying one of 20 amino acids
  • The order of the codons sets the order of amino acids in the protein made in translation

The genetic code, recap

  • Redundant: 61 codons for 20 amino acids
  • Near universal
  • Has a start codon (AUG) and three stop codons
  • Codons are written 5′ → 3′
  • The third base matters less than the first two (wobble)
The central dogma: DNA is transcribed to mRNA, and mRNA codons are translated into amino acids (Lecture 7, slide 5)

Learning outcomes

  • Ribosomes decode mRNAs and synthesise proteins by catalysing peptide bond formation between amino acids
  • Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge tRNAs with the correct amino acid
  • Complementary base pairing between mRNA codons and tRNA anticodons specifies the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide

Questions

What are the three learning outcomes of this lecture in one line each?

Ribosomes catalyse peptide bonds while decoding mRNA; synthetases charge each tRNA with the right amino acid; codon-anticodon pairing sets the amino acid order.

Why can a single nucleotide not code for one amino acid?

4 bases could only specify 4 amino acids. Triplets give 64 codons, enough for 20.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
The ribosome and its three tRNA sites

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Translation (Lecture 7)

Source: Lecture 7: Translation (PowerPoint)

  • Translation needs many components: mRNA, tRNAs, amino acids, the ribosome, protein factors and energy (GTP and ATP)
  • The key chemical reaction is forming peptide bonds between amino acids
  • Bacterial ribosome = 70S: a 30S small subunit (16S rRNA) and a 50S large subunit (23S and 5S rRNA)
  • The small subunit matches tRNAs to codons. The large subunit makes the peptide bonds
Site Holds Name
A site the incoming aminoacyl-tRNA (charged tRNA) aminoacyl
P site the peptidyl-tRNA, carrying the growing chain peptidyl
E site the free, uncharged tRNA, before it leaves exit

Order a tRNA passes through: A → P → E.

The components of translation: small and large ribosomal subunits with A and P sites, mRNA, initiator tRNA and the initiation, elongation and release factors (Lecture 7, slide 7)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 365

To maintain the correct reading frame and to ensure accuracy (about 1 mistake every 10,000 amino acids), protein synthesis is performed by the ribosome, a complex catalytic machine made from more than 50 different proteins (the ribosomal proteins) and several RNA molecules, the ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs).

Alberts 7e, p. 366

The small subunit provides the framework on which the tRNAs are accurately matched to the codons of the mRNA, while the large subunit catalyzes the formation of the peptide bonds that link the amino acids together into a polypeptide chain.

Alberts 7e, p. 367

Each ribosome has one binding site for mRNA and three binding sites for tRNA: the A, P, and E sites (short for aminoacyl-tRNA, peptidyl-tRNA, and exit, respectively).

Figure 6–65: A comparison of bacterial and eukaryotic ribosomes. (Alberts 7e, p. 366)

Figure 6–66: The RNA-binding sites in the ribosome. (Alberts 7e, p. 367)

Questions

Name the three tRNA sites on the ribosome and what each holds.

A site: incoming aminoacyl-tRNA. P site: peptidyl-tRNA with the growing chain. E site: uncharged tRNA about to leave.

What are the subunits of a bacterial ribosome?

70S overall: 30S small subunit and 50S large subunit.

props.title: Overview of translation
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: Ribosomes bind mRNA, recruit charged tRNAs and shift one codon at a time

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Overview of translation

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Translation (Lecture 7)

Source: Lecture 7: Translation (PowerPoint)

  1. Ribosomes bind to mRNAs and recruit tRNAs charged with amino acids
  2. tRNA anticodons pair with the matching (cognate) codons in the mRNA
  3. The catalytic activity of the 23S rRNA forms a peptide bond between the amino acids on the tRNAs in the P and A sites
  4. The ribosome moves one codon 5′ → 3′ along the mRNA: the tRNA in the P site moves to the E site, and the tRNA in the A site moves to the P site
  5. A new charged tRNA fills the empty A site
  • The peptide bond is made by RNA, not protein, so the ribosome is a ribozyme. The enzyme activity is called peptidyl transferase
Ribosomes move one codon at a time along the mRNA while the 23S rRNA forms each peptide bond (Lecture 7, slide 8)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 366

The mRNA is then pulled through the ribosome, three nucleotides at a time.

Alberts 7e, p. 372

Instead, it is believed that the 23S rRNA forms a highly structured pocket that, through a network of hydrogen bonds, precisely orients the two reactants (the growing peptide chain and an aminoacyl-tRNA) and thereby greatly accelerates their covalent joining.

Alberts 7e, p. 372

RNA molecules that possess catalytic activity are known as ribozymes.

Figure 6–68: Translating an mRNA molecule. (Alberts 7e, p. 368)

Questions

Which part of the ribosome catalyses peptide bond formation?

The 23S rRNA of the large subunit (peptidyl transferase), so the ribosome is a ribozyme.

After a peptide bond forms, where do the two tRNAs move?

The ribosome shifts one codon: the P-site tRNA moves to the E site and the A-site tRNA, now carrying the chain, moves to the P site.

props.title: Charging tRNAs
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach the right amino acid to each tRNA

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Charging tRNAs

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Translation (Lecture 7)

Source: Lecture 7: Translation (PowerPoint)

  • Charging = aminoacylation: attaching an amino acid to the 3′ end of its tRNA, making an aminoacyl-tRNA
  • Carried out by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, one for each amino acid
  • Charging uses ATP: the amino acid is first activated as aminoacyl-AMP, then transferred to the tRNA
DNA-encoded amino acids Codons for amino acids Minimum tRNAs, allowing for wobble Actual tRNAs in an organism Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases
20 61 31 more than 31, fewer than 61 20
  • Wobble is why fewer than 61 tRNAs are needed: one tRNA can read several codons that differ only at the third base
  • The synthetase is the first "adaptor" (amino acid to tRNA); the tRNA is the second (anticodon to codon). A mistake at either step puts the wrong amino acid in the protein
tRNA structure, and an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase using ATP to attach an amino acid to its tRNA (Lecture 7, slide 10)

20 amino acids, 61 sense codons, at least 31 tRNAs thanks to wobble, and 20 synthetases (Lecture 7, slide 11)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 362

Most cells have a different synthetase enzyme for each amino acid (that is, 20 synthetases in all); one attaches glycine to all tRNAs that recognize codons for glycine, another attaches alanine to all tRNAs that recognize codons for alanine, and so on.

Alberts 7e, p. 363

The synthetase-catalyzed reaction that attaches the amino acid to the 3′ end of the tRNA is one of many reactions coupled to the energy-releasing hydrolysis of ATP (see pp. 70–72), and it produces a high-energy bond between the tRNA and the amino acid.

Alberts 7e, p. 363

The first adaptor is the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, which couples a particular amino acid to its corresponding tRNA; the second adaptor is the tRNA molecule itself, whose anticodon forms base pairs with the appropriate codon on the mRNA.

Alberts 7e, p. 364

This hydrolytic editing, which is analogous to the exonucleolytic proofreading by DNA polymerases, increases the overall accuracy of tRNA charging so that only about one mistake is made in 40,000 couplings (Figure 6–61).

Figure 6–58: Amino acid activation by synthetase enzymes. (Alberts 7e, p. 362)

Figure 6–60: The genetic code is translated by means of two adaptors that act one after another. (Alberts 7e, p. 363)

Questions

What do aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases do, and how many are there?

They attach each amino acid to its matching tRNAs (charging). There are 20, one per amino acid.

Why does an organism need fewer than 61 tRNAs?

Wobble at the third codon position lets one tRNA read more than one codon, so a minimum of 31 is enough.

props.title: Initiation of translation
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: IF proteins assemble the 30S subunit, mRNA and fMet-tRNA, then the 50S joins

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Initiation of translation

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Translation (Lecture 7)

Source: Lecture 7: Translation (PowerPoint)

In bacteria:

  1. Initiation factors and the mRNA bind the small (30S) subunit. The mRNA binds through its ribosome binding site, the Shine-Dalgarno sequence (AGGAGG), which pairs with the 16S rRNA a few bases before the start codon
  2. IF2 brings the initiator fMet-tRNA (N-formylmethionine) to the 30S-mRNA complex. Its anticodon UAC pairs with the AUG start codon in the P site. IF3 is released
  3. The large (50S) subunit binds. IF1 and IF2 are released, leaving a complete 70S ribosome with fMet-tRNA in the P site and an empty A site
  • The initiator tRNA is the only one that enters the P site directly; every other tRNA enters at the A site
  • Eukaryotes differ: the small subunit binds the 5′ cap and scans for the first AUG, and the initiator carries ordinary methionine
The Shine-Dalgarno sequence pairs with the 3′ end of 16S rRNA, a few bases upstream of the AUG start codon (Lecture 7, slide 12)

Initiation: IF2 brings fMet-tRNA to the 30S–mRNA complex, then the 50S subunit joins and IF1 and IF2 leave (Lecture 7, slide 13)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 374

Instead, each bacterial mRNA contains a specific ribosome-binding site (called the Shine–Dalgarno sequence, named after its discoverers) that is located a few nucleotides upstream of the AUG at which translation is to begin.

Alberts 7e, p. 374

This nucleotide sequence, with the consensus 5′-AGGAGGU-3′, forms base pairs with the 16S rRNA of the small ribosomal subunit to position the initiating AUG codon in the ribosome.

Alberts 7e, p. 373

This initiator tRNA always carries the amino acid methionine (in bacteria, a modified form of methionine—formylmethionine—is used), with the result that all newly made proteins have methionine as the first amino acid at their N-terminus, the end of a protein that is synthesized first.

Figure 6–75: Structure of a typical bacterial mRNA molecule. (Alberts 7e, p. 374)

Questions

What is the Shine-Dalgarno sequence and what does it do?

The ribosome binding site on bacterial mRNA (AGGAGG). It base pairs with the 16S rRNA to position the start codon AUG in the ribosome.

Which tRNA sits in the P site at the start, and what pairs with what?

fMet-tRNA. Its UAC anticodon pairs with the AUG start codon.

props.title: Elongation
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: Each cycle adds one amino acid: bind, bond, move

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Elongation

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Translation (Lecture 7)

Source: Lecture 7: Translation (PowerPoint)

  1. The next charged tRNA enters the A site, brought in by EF-Tu (with GTP)
  2. A peptide bond forms between the chain on the P-site tRNA and the amino acid on the A-site tRNA. The uncharged tRNA exits, and the mRNA translocates three nucleotides
  3. The first elongation step is complete, and the third tRNA enters the A site
    4, 5, 6 … the cycle repeats
  • Rate in E. coli at 37 °C: about 15 amino acids per second
  • Error rate: about 10⁻⁴, one wrong amino acid in every 10,000
  • Translocation is driven by a second elongation factor, EF-G, using GTP
  • EF-Tu only lets go of the tRNA once a correct codon-anticodon match triggers GTP hydrolysis, which proofreads the pairing

Slide example: UUC = phenylalanine, GGU = glycine.

One elongation cycle: EF-Tu delivers a charged tRNA to the A site, a peptide bond forms, and the mRNA translocates 3 nucleotides (Lecture 7, slide 15)

The cycle repeats at about 15 amino acids per second, with an error rate of about 10⁻⁴ (Lecture 7, slide 16)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 368

In step 1, a tRNA carrying the next amino acid in the chain binds to the ribosomal A site by forming base pairs with the mRNA codon positioned there, so that the P site and the A site contain adjacent bound tRNAs.

Alberts 7e, p. 368

In step 2, the carboxyl end of the polypeptide chain is released from the tRNA at the P site (by breakage of the high-energy bond between the tRNA and its amino acid) and joined to the free amino group of the amino acid linked to the tRNA at the A site, forming a new peptide bond.

Alberts 7e, p. 368

These factors are called EF-Tu and EF-G in bacteria, and EF1 and EF2 in eukaryotes.

Alberts 7e, p. 369

Only when GTP is hydrolyzed does EF-Tu release its grip on the aminoacyl-tRNA and allow it to be used in protein synthesis.

Alberts 7e, p. 369

The two proofreading steps, acting in series, are largely responsible for the 99.99% accuracy of the ribosome in translating RNA into protein.

Figure 6–69: Detailed view of the translation cycle. (Alberts 7e, p. 369)

Questions

Describe one cycle of elongation.

A charged tRNA enters the A site with EF-Tu; a peptide bond joins the chain to its amino acid; the ribosome moves three nucleotides so the tRNAs shift to E and P, and the empty tRNA leaves.

How fast and how accurate is translation in E. coli?

About 15 amino acids per second, with about 1 error in 10,000 amino acids.

props.title: Polyribosomes
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: Several ribosomes can translate one mRNA at the same time

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Polyribosomes

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Translation (Lecture 7)

Source: Lecture 7: Translation (PowerPoint)

  • A single mRNA can be translated by several ribosomes at once. These structures are polyribosomes (polysomes)
  • Each ribosome starts at the start codon and moves 5′ → 3′, so ribosomes further along carry longer chains
  • The slide's electron micrograph is from the salivary glands of the midge Chironomus thummi
  • This lets a cell make many copies of a protein from one mRNA
Electron micrograph of a polyribosome: many ribosomes translating one mRNA at once (Lecture 7, slide 17)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 375

For this reason, most mRNA molecules, and particularly those being translated at high rates, are found in the form of polyribosomes (or polysomes): large cytoplasmic assemblies made up of several ribosomes spaced as close as 80 nucleotides apart along a single mRNA molecule (Figure 6–77).

Figure 6–77: A polyribosome. (Alberts 7e, p. 375)

Questions

What is a polyribosome?

One mRNA being translated by several ribosomes at the same time.
