props.title: Termination of translation
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: A stop codon in the A site recruits a release factor

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Termination of translation

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Translation (Lecture 7)

Source: Lecture 7: Translation (PowerPoint)

  1. A termination codon enters the A site. No tRNA matches it. A release factor binds instead:
    • RF1 recognises UAA and UAG
    • RF2 recognises UAA and UGA
  2. The release factor causes hydrolysis: water is added in place of an amino acid, freeing the polypeptide from the P-site tRNA
  3. The ribosomal subunits separate, and the mRNA and tRNA dissociate
A stop codon in the A site recruits RF1 or RF2, the polypeptide is released and the ribosome dissociates (Lecture 7, slide 18)

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 374

Proteins known as release factors bind to any ribosome with a stop codon positioned in the A site, forcing the peptidyl transferase in the ribosome to catalyze the addition of a water molecule instead of an amino acid to the peptidyl-tRNA (Figure 6–76).

Alberts 7e, p. 374

This reaction frees the carboxyl end of the growing polypeptide chain from its attachment to a tRNA molecule, and as only this attachment normally holds the growing polypeptide to the ribosome, the completed protein chain is released into the cytoplasm.

Figure 6–76: The final phase of eukaryotic protein synthesis. (Alberts 7e, p. 374)

Questions

Which release factors recognise which stop codons?

RF1: UAA and UAG. RF2: UAA and UGA.

How is the finished polypeptide released?

The release factor triggers hydrolysis of the bond between the polypeptide and the P-site tRNA, so water is added instead of an amino acid.

props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: This session builds and uses a standard curve (also called a calibration curve) to work out the concentration of a DNA sample.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Aim and setup

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Concentration practical

Source: Practical Manual 1 4018A (Molecular Biology).pdf (open)

This session builds and uses a standard curve (also called a calibration curve) to work out the concentration of a DNA sample. A series of diluted samples get made from a solution of known concentration, each measured on a spectrophotometer, then concentration gets plotted against absorbance to produce the standard curve. That curve is then used to read off the concentration of an unknown sample.

  • Sample A: 2 mL of a 0.5 mg/mL DNA solution, used to build the standard curve
  • Sample B: 0.5 mL of DNA at an unknown concentration, the one this session solves for
  • TE Buffer (20 mL): TRIS keeps the pH stable; EDTA binds the metal ions that DNA-degrading enzymes need as cofactors, so it protects the DNA from being broken down

Test

What's the purpose of building a standard curve in the DNA concentration practical?

To convert an absorbance reading into a DNA concentration, by measuring several samples of known concentration, plotting concentration against absorbance, and fitting a line through the points.

What do TRIS and EDTA each do in TE buffer?

TRIS keeps the pH stable. EDTA binds the metal ions that DNA-degrading enzymes need as cofactors, so it protects the DNA from being broken down.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Building the standard curve

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Concentration practical

Source: Practical Manual 1 4018A (Molecular Biology).pdf (open)

Six dilutions of sample A get made, each in triplicate (18 tubes total, three sets labelled 1 to 6).

Tube TE Buffer (µL) DNA sample A (µL)
1 840 160
2 880 120
3 920 80
4 940 60
5 960 40
6 1000 0
  • Double-check the pipette is set correctly before each transfer, especially if the same volume gets pipetted twice in a row
  • Watch the tip while it draws up liquid, and don't remove the pipette until it's finished filling
  • Empty the pipette by pressing the tip gently against the side of the tube, or into liquid already there. That stops surface tension holding the last drop on the tip

Test

How many tubes are made for the standard curve, and why?

Six dilutions of sample A, each made in triplicate, so 18 tubes in total.

Why press the pipette tip gently against the side of the tube when emptying it?

Surface tension can otherwise hold the last drop on the tip.

props.title: Measuring absorbance
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: DNA absorbs light maximally at a wavelength of 260 nm.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Measuring absorbance

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Concentration practical

Source: Practical Manual 1 4018A (Molecular Biology).pdf (open)

DNA absorbs light maximally at a wavelength of 260 nm. There should be a linear relationship between absorbance and concentration.

  • Start with tube 6 (buffer only, no DNA). Place it in a cuvette, avoiding the clear windows, load it into the spectrophotometer aligned with the light-path arrows, then press the blue Zero (0A/100%T) button
  • Return that solution to its tube, then measure tube 6 again with the green button. The reading should sit close to zero
  • Work through tubes 1 to 5 the same way, then measure the diluted unknown sample too

A negative reading isn't a mistake

A small negative absorbance for tube 6 is normal: no instrument reads exactly zero, and this one has some inherent inaccuracy. Anything within about ±0.1 is fine (this is part of why the measurements get taken in triplicate). Anything further off than that points to an error in a solution or the technique, worth flagging to a demonstrator.

Test

Why does tube 6 (buffer only, no DNA) get used to zero the spectrophotometer first?

It contains no DNA, so its reading represents the baseline. The instrument gets zeroed against it before any of the actual DNA samples get measured.

A tube with no DNA gives a slightly negative absorbance reading. Is that a problem?

No. Every instrument has some inherent inaccuracy, so a small reading close to zero (within about ±0.1) is expected. Anything further off than that suggests an error in the solution or technique.

props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: Plotting concentration (or, to save a step, just the volume of DNA standard added) on the x-axis against absorbance on the y-axis should give a straight line.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Analysing the results

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Concentration practical

Source: Practical Manual 1 4018A (Molecular Biology).pdf (open)

Plotting concentration (or, to save a step, just the volume of DNA standard added) on the x-axis against absorbance on the y-axis should give a straight line. That line's equation, in the familiar y = mx + c form, converts any new absorbance reading into a concentration by substituting in and solving.

R² measures how well the data actually fits that line: values close to 1.0 mean a strong, highly linear fit; values close to 0 mean the line barely describes the data.

Test

What do you plot for the standard curve, and what do you do with the line?

Concentration (or the volume of DNA standard added) on the x-axis against absorbance on the y-axis gives a straight line. Its equation, y = mx + c, converts a new absorbance reading into a concentration.

What does an R² value close to 1 tell you?

A strong, highly linear fit of the data to the line. Values close to 0 mean the line barely describes the data.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Pre-lab prep

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Concentration practical

Source: The Use of Adjustable Pipettes.pdf (open)

Adjustable pipettes are safe, easy and quick to use, provided the first 5 minutes go into getting familiar with how they work.

Two get used throughout: a P200, adjustable from 20 to 200 µL (small white or yellow tips), and a P1000, adjustable from 200 to 1000 µL (larger white tips). The volume is set by twisting the plunger or knurled ring; a window on the pipette shows the set volume.

  • Set the P200 to dispense 200 µL, fit a tip by pushing the barrel into it inside the tip box (fingers never touch the tip itself), then press the plunger to the first stop and release slowly over a 2-second count
  • Press to the first stop again (expels most of the liquid), then to the second stop (expels the last drops)
  • When dispensing: wipe stray drops off the tip, touch it lightly to the inside wall of the tube, press to the first stop then the second, then eject into the WASTE tub (contains antiseptic)
  • Checking it works: hold the pipette up after drawing liquid. Dripping means either the tip isn't seated properly, or the seal is damaged and needs replacing

Two further pre-lab items sit on Blackboard's 'Pre-lab activities - Practical 1' folder without a downloadable file behind them: Practical 1 Introduction to Spectroscopy of DNA, and Operating an Automated Pipette (Biohit). Neither has been added here yet.

  • Equipment for this experiment (Blackboard)
  • How to use the Bench Top Spec (Blackboard)

Test

What volume ranges do the P200 and P1000 pipettes cover?

P200: 20 to 200 µL (small white or yellow tips). P1000: 200 to 1000 µL (larger white tips).

What does a pipette that drips after drawing up liquid tell you?

Either the tip is not seated properly, or the seal is damaged and needs replacing.

Why press to the second stop when dispensing?

The first stop expels most of the liquid and the second stop expels the last drops.

Set the P200 to dispense 200 µL, fit a tip by pushing the barrel into it inside the tip box (fingers never touch the tip itself), then press the plunger to the first stop and release slowly over a 2-second count Press to the first stop again (expels most of the liquid), then to the second stop (expels the last drops) When dispensing: wipe stray drops off the tip, touch it lightly to the inside wall of the tube, press to the first stop then the second, then eject into the WASTE tub (contains antiseptic) Checking it works : hold the pipette up after drawing liquid. Dripping means either the tip isn't seated properly, or the seal is damaged and needs replacing Two further pre-lab items sit on Blackboard's 'Pre-lab activities - Practical 1' folder without a downloadable file behind them: Practical 1 Introduction to Spectroscopy of DNA , and Operating an Automated Pipette (Biohit) . Neither has been added here yet. Equipment for this experiment (Blackboard) How to use the Bench Top Spec (Blackboard) Test What volume ranges do the P200 and P1000 pipettes cover? P200: 20 to 200 µL (small white or yellow tips). P1000: 200 to 1000 µL (larger white tips). What does a pipette that drips after drawing up liquid tell you? Either the tip is not seated properly, or the seal is damaged and needs replacing. Why press to the second stop when dispensing? The first stop expels most of the liquid and the second stop expels the last drops.

props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: The aim is to produce a restriction map of the plasmid pBR322.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Aim and background

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Restriction Mapping practical

Source: Practical Manual 1 4018A (Molecular Biology).pdf (open)

The aim is to produce a restriction map of the plasmid pBR322. Lectures on plasmids, restriction enzymes and restriction mapping (from Richard Bowater) run around the same time as this practical.

What a restriction enzyme actually does

  • A restriction enzyme cuts double-stranded DNA only at one specific short sequence, its recognition site
  • These sequences are usually palindromic: read 5′→3′, the sequence is identical on both strands
  • A 'site' means every place in a DNA molecule where that exact sequence occurs. Cutting DNA at these sites is digestion

Why cutting a circle matters

  • Plasmids are circular. Cutting a circle once just opens it into a single linear fragment; the fragment count only rises once there are 2 or more cuts
  • Cut at 2 sites and 2 fragments result; cut at 3 sites and 3 fragments result, and so on

Test

What is special about the sequence a restriction enzyme recognises?

It is one specific short sequence (its recognition site), usually palindromic: read 5′ to 3′, it is identical on both strands.

How many fragments do you get by cutting a circular plasmid at 1, 2 and 3 sites?

One cut just opens the circle into a single linear fragment. Two cuts give 2 fragments and 3 cuts give 3.

Related

  • Transformation in the lab

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 499

These enzymes, which are purified from bacteria, cut the DNA double helix at specific sites defined by the local nucleotide sequence, thereby cleaving a long, double-strand DNA molecule into fragments of strictly defined sizes.

Alberts 7e, p. 499

Different bacterial species produce different restriction nucleases, each cutting at a different, specific nucleotide sequence (Figure 8–23).

Alberts 7e, p. 499

The reason restriction nucleases are so useful in the laboratory is that each enzyme will always cut a particular DNA molecule at the same sites.

Alberts 7e, p. 499

Restriction nucleases are usually obtained from bacteria, and their names reflect their origins; for example, the enzyme EcoRI comes from Escherichia coli.

Figure 8–23: Restriction nucleases cleave DNA at specific nucleotide sequences. (Alberts 7e, p. 499)

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Setting up the digest

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Restriction Mapping practical

Source: Practical Manual 1 4018A (Molecular Biology).pdf (open)

Three enzymes get used, alone and in every combination:

Enzyme Recognition sequence
HindIII AAGCTT
PstI CTGCAG
PvuII CAGCTG

That gives 7 possible digests: 3 single (HindIII, PstI, PvuII), 3 double (HindIII+PstI, HindIII+PvuII, PstI+PvuII), and 1 triple (all three). Each student runs one of the seven, then the group of 7 analyses all the results together.

  • To a microcentrifuge tube, add 5 µL pBR322 plasmid DNA, 2 µL of 10x restriction enzyme buffer, and 12 µL nuclease-free water
  • Spin briefly, then pipette the mix into the labelled restriction enzyme tube (E1 = HindIII, E2 = PstI, E3 = PvuII, E4 = HindIII+PstI, E5 = HindIII+PvuII, E6 = PstI+PvuII, E7 = all three), mixing gently without introducing air bubbles
  • Incubate at 37°C for 20 minutes, then spin briefly and store on ice

Test

Which three enzymes are used in Practical 2, and how many different digests do they give?

HindIII, PstI and PvuII, giving 7 digests: 3 single, 3 double and 1 triple.

How long, and at what temperature, is the digest incubated?

20 minutes at 37°C.

props.title: Running the gel
props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: Agarose gels containing ethidium bromide get provided ready-made.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Running the gel

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Restriction Mapping practical

Source: Practical Manual 1 4018A (Molecular Biology).pdf (open)

Agarose gels containing ethidium bromide get provided ready-made. Ethidium bromide is a teratogen and potential carcinogen, so gloves stay on throughout.

  • Mix the 20 µL digest with 5 µL of loading buffer, then load it alongside the other six digests so every single, double, and the triple digest sit next to each other on the gel, plus a 1 kb ladder lane
  • Run at 120 V until the dye front has migrated at least two-thirds of the way down the gel
  • View under UV light on a transilluminator and photograph (photos get posted to Blackboard either way, in case there isn't time in the session itself)

Reading the gel

  • DNA's negatively charged backbone pulls fragments toward the positive electrode; smaller fragments move further through the gel's mesh in the same time, larger fragments move less far
  • The 1 kb ladder (fragments of known size) runs alongside the samples, so an unknown fragment's size can be estimated by comparing migration distance against it

Test

Why do smaller DNA fragments travel further through the gel?

DNA's negatively charged backbone pulls it toward the positive electrode, and smaller fragments move further through the gel's mesh in the same time.

What is the 1 kb ladder for?

It is a set of fragments of known size run alongside the samples, so an unknown fragment's size can be estimated from how far it migrated.

Why do gloves stay on when handling the gel?

The gels contain ethidium bromide, which is a teratogen and a potential carcinogen.

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 500

In less than an hour, the DNA fragments become spread out across the gel according to size, forming a ladder of discrete bands, each composed of a collection of DNA molecules of identical length (Figure 8–24A and B).

Alberts 7e, p. 500

To separate DNA molecules longer than 500 nucleotide pairs, the gel is made of a diluted solution of agarose (a polysaccharide isolated from seaweed).

Alberts 7e, p. 501

A particularly sensitive method of staining DNA is to soak the gel in the dye ethidium bromide, which fluoresces under ultraviolet light when it is bound to DNA (see Figure 8–24B and D).

Figure 8–24: DNA molecules can be separated by size using gel electrophoresis. (Alberts 7e, p. 500)

props.subject: Molecular Biology and Genetics
props.summary: Plotting log₁₀(fragment size in bp) on the x-axis against distance migrated (mm) on the y-axis, for the marker bands, produces a standard curve.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Building a restriction map from the data

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Restriction Mapping practical

Source: Practical Manual 1 4018A (Molecular Biology).pdf (open)

Plotting log₁₀(fragment size in bp) on the x-axis against distance migrated (mm) on the y-axis, for the marker bands, produces a standard curve. Measuring how far a digest's own fragments travelled and reading them against that curve gives their size.

Worked example

Take a plasmid pABC123, digested with BamHI, EcoRI and HindIII:

Enzyme(s) Fragment sizes (bp)
BamHI 6000
EcoRI 6000
HindIII 6000
BamHI + EcoRI 1000 + 5000
BamHI + HindIII 2500 + 3500
EcoRI + HindIII 1500 + 4500
BamHI + EcoRI + HindIII 1000 + 1500 + 3500

Each single digest gives one fragment (6000 bp, the full plasmid), so each enzyme has exactly one site. Starting with BamHI alone gives the first point on the map:

Step 1: mark BamHI's single site, position 1, on the circular 6000 bp plasmid

BamHI + EcoRI gives 1000 + 5000 bp, so those two sites sit 1000 bp apart going one way round the circle, and 5000 bp apart the other way:

Step 2: add EcoRI at position 1000, since that's the shorter of the two fragment sizes

BamHI + HindIII gives 2500 + 3500 bp, placing HindIII at one of two possible positions relative to BamHI, either of which fits that pair of fragment sizes on its own:

Option 1: HindIII placed at position 2500

Option 2: HindIII placed at position 3500 (measuring the other way round)

The triple digest (1000, 1500, 3500 bp) only matches Option 1: going around the circle BamHI (0) to EcoRI (1000) is 1000 bp, EcoRI (1000) to HindIII (2500) is 1500 bp, and HindIII (2500) back to BamHI (6000/0) is 3500 bp. Option 2 would instead give a 2500 bp gap between EcoRI and HindIII, which doesn't match. So Option 1 is the correct map.

The real digest for this practical works exactly the same way, just with pBR322 and the HindIII/PstI/PvuII combination instead.

Test

In the pABC123 worked example, why does each single-enzyme digest produce only one fragment?

Because the plasmid is circular. Cutting a circular molecule once just opens it into a single linear fragment, rather than producing multiple pieces. Multiple fragments only appear once there are 2 or more cuts.

How do you work out the size of an unknown DNA fragment from a gel?

Plot log₁₀(marker fragment size in bp) against distance migrated (mm) for the marker/ladder bands, producing a standard curve. Measure the unknown fragment's migration distance and read its size off that curve.

Why do two different arrangements (Option 1 and Option 2) both fit a double digest's fragment sizes equally well?

A double digest only tells you the distances between two sites going each way round the circle, it doesn't tell you which direction each site sits in relative to a third site already placed. Both arrangements satisfy that same pair of distances until further data rules one out.

How do you decide which of two candidate restriction maps is actually correct?

Compare the fragment sizes each candidate map predicts for the triple digest against the fragment sizes actually observed. Only the correct map's prediction matches the real result.

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 500

Because larger fragments migrate more slowly than smaller ones, the lowermost bands on the gel contain the smallest DNA fragments.

Alberts 7e, p. 500

The sizes of the fragments can be estimated by comparing them to a set of DNA fragments of known sizes (left).

props.summary: The aim is to transform E. coli strain HB101 with plasmid pBR322, then work out the transformation efficiency.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Aim and background

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transformation practical

Source: Practical Manual 1 4018A (Molecular Biology).pdf (open)

The aim is to transform E. coli strain HB101 with plasmid pBR322, then work out the transformation efficiency.

  • Transformation is the uptake of DNA by an organism, a naturally rare event. Growing the transformed cells on antibiotic-containing media means only the ones that actually took up the plasmid survive
  • Competency (the physiological state needed to take up DNA) gets artificially induced with calcium chloride. Cells sit on ice with the plasmid (which slows the membrane), then get heat-shocked at 42°C briefly, which lets the plasmid cross into the cell, before returning to ice
  • pBR322 carries an ampicillin resistance gene (bla), so growth on ampicillin plates selects specifically for successfully transformed cells

Test

Why are transformed cells grown on ampicillin plates?

pBR322 carries an ampicillin resistance gene (bla), so only cells that took up the plasmid survive.

How is competency induced in the practical?

Artificially, with calcium chloride. Cells sit on ice with the plasmid, then get a brief heat shock at 42°C that lets the plasmid cross into the cell.

Related

  • Transformation in the lab

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 502

The plasmid vectors most widely used for gene cloning are small, circular molecules of double-stranded DNA derived from plasmids that occur naturally in bacterial cells.

Alberts 7e, p. 503

The resulting recombinant plasmid DNA is then introduced into a bacterium, where it is replicated many millions of times as the bacterium multiplies.

Figure 8–28: A DNA fragment can be replicated inside a bacterial cell. (Alberts 7e, p. 503)

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Transforming the cells

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transformation practical

Source: Practical Manual 1 4018A (Molecular Biology).pdf (open)

  • Add 5 µL of pBR322 plasmid DNA to 40 µL of E. coli HB101 cells, then place on ice for 10 minutes
  • Heat-shock at 42°C for precisely 50 seconds, then straight back onto ice for 2 minutes
  • Add the reaction to 1 mL of LB broth, then incubate at 37°C for 30 minutes (this recovery step lets the ampicillin-resistance gene get expressed)
  • Spin for 2 minutes at 14,000 rpm, remove the supernatant, resuspend the pellet in 100 µL LB broth, then spread onto an ampicillin plate and incubate at 37°C overnight

Test

Why is there a 30 minute recovery step in LB broth at 37°C?

It lets the ampicillin-resistance gene get expressed before the cells meet the antibiotic.

What are the heat shock conditions?

42°C for precisely 50 seconds, then straight back onto ice for 2 minutes.

What happens to the cells after the recovery step?

Spin for 2 minutes at 14,000 rpm, remove the supernatant, resuspend the pellet in 100 µL LB broth, then spread onto an ampicillin plate and incubate at 37°C overnight.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Setting up the dilution series

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transformation practical

Source: Practical Manual 1 4018A (Molecular Biology).pdf (open)

Before the heat shock (Transforming the cells), a separate tube (990 µL LB broth + 10 µL of the original E. coli cells, labelled '10⁻²') gets set aside to work out how many living cells were used in total.

  • Label 5 tubes −3 to −7, each with 900 µL sterile LB broth
  • Transfer 100 µL from the 10⁻² tube into tube −3, mix, then carry 100 µL from −3 into −4, from −4 into −5, and so on through to −7
Each tube gets 100 µL passed forward into the next, starting from the '10⁻²' tube through to tube −7

Spread 100 µL from each of −3 through −7 onto its own LB agar plate, plus a control plate (100 µL from −3 spread onto an ampicillin plate, to confirm the untransformed cells aren't already resistant).

Test

Why does the transformation experiment include a control plate of untransformed cells on ampicillin?

To confirm the bacteria weren't already ampicillin-resistant before transformation, so any growth on the actual transformation's ampicillin plate can be attributed to the plasmid.

Why is a separate 10⁻² tube set aside before the heat shock?

To work out how many living cells were used in total. It is 990 µL LB broth plus 10 µL of the original E. coli cells.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Calculating transformation efficiency

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transformation practical

Source: Practical Manual 1 4018A (Molecular Biology).pdf (open)

Each live cell produces one colony (a colony-forming unit, CFU). Counting colonies on a plate with 10 to 200 of them gives:

Cells per mL = colonies counted × 10^|dilution| × 10

Worked example: 51 colonies on the −7 plate gives 51 × 10⁷ × 10 = 5.1 × 10⁹ CFU/mL in the original suspension.

The same formula applied to the ampicillin plate spread with transformed cells gives the transformed CFU/mL. Dividing transformed CFU/mL by total CFU/mL gives the frequency of transformation. Worked example: 6 × 10³ transformed cells out of 3 × 10⁸ total gives 2 × 10⁻⁵, meaning roughly 1 cell in every 50,000 was transformed.

Test

What is a colony-forming unit (CFU)?

A single live bacterial cell capable of growing into one visible colony on an agar plate.

What's the formula for calculating cells per mL from a dilution plate count?

Cells per mL = colonies counted × 10^|dilution| × 10.

How do you calculate the frequency of transformation?

Divide the number of transformed cells (CFU/mL) by the total number of cells (CFU/mL) used in the transformation.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Transcription (Lecture 6): questions

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transcription (Lecture 6)

20 questions

Transcription: making an RNA copy of DNA

Which DNA strand does RNA polymerase read, and which strand does the mRNA match?

It reads the template strand. The mRNA is complementary to the template and has the same sequence as the coding strand, with U in place of T.

A coding strand reads 5′-ATGCTTTTGCCAATT-3′. What is the mRNA and the peptide?

mRNA 5′-AUGCUUUUGCCAAUU-3′, read as AUG CUU UUG CCA AUU: Met, Leu, Leu, Pro, Ile.

Gene and mRNA structure

What are the 5′ and 3′ UTRs?

Untranslated regions of the mRNA: the 5′ UTR lies between the start of transcription and AUG, the 3′ UTR between the stop codon and the end of transcription.

Prokaryotic promoters and RNA polymerase

What do 'cis-acting' and 'trans-acting' mean for a promoter and RNA polymerase?

The promoter is cis-acting: a DNA sequence that only controls its own gene. RNA polymerase is trans-acting: a protein that can act on any matching promoter.

What are the subunits of E. coli RNA polymerase?

2 α, 1 β, 1 β′ and 1 σ (sigma) subunit.

What are the −10 and −35 consensus sequences of an E. coli promoter?

−35: TTGACA. −10: TATAAT. They are 15 to 20 bp apart, and the −10 box is 5 to 9 bp before +1.

What does the sigma factor do?

It binds the −10 and −35 boxes so RNA polymerase starts at the right place. Different sigma factors recognise different sets of promoters.

Termination of transcription

How do intrinsic and extrinsic terminators differ?

Intrinsic: the RNA forms a hairpin loop and polymerase and RNA are released. Extrinsic: the rho protein is needed to end transcription.

Prokaryotic genomes and gene regulation

How big is the E. coli genome?

4,639,221 bp with about 4,300 tightly packed genes, not all expressed at once.

The lac operon

What is an operon? Name the lac operon genes and their products.

Linked genes under one promoter. lacZ: β-galactosidase (splits lactose). lacY: permease (brings lactose in). lacA: transacetylase.

Repression and induction

How does lactose switch on the lac operon?

Without lactose the lacI repressor sits on the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. Lactose (strictly allolactose) binds the repressor so it releases the operator.

Glucose control: cAMP and CAP

How does glucose control the lac operon?

No glucose: cAMP rises, binds CAP, and cAMP-CAP binds next to the promoter to strongly activate transcription. With glucose, cAMP is low and activation is weak.

Lactose present, glucose present: what happens to lac gene expression and why?

Low. The repressor is released, but with little cAMP, CAP does not activate, so transcription is weak.

lac operon mutants

What do lacI mutants that can't bind the operator, and operator Oᶜ mutants, have in common?

Both give constitutive expression: the repressor can't block transcription, so the genes are always on.

What happens with a lacI mutant whose repressor can't bind lactose?

The operon stays repressed even with lactose present, because the repressor never leaves the operator.

Eukaryotic transcription: an overview

What is in a eukaryotic primary transcript, and which polymerase makes mRNA?

Exons (coding) and introns (non-coding). RNA Pol II makes all protein-coding mRNAs and microRNAs.

Starting eukaryotic transcription

How does transcription start in eukaryotes?

Chromatin remodelling exposes the promoter, TBP binds the TATA box, TAFs help RNA Pol II bind to form the basal transcription complex, and transcription factors on enhancers boost initiation up to 100 times.

Capping and tailing

How is a eukaryotic mRNA capped and tailed?

A G is added to the 5′ end by a 5′-5′ triphosphate link and methylated. The 3′ end is cut after AAUAAA and poly-A polymerase adds 100 to 200 A.

Splicing

What are the three key intron motifs, and what removes introns?

Splice donor, branch site and splice acceptor. The spliceosome, which contains snRNPs that base pair with the intron, removes them.

Alternative splicing

What is alternative splicing and why does it matter?

Joining exons in different combinations, so one gene gives several mRNAs and proteins: it generates protein diversity.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.title: Translation (Lecture 7) questions
01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Translation (Lecture 7): questions

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Translation (Lecture 7)

15 questions

Translation and the central dogma

What are the three learning outcomes of this lecture in one line each?

Ribosomes catalyse peptide bonds while decoding mRNA; synthetases charge each tRNA with the right amino acid; codon-anticodon pairing sets the amino acid order.

Why can a single nucleotide not code for one amino acid?

4 bases could only specify 4 amino acids. Triplets give 64 codons, enough for 20.

The ribosome and its three tRNA sites

Name the three tRNA sites on the ribosome and what each holds.

A site: incoming aminoacyl-tRNA. P site: peptidyl-tRNA with the growing chain. E site: uncharged tRNA about to leave.

What are the subunits of a bacterial ribosome?

70S overall: 30S small subunit and 50S large subunit.

Overview of translation

Which part of the ribosome catalyses peptide bond formation?

The 23S rRNA of the large subunit (peptidyl transferase), so the ribosome is a ribozyme.

After a peptide bond forms, where do the two tRNAs move?

The ribosome shifts one codon: the P-site tRNA moves to the E site and the A-site tRNA, now carrying the chain, moves to the P site.

Charging tRNAs

What do aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases do, and how many are there?

They attach each amino acid to its matching tRNAs (charging). There are 20, one per amino acid.

Why does an organism need fewer than 61 tRNAs?

Wobble at the third codon position lets one tRNA read more than one codon, so a minimum of 31 is enough.

Initiation of translation

What is the Shine-Dalgarno sequence and what does it do?

The ribosome binding site on bacterial mRNA (AGGAGG). It base pairs with the 16S rRNA to position the start codon AUG in the ribosome.

Which tRNA sits in the P site at the start, and what pairs with what?

fMet-tRNA. Its UAC anticodon pairs with the AUG start codon.

Elongation

Describe one cycle of elongation.

A charged tRNA enters the A site with EF-Tu; a peptide bond joins the chain to its amino acid; the ribosome moves three nucleotides so the tRNAs shift to E and P, and the empty tRNA leaves.

How fast and how accurate is translation in E. coli?

About 15 amino acids per second, with about 1 error in 10,000 amino acids.

Polyribosomes

What is a polyribosome?

One mRNA being translated by several ribosomes at the same time.

Termination of translation

Which release factors recognise which stop codons?

RF1: UAA and UAG. RF2: UAA and UGA.

How is the finished polypeptide released?

The release factor triggers hydrolysis of the bond between the polypeptide and the P-site tRNA, so water is added instead of an amino acid.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.title: DNA Concentration practical quiz
01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
DNA Concentration practical: quiz

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Concentration practical
How to use this

Read a question and answer it out loud or on paper first. Then click the question to reveal the answer. Questions are grouped by topic, in lecture order, and the same questions sit at the bottom of each topic note.

13 questions

Aim and setup

What's the purpose of building a standard curve in the DNA concentration practical?

To convert an absorbance reading into a DNA concentration, by measuring several samples of known concentration, plotting concentration against absorbance, and fitting a line through the points.

What do TRIS and EDTA each do in TE buffer?

TRIS keeps the pH stable. EDTA binds the metal ions that DNA-degrading enzymes need as cofactors, so it protects the DNA from being broken down.

Preparing the unknown sample

How do you prepare the unknown sample for measurement?

Pipette 950 µL of TE buffer into a microcentrifuge tube, then add 50 µL of DNA sample B.

What are samples A and B used for?

Sample A (2 mL of 0.5 mg/mL DNA) is used to build the standard curve. Sample B is DNA of unknown concentration, the one the session solves for.

Building the standard curve

How many tubes are made for the standard curve, and why?

Six dilutions of sample A, each made in triplicate, so 18 tubes in total.

Why press the pipette tip gently against the side of the tube when emptying it?

Surface tension can otherwise hold the last drop on the tip.

Measuring absorbance

Why does tube 6 (buffer only, no DNA) get used to zero the spectrophotometer first?

It contains no DNA, so its reading represents the baseline. The instrument gets zeroed against it before any of the actual DNA samples get measured.

A tube with no DNA gives a slightly negative absorbance reading. Is that a problem?

No. Every instrument has some inherent inaccuracy, so a small reading close to zero (within about ±0.1) is expected. Anything further off than that suggests an error in the solution or technique.

Analysing the results

What do you plot for the standard curve, and what do you do with the line?

Concentration (or the volume of DNA standard added) on the x-axis against absorbance on the y-axis gives a straight line. Its equation, y = mx + c, converts a new absorbance reading into a concentration.

What does an R² value close to 1 tell you?

A strong, highly linear fit of the data to the line. Values close to 0 mean the line barely describes the data.

Pre-lab prep

What volume ranges do the P200 and P1000 pipettes cover?

P200: 20 to 200 µL (small white or yellow tips). P1000: 200 to 1000 µL (larger white tips).

What does a pipette that drips after drawing up liquid tell you?

Either the tip is not seated properly, or the seal is damaged and needs replacing.

Why press to the second stop when dispensing?

The first stop expels most of the liquid and the second stop expels the last drops.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
DNA Replication: quiz

Molecular Biology and Genetics › DNA Replication
How to use this

Read a question and answer it out loud or on paper first. Then click the question to reveal the answer. Questions are grouped by topic, in lecture order, and the same questions sit at the bottom of each topic note.

27 questions

Three theoretical ways DNA could replicate

What are the three theoretical models for how DNA could replicate, and which one is correct?

Conservative (both parental strands stay together), semiconservative (each daughter has one parental and one new strand), and dispersive (parental and new DNA mixed throughout). Semiconservative is correct.

How do the conservative and dispersive models differ?

Conservative: both parental strands stay together and an entirely new molecule forms. Dispersive: parental and new DNA are mixed throughout each strand.

The Meselson-Stahl experiment

How did Meselson and Stahl's experiment distinguish between the three replication models?

They grew E. coli in heavy (¹⁵N) nitrogen medium, switched them to light (¹⁴N) medium, then used density gradient centrifugation to separate DNA by weight across successive generations.

What banding pattern did Meselson and Stahl actually observe, and why did it confirm semiconservative replication?

Generation 0 gave one heavy band; Generation I gave one intermediate band; Generation II gave one intermediate and one light band. This matches semiconservative replication exactly, since each new duplex should contain one old (heavy) and one new (light) strand.

Which model of DNA replication was confirmed by the Meselson-Stahl experiment?
  • A. Conservative
  • B. Semiconservative
  • C. Dispersive
  • D. Discontinuous

Answer: B. Semiconservative

In the Meselson-Stahl experiment, what banding pattern appeared after one round of replication in light medium?
  • A. One heavy band
  • B. One light band
  • C. One intermediate band
  • D. Two bands, heavy and light

Answer: C. One intermediate band

The semiconservative model

What role do the parental strands play in DNA replication?

They act as templates that determine the sequence of the daughter strands.

In which direction is new DNA always synthesised, and where else have you met this rule?

5′ to 3′. It is the same directionality rule as in DNA structure, where the two strands are antiparallel, now applied to copying.

How new nucleotides get added

Which enzyme does most of the DNA synthesis in E. coli?

DNA polymerase III, with DNA polymerase I playing a lesser role.

What decides which base is added opposite a base on the parental strand?

The parental strand is the template: it determines which base is incorporated opposite it into the new strand.

How does a new nucleotide join the growing DNA chain?

The incoming nucleotide (a dNTP, carrying three phosphates) attaches its 5′ end to the free 3′-OH end of the growing chain, releasing a pyrophosphate.

Starting a new strand: primers

Why can't DNA polymerase start building a new strand from scratch?

It can only add nucleotides onto an existing free 3′ end. Primase first makes a short RNA primer to provide that starting point.

What is the role of primase in DNA replication?
  • A. It unwinds the double helix
  • B. It synthesises a short RNA primer
  • C. It joins Okazaki fragments
  • D. It removes supercoiling

Answer: B. It synthesises a short RNA primer

Visualising replication: the growing bubble

What did electron microscope images of replicating E. coli DNA show?

The replication bubble gets bigger as replication proceeds. It is direct physical evidence that replication spreads outward from a starting point.

Replication forks: leading and lagging strands

What's the difference between the leading strand and the lagging strand?

The leading strand is synthesised continuously in the same direction the replication fork moves. The lagging strand is synthesised discontinuously, in short Okazaki fragments, running in the opposite direction to fork movement.

Why is the lagging strand synthesised as Okazaki fragments?
  • A. DNA polymerase can only synthesise 5' to 3', so the strand running the other way must be copied in short pieces
  • B. The lagging strand has a different chemical composition
  • C. Ligase requires fragmented DNA to function
  • D. The leading strand is synthesised in the opposite direction

Answer: A. DNA polymerase can only synthesise 5' to 3', so the strand running the other way must be copied in short pieces

The enzymes of replication

Name the six key enzymes/proteins in E. coli DNA replication and what each one does.

Helicase (DnaB): unwinds the helix. Primase: makes the RNA primer. DNA polymerase III: does most of the actual DNA synthesis. DNA polymerase I: removes RNA primers and replaces them with DNA. Ligase: joins Okazaki fragments together. DNA gyrase: removes supercoiling ahead of the fork.

Which enzyme removes the RNA primers, and which seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments?

DNA polymerase I removes the primers and replaces them with DNA. DNA ligase seals the phosphodiester bonds joining the Okazaki fragments.

What does DNA gyrase do?

It is a topoisomerase that removes the supercoiling caused by unwinding the helix ahead of the fork.

Origins of replication: oriC

What is oriC, and what does it consist of?

The E. coli chromosomal origin of replication: 245 bp, containing three repeats of a 13 bp sequence and four repeats of a 9 bp sequence.

Describe the three stages of initiation at oriC.

(a) Around 20 DnaA proteins, each bound to ATP, bind the four 9 bp repeats and wrap the DNA around the complex. (b) The three 13 bp repeats are denatured in sequence. (c) DnaB helicase hexamers, helped by DnaC, bind each strand and start unwinding, ready for priming and synthesis.

Termination of replication

How does replication terminate in E. coli?

The two replication forks, moving in opposite directions from the single origin, meet at a terminus region containing Ter sequences. These are bound by the Tus protein, which arrests a fork approaching from one particular direction only (a 'fork trap').

What does the Tus protein do at Ter sites during replication termination?
  • A. It initiates a new round of replication
  • B. It arrests a replication fork approaching from one particular direction
  • C. It synthesises the final Okazaki fragment
  • D. It removes RNA primers

Answer: B. It arrests a replication fork approaching from one particular direction

Eukaryotic replication: multiple origins

How does eukaryotic DNA replication differ from bacterial replication in terms of origins?

Eukaryotes replicate from many origins at once (replicons of roughly 40 to 100 kbp each), rather than the single origin bacterial chromosomes use, since eukaryotic chromosomes are far larger.

What is a replicon, and how big are eukaryotic ones?

The stretch of DNA replicated from one origin. In eukaryotes they are 40 to 100 kbp, and replication starts from many origins at once.

Replication of chromosome ends: telomeres

What problem does telomerase solve, and how?

Because of how lagging-strand synthesis works, a linear chromosome would lose a little DNA from its ends with every round of replication. Telomerase solves this by adding new repeat sequences onto the chromosome ends, using its own internal RNA template.

What problem does telomerase solve in eukaryotic cells?
  • A. It prevents mutations during replication
  • B. It compensates for DNA lost from chromosome ends each replication cycle
  • C. It speeds up the replication fork
  • D. It joins multiple origins of replication together

Answer: B. It compensates for DNA lost from chromosome ends each replication cycle

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Heredity and DNA: quiz

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Heredity and DNA
How to use this

Read a question and answer it out loud or on paper first. Then click the question to reveal the answer. Questions are grouped by topic, in lecture order, and the same questions sit at the bottom of each topic note.

23 questions

Genetics: from Mendel to chromosomes

What does 'heredity' mean?

The passing on of physical or mental characteristics from one generation to the next.

What ratio did Mendel observe in the F2 pea generation for tall:dwarf?

Approximately 3:1 (tall:dwarf).

Which chromosome carries the pea height gene (Le/le)?

Chromosome 3 (pea has 7 chromosomes total).

What ratio did Mendel observe for tall:dwarf pea plants in the F2 generation?
  • A. 1:1
  • B. 1:3
  • C. 3:1
  • D. 9:3:3:1

Answer: C. 3:1

Proving DNA is the hereditary material

What did Griffith's experiment show?

Live IIR plus heat-killed IIIS together kills the mouse and produces living IIIS bacteria. Something from the dead bacteria transformed the harmless ones. He called it the transforming principle.

How did Avery, MacLeod and McCarty identify the transforming principle as DNA?

Only the DNase-treated batch of IIIS filtrate failed to transform IIR cells. RNase and protease treatment didn't stop transformation. By elimination, DNA is the active factor.

What isotopes did Hershey and Chase use, and why?

³²P labels DNA (phosphorus is in the DNA backbone, not protein); ³⁵S labels protein (sulfur is in some amino acids, not DNA).

What did Griffith's 1928 experiment demonstrate?
  • A. DNA is the genetic material
  • B. Something from dead bacteria could transform living bacteria
  • C. RNA carries hereditary information
  • D. Bacteria can exchange plasmids directly

Answer: B. Something from dead bacteria could transform living bacteria

In the Hershey-Chase experiment, which isotope was used to label bacteriophage protein?
  • A. ³²P
  • B. ¹⁴C
  • C. ³⁵S
  • D. ¹⁵N

Answer: C. ³⁵S

Which enzyme treatment abolished the transforming activity in Avery, MacLeod and McCarty's experiment?
  • A. Protease
  • B. RNase
  • C. DNase
  • D. Lipase

Answer: C. DNase

Transformation in the lab

Why does CaCl₂ make E. coli 'competent'?

It provides positive ions that neutralise the negative charge on both the cell membrane and DNA's phosphate backbone, reducing repulsion so DNA can approach the cell.

What does the pGLO experiment demonstrate?

That foreign DNA (a jellyfish GFP gene) was taken up by E. coli and actively expressed. The bacteria glow green under UV.

What does CaCl2 do in making E. coli cells competent?
  • A. Breaks down the cell wall
  • B. Neutralises negative charges to reduce repulsion between DNA and the membrane
  • C. Provides nutrients for growth
  • D. Activates restriction enzymes

Answer: B. Neutralises negative charges to reduce repulsion between DNA and the membrane

Natural transformation

What is T-DNA, and what does Agrobacterium do with it?

T-DNA is the segment of the Ti plasmid that gets physically transferred into a plant cell's genome during infection, hijacking its growth to form a gall.

What is the function of T-DNA in Agrobacterium-mediated transformation?
  • A. It degrades plant cell walls
  • B. It gets physically transferred into the plant genome
  • C. It produces the Ti plasmid
  • D. It encodes antibiotic resistance only

Answer: B. It gets physically transferred into the plant genome

Physical and chemical properties of DNA and RNA

At what wavelength do DNA and RNA absorb UV light most strongly, and what is that used for?

260 nm, because of the bases. It is the standard way to measure nucleic acid concentration and purity.

What is denaturation of DNA, and what does it leave intact?

Separating the two strands by breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases (using heat or chemicals). The covalent sugar-phosphate backbone stays intact.

What is the hyperchromic effect?

UV absorbance at 260 nm increases as DNA denatures, because unstacked single-stranded bases absorb more UV than stacked double-stranded ones.

What is melting temperature (Tm), and why does more G and C raise it?

The temperature at which half the DNA sample is denatured. G≡C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds, which take more energy to break than the 2 in A=T.

What is molecular hybridization?

Complementary single strands from different sources re-annealing and base-pairing with each other. It is the principle behind PCR, probes and primers.

Perspectives: where inheritance gets stranger

What is a tsRNA?

A tRNA-derived small RNA: a fragment chopped from a full tRNA molecule, found in sperm, which can carry non-DNA hereditary information to a zygote.

What enzyme does the Le gene encode, and what happens in the dwarf mutant?

Gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase. The mutant (le) has an A→G DNA change causing an ala229→thr amino acid swap, crippling the enzyme and reducing the height-promoting hormone.

What is a tsRNA, as discussed in the lecture on inheritance beyond DNA sequence?
  • A. A type of ribosomal RNA
  • B. A tRNA-derived small RNA fragment found in sperm
  • C. A transfer RNA synthase
  • D. A bacterial transformation vector

Answer: B. A tRNA-derived small RNA fragment found in sperm

Restriction Mapping practical: quiz

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Restriction Mapping practical
How to use this

Read a question and answer it out loud or on paper first. Then click the question to reveal the answer. Questions are grouped by topic, in lecture order, and the same questions sit at the bottom of each topic note.

11 questions

Aim and background

What is special about the sequence a restriction enzyme recognises?

It is one specific short sequence (its recognition site), usually palindromic: read 5′ to 3′, it is identical on both strands.

How many fragments do you get by cutting a circular plasmid at 1, 2 and 3 sites?

One cut just opens the circle into a single linear fragment. Two cuts give 2 fragments and 3 cuts give 3.

Setting up the digest

Which three enzymes are used in Practical 2, and how many different digests do they give?

HindIII, PstI and PvuII, giving 7 digests: 3 single, 3 double and 1 triple.

How long, and at what temperature, is the digest incubated?

20 minutes at 37°C.

Running the gel

Why do smaller DNA fragments travel further through the gel?

DNA's negatively charged backbone pulls it toward the positive electrode, and smaller fragments move further through the gel's mesh in the same time.

What is the 1 kb ladder for?

It is a set of fragments of known size run alongside the samples, so an unknown fragment's size can be estimated from how far it migrated.

Why do gloves stay on when handling the gel?

The gels contain ethidium bromide, which is a teratogen and a potential carcinogen.

Building a restriction map from the data

In the pABC123 worked example, why does each single-enzyme digest produce only one fragment?

Because the plasmid is circular. Cutting a circular molecule once just opens it into a single linear fragment, rather than producing multiple pieces. Multiple fragments only appear once there are 2 or more cuts.

How do you work out the size of an unknown DNA fragment from a gel?

Plot log₁₀(marker fragment size in bp) against distance migrated (mm) for the marker/ladder bands, producing a standard curve. Measure the unknown fragment's migration distance and read its size off that curve.

Why do two different arrangements (Option 1 and Option 2) both fit a double digest's fragment sizes equally well?

A double digest only tells you the distances between two sites going each way round the circle, it doesn't tell you which direction each site sits in relative to a third site already placed. Both arrangements satisfy that same pair of distances until further data rules one out.

How do you decide which of two candidate restriction maps is actually correct?

Compare the fragment sizes each candidate map predicts for the triple digest against the fragment sizes actually observed. Only the correct map's prediction matches the real result.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.text: Restriction Mapping practical: quiz Molecular Biology and Genetics › Restriction Mapping practical How to use this Read a question and answer it out loud or on paper first . Then click the question to reveal the answer. Questions are grouped by topic, in lecture order, and the same questions sit at the bottom of each topic note. 11 questions Aim and background What is special about the sequence a restriction enzyme recognises? It is one specific short sequence (its recognition site), usually palindromic: read 5′ to 3′, it is identical on both strands. How many fragments do you get by cutting a circular plasmid at 1, 2 and 3 sites? One cut just opens the circle into a single linear fragment. Two cuts give 2 fragments and 3 cuts give 3. Setting up the digest Which three enzymes are used in Practical 2, and how many different digests do they give? HindIII, PstI and PvuII, giving 7 digests: 3 single, 3 double and 1 triple. How long, and at what temperature, is the digest incubated? 20 minutes at 37°C. Running the gel Why do smaller DNA fragments travel further through the gel? DNA's negatively charged backbone pulls it toward the positive electrode, and smaller fragments move further through the gel's mesh in the same time. What is the 1 kb ladder for? It is a set of fragments of known size run alongside the samples, so an unknown fragment's size can be estimated from how far it migrated. Why do gloves stay on when handling the gel? The gels contain ethidium bromide, which is a teratogen and a potential carcinogen. Building a restriction map from the data In the pABC123 worked example, why does each single-enzyme digest produce only one fragment? Because the plasmid is circular. Cutting a circular molecule once just opens it into a single linear fragment, rather than producing multiple pieces. Multiple fragments only appear once there are 2 or more cuts. How do you work out the size of an unknown DNA fragment from a gel? Plot log₁₀(marker fragment size in bp) against distance migrated (mm) for the marker/ladder bands, producing a standard curve. Measure the unknown fragment's migration distance and read its size off that curve. Why do two different arrangements (Option 1 and Option 2) both fit a double digest's fragment sizes equally well? A double digest only tells you the distances between two sites going each way round the circle, it doesn't tell you which direction each site sits in relative to a third site already placed. Both arrangements satisfy that same pair of distances until further data rules one out. How do you decide which of two candidate restriction maps is actually correct? Compare the fragment sizes each candidate map predicts for the triple digest against the fragment sizes actually observed. Only the correct map's prediction matches the real result.

Structure of DNA and RNA: quiz

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Structure of DNA and RNA
How to use this

Read a question and answer it out loud or on paper first. Then click the question to reveal the answer. Questions are grouped by topic, in lecture order, and the same questions sit at the bottom of each topic note.

26 questions

The nucleotide: DNA and RNA's shared building block

What three parts make up a nucleotide?

A 5-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base.

What's the chemical difference between ribose and deoxyribose?

Ribose has an -OH group on its 2′ carbon; deoxyribose has just -H there instead.

Name the two purines and three pyrimidines.

Purines: Adenine, Guanine. Pyrimidines: Cytosine, Thymine (DNA only), Uracil (RNA only).

What distinguishes ribose from deoxyribose?
  • A. Ribose has a phosphate group, deoxyribose doesn't
  • B. Ribose has an -OH at the 2' carbon, deoxyribose has -H
  • C. Deoxyribose is found only in RNA
  • D. Ribose lacks a nitrogenous base

Answer: B. Ribose has an -OH at the 2' carbon, deoxyribose has -H

Linking nucleotides: the phosphodiester bond

What bond links nucleotides together, and between which carbons?

A phosphodiester bond, between the 5′ carbon of one sugar and the 3′ carbon of the next.

What direction is DNA/RNA always synthesised, transcribed, and translated in?

5′ to 3′, in all three processes.

What type of bond links adjacent nucleotides in a DNA strand?
  • A. Hydrogen bond
  • B. Glycosidic bond
  • C. Phosphodiester bond
  • D. Peptide bond

Answer: C. Phosphodiester bond

Discovering the structure: Franklin, Chargaff, Watson and Crick

What did Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction photographs show?

They distinguished A-form from B-form DNA and suggested the molecule was probably helical. Watson and Crick used this data, shared via Maurice Wilkins, to build the double-helix model in 1953.

What is Chargaff's rule, and why was it an important clue?

%A is roughly equal to %T and %G roughly equal to %C in every species, even though the overall A+T versus G+C ratio varies widely. It was a direct clue toward complementary base pairing.

Sarcina DNA is about 13% A and 37% G. What does that show about Chargaff's rule?

A is still roughly equal to T (13.4 and 12.4) and G equal to C (37.1 and 37.1), even though the balance of A+T to G+C is very different from other species.

Which experimental technique did Rosalind Franklin use that was central to solving DNA's structure?
  • A. Mass spectrometry
  • B. X-ray diffraction
  • C. Electron microscopy
  • D. Gel electrophoresis

Answer: B. X-ray diffraction

The double helix: full structure

How many hydrogen bonds hold A=T together, vs G≡C?

A=T: 2 hydrogen bonds. G≡C: 3 hydrogen bonds.

What does 'antiparallel' mean for the two DNA strands?

One strand runs 5′→3′, the other runs 3′→5′: opposite directions.

What are the double helix's key dimensions?

2 nm diameter, 0.34 nm rise per base pair, ~10 (precisely 10.4) base pairs per turn.

Why does the major groove matter more than the minor groove for protein binding?

The major groove exposes more of each base pair's distinguishing chemical detail, making it the site where sequence-reading proteins (e.g. transcription factors) typically bind.

How many hydrogen bonds hold a G-C base pair together?
  • A. 1
  • B. 2
  • C. 3
  • D. 4

Answer: C. 3

What is the approximate diameter of the DNA double helix?
  • A. 0.34 nm
  • B. 1 nm
  • C. 2 nm
  • D. 3.4 nm

Answer: C. 2 nm

Why do most sequence-reading proteins bind in the major groove rather than the minor groove?
  • A. The major groove is narrower
  • B. The major groove exposes more distinguishing chemical detail of each base pair
  • C. The minor groove is inaccessible
  • D. The minor groove only forms in RNA

Answer: B. The major groove exposes more distinguishing chemical detail of each base pair

RNA: structure and the three main types

What are the three main types of RNA and their roles?

mRNA carries the genetic message, tRNA delivers amino acids to ribosomes, rRNA is a structural and functional component of ribosomes.

tRNA is made single-stranded. Why does it still contain double-stranded regions?

It folds back on itself, and complementary base pairing within the same molecule forms the double-stranded regions.

Which RNA type carries amino acids to the ribosome during translation?
  • A. mRNA
  • B. rRNA
  • C. tRNA
  • D. snRNA

Answer: C. tRNA

The central dogma

State the central dogma of molecular biology.

Information flows one-way: DNA → RNA → protein. It cannot flow back from protein to nucleic acid.

What does the central dogma say can never happen?

Information can pass between nucleic acids and from nucleic acid to protein, but never back from protein to nucleic acid or to another protein (Crick, 1970).

Extra depth: semiconservative replication

What is semiconservative replication?

DNA replication where each daughter molecule contains one original (old) strand and one newly synthesised strand.

Why is the lagging strand synthesised in fragments (Okazaki fragments)?

DNA polymerase only builds in the 5′→3′ direction, so the strand running the wrong way relative to the replication fork has to be copied backwards in short pieces.

What are the three enzyme roles in DNA replication?

Helicase and topoisomerase unwind strands and prevent tangling, DNA polymerase adds nucleotides and proofreads, DNA ligase joins Okazaki fragments.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
The Genetic Code: questions

Molecular Biology and Genetics › The Genetic Code

16 questions

Information flow: DNA to mRNA to protein

What is the central dogma of molecular biology?

Information flows DNA → RNA → protein (Crick, 1970). Sequence information cannot be transferred back from protein to protein or nucleic acid. Often put as 'DNA makes RNA and RNA makes protein'.

What happens in transcription and in translation?

Transcription copies the DNA sequence into mRNA. Translation reads the mRNA codons on ribosomes, and the order of codons sets the order of amino acids in the protein.

Why the code must be a triplet

Why must the genetic code be read in triplets?

DNA has 4 bases. Singles give 4 combinations and pairs give 16, too few for 20 amino acids. Triplets give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons, enough with redundancy (Brenner).

Proving the triplet code: frameshift mutations

What did Crick's frameshift experiments in phage T4 rII show?

Inserting or deleting 1 or 2 nucleotides abolished gene function, but 3 often did not, because three restores the reading frame. So the code is read in triplets.

Cracking the code: Nirenberg and Matthaei

What was in Nirenberg and Matthaei's cell-free system?

An RNA polymer (e.g. poly-U), tRNAs each coupled to a radioactive amino acid, ribosomes, and an energy source (GTP). Protein was precipitated with acetone and its radioactivity measured.

What did the poly-U experiment show, and how was the RNA made?

Poly-U gave about 39,800 counts/min of phenylalanine in protein versus about 40 to 50 for poly-A, poly-C or none, so UUU = phenylalanine. The RNA was made with polynucleotide phosphorylase, which needs no DNA template.

Who shared the 1968 Nobel Prize for deciphering the genetic code?

Marshall Nirenberg, Har Gobind Khorana and Robert W. Holley.

Repeating copolymers: Khorana

How did Khorana's repeating copolymers assign codons? Give an example.

A repeat read in different frames gives a known set of codons. Repeating UC gives UCU and CUC, and the product contained leucine and serine.

Which codons did Khorana's GUA, GAU and GUAA repeats reveal?

The stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA: these repeats did not prime synthesis of a polypeptide product.

The code is redundant

What does it mean that the genetic code is redundant?

64 codons: 61 encode the 20 amino acids and 3 are stops, so most amino acids have several codons, which usually differ at the third base (e.g. valine: GUU, GUC, GUA, GUG).

The wobble hypothesis

What is the wobble hypothesis?

Crick's proposal that the first two codon bases pair strictly with the tRNA, but pairing at the third base is less constrained and can break standard rules, so one tRNA can read more than one codon.

Start and stop: AUG and the stop codons

What is the start codon, and what is the first amino acid in bacteria?

AUG, which encodes methionine. In bacteria the first amino acid is the modified form N-formylmethionine (fMet).

mRNA 5′-UGAUUCCUAGGAGGUUUGACCUAUGCGAUCUGUUGGU-3′ has one start codon. What are the first five amino acids?

Met, Arg, Ser, Val, Gly: reading from AUG gives AUG CGA UCU GUU GGU.

Which peptide starts at the AUG in 5′-UCGGGUGUCGAUACGCUGGUGUCAAAUAUGCUUUUGCCAAUU-3′?

Met, Leu, Leu, Pro, Ile: AUG CUU UUG CCA AUU.

Non-overlapping and commaless

What do 'non-overlapping' and 'commaless' mean for the genetic code?

Non-overlapping: each nucleotide is part of only one codon. Commaless: codons are read one after the other with no gaps between them.

A (nearly) universal code: selenocysteine and pyrrolysine

Why is the genetic code only 'nearly' universal?

In some proteins in some species, UGA encodes selenocysteine (cysteine with selenium for sulphur) and UAG encodes pyrrolysine (lysine plus a pyrroline group).

Transformation practical: quiz

Molecular Biology and Genetics › Transformation practical
How to use this

Read a question and answer it out loud or on paper first. Then click the question to reveal the answer. Questions are grouped by topic, in lecture order, and the same questions sit at the bottom of each topic note.

10 questions

Aim and background

Why are transformed cells grown on ampicillin plates?

pBR322 carries an ampicillin resistance gene (bla), so only cells that took up the plasmid survive.

How is competency induced in the practical?

Artificially, with calcium chloride. Cells sit on ice with the plasmid, then get a brief heat shock at 42°C that lets the plasmid cross into the cell.

Transforming the cells

Why is there a 30 minute recovery step in LB broth at 37°C?

It lets the ampicillin-resistance gene get expressed before the cells meet the antibiotic.

What are the heat shock conditions?

42°C for precisely 50 seconds, then straight back onto ice for 2 minutes.

What happens to the cells after the recovery step?

Spin for 2 minutes at 14,000 rpm, remove the supernatant, resuspend the pellet in 100 µL LB broth, then spread onto an ampicillin plate and incubate at 37°C overnight.

Setting up the dilution series

Why does the transformation experiment include a control plate of untransformed cells on ampicillin?

To confirm the bacteria weren't already ampicillin-resistant before transformation, so any growth on the actual transformation's ampicillin plate can be attributed to the plasmid.

Why is a separate 10⁻² tube set aside before the heat shock?

To work out how many living cells were used in total. It is 990 µL LB broth plus 10 µL of the original E. coli cells.

Calculating transformation efficiency

What is a colony-forming unit (CFU)?

A single live bacterial cell capable of growing into one visible colony on an agar plate.

What's the formula for calculating cells per mL from a dilution plate count?

Cells per mL = colonies counted × 10^|dilution| × 10.

How do you calculate the frequency of transformation?

Divide the number of transformed cells (CFU/mL) by the total number of cells (CFU/mL) used in the transformation.

01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics.html:
Written questions

Molecular Biology and Genetics
How to use this

Write your own answer first, on paper. Then open the model answer and compare. Exam answers are marked on how well you explain, so practise explaining.

Describe the experimental evidence that established DNA, rather than protein, as the hereditary material. Refer to at least two separate experiments.

Griffith (1928) showed that something from heat-killed virulent bacteria could transform harmless bacteria into virulent ones, proving a 'transforming principle' existed without identifying it. Avery, MacLeod and McCarty narrowed this down by treating the transforming extract with different enzymes: only DNase (not RNase or protease) abolished transformation, pointing to DNA as the active molecule. Hershey and Chase then confirmed this directly using isotope labelling: phage DNA was labelled with ³²P and phage protein with ³⁵S. After infection, mostly ³²P (DNA) entered the bacterial cells and was passed to phage progeny, while ³⁵S (protein) stayed outside. Together, these three experiments built an increasingly direct case for DNA as the hereditary material.

Explain how the structure of DNA relates to its function as the molecule of heredity. Refer to base pairing, strand directionality, and the semiconservative model of replication.

Complementary base pairing (A with T, G with C) means each strand specifies the exact sequence of its partner, so either strand can act as a template to accurately reconstruct the other. The two strands are antiparallel, running 5' to 3' in opposite directions, which dictates how replication machinery works: DNA polymerase only synthesises 5' to 3', so one new strand (leading) is built continuously while the other (lagging) is built discontinuously as Okazaki fragments. Because replication is semiconservative, each daughter molecule ends up with one original (template) strand and one newly synthesised strand. This means genetic information is preserved and faithfully passed on at every cell division, which is exactly what's needed for a hereditary molecule.

Questions

Name the seven SI base units.

Metre (m), second (s), kilogram (kg), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd).

Is the litre an SI unit?

No, but it is accepted with SI: 1 L = 1 dm³ = 1/1000 m³.

props.title: Converting units
props.subject: Professional Skills for Biosciences
props.summary: Method 1: 5 nL = 5 × 10⁻⁹ L = 5 × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁻³ L = 5 × 10⁻⁶ mL. Method 2: nL and mL are 10⁶ apart, and mL is the bigger unit, so 5 nL = 5 × 10⁻⁶ mL.
props.source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Measurements and Dilutions, Dr Beth Williams (PDF)

01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosci.html:
Converting units

Professional Skills for Biosciences › Measurements and Dilutions

Source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Measurements and Dilutions, Dr Beth Williams (PDF)

5 nL in mL

Method 1: 5 nL = 5 × 10⁻⁹ L = 5 × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁻³ L = 5 × 10⁻⁶ mL. Method 2: nL and mL are 10⁶ apart, and mL is the bigger unit, so 5 nL = 5 × 10⁻⁶ mL.

2.5 μL in nL

μL and nL are 10³ apart, and nL is the smaller unit, so 2.5 μL = 2.5 × 10³ nL = 2500 nL.

Units with powers: 150 m² in mm²

1 m = 10³ mm, so 1 m² = (10³ mm)² = 10⁶ mm². 150 m² = 150 × 10⁶ mm² = 1.5 × 10⁸ mm². The power on the unit applies to the conversion factor too.

Questions

Convert 5 nL to mL.

5 × 10⁻⁶ mL (nL and mL are 10⁶ apart).

Convert 2.5 μL to nL.

2500 nL (2.5 × 10³ nL).

Convert 150 m² to mm².

1 m² = 10⁶ mm², so 1.5 × 10⁸ mm².

props.title: Scale and scale bars
props.subject: Professional Skills for Biosciences
props.summary: Biological drawings and micrographs are drawn to scale, like a map. A scale of 10,000:1 means 1 μm in real life is drawn as 10,000 μm (10 mm) on the page.
props.source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Measurements and Dilutions, Dr Beth Williams (PDF)

01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosci.html:
Scale and scale bars

Professional Skills for Biosciences › Measurements and Dilutions

Source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Measurements and Dilutions, Dr Beth Williams (PDF)

Biological drawings and micrographs are drawn to scale, like a map. A scale of 10,000:1 means 1 μm in real life is drawn as 10,000 μm (10 mm) on the page.

Real size = size in the picture ÷ scale. Worked example: a mitochondrion measures 0.8 mm in a picture at 10,000:1, so its real size is 0.8 mm ÷ 10,000 = 8 × 10⁻⁵ mm = 80 nm.

A scale bar is a line on the image labelled with the real length it represents, so the scale still holds if the image is resized.

Questions

A mitochondrion measures 0.8 mm in a picture at 10,000:1. What is its real size?

0.8 mm ÷ 10,000 = 8 × 10⁻⁵ mm = 80 nm.

props.title: Dilutions
props.subject: Professional Skills for Biosciences
props.summary: A dilution needs two things: the property of the original solution (for example its concentration of bacteria), and the dilution factor, the amount it is diluted by.
props.source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Measurements and Dilutions, Dr Beth Williams (PDF)

01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosci.html:
Dilutions

Professional Skills for Biosciences › Measurements and Dilutions

Source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Measurements and Dilutions, Dr Beth Williams (PDF)

A dilution needs two things: the property of the original solution (for example its concentration of bacteria), and the dilution factor, the amount it is diluted by.

A 1 in 5 dilution

1 part culture + 4 parts medium = 5 parts total. A culture of 10⁵ bacteria per mL diluted 1 in 5 has 10⁵ ÷ 5 = 2 × 10⁴ bacteria per mL. The same ratio works at any volume: 1 mL + 4 mL, or 2 mL + 8 mL.

Questions

How is a 1 in 5 dilution made, and what does it do to 10⁵ bacteria mL⁻¹?

1 part culture + 4 parts medium. It gives 2 × 10⁴ bacteria mL⁻¹.

props.title: Serial dilutions
props.subject: Professional Skills for Biosciences
props.summary: In a serial dilution a solution is diluted by the same factor again and again, usually 10 (a 10-fold dilution). Each tube is 1/10 the concentration of the one before.
props.source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Measurements and Dilutions, Dr Beth Williams (PDF)

01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosci.html:
Serial dilutions

Professional Skills for Biosciences › Measurements and Dilutions

Source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Measurements and Dilutions, Dr Beth Williams (PDF)

In a serial dilution a solution is diluted by the same factor again and again, usually 10 (a 10-fold dilution). Each tube is 1/10 the concentration of the one before.

1 mL into 9 mL each time: 10⁸ → 10⁷ → 10⁶ → 10⁵ → 10⁴ cells mL⁻¹

Tube Made by Dilution Cells mL⁻¹
Stock 10 mL culture 1 10⁸
1 1 mL + 9 mL 10⁻¹ 10⁷
2 1 mL + 9 mL 10⁻² 10⁶
3 1 mL + 9 mL 10⁻³ 10⁵
4 1 mL + 9 mL 10⁻⁴ 10⁴

A 1 in 2 dilution mixes a volume of solution with the same volume of medium, for example 5 mL + 5 mL, halving the concentration: 10⁸ → 5 × 10⁷ cells mL⁻¹.

After a dilution series, a graph of concentration against a measured property (such as reaction rate or UV absorbance) can be drawn, as in the DNA concentration practical.

Questions

A 10⁸ cells mL⁻¹ culture goes through four 1 in 10 dilutions. What is the final concentration?

10⁴ cells mL⁻¹.

What does a 1 in 2 dilution of 10⁸ cells mL⁻¹ give?

5 × 10⁷ cells mL⁻¹ (equal volumes of culture and medium).

01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosci.html:
Rearranging equations

Professional Skills for Biosciences › Maths for Biologists

Source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Maths Workbook 2024/25 (Word); answers worked here

Do the same operation to both sides until the wanted letter is alone.

  • C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ → V₂ = C₁V₁ / C₂
  • n = m / M (moles = mass / molar mass) → M = m / n, units g mol⁻¹
  • °F = (9/5) × °C + 32, so 25 °C = 45 + 32 = 77 °F

Questions

Make V₂ the subject of C₁V₁ = C₂V₂.

V₂ = C₁V₁ / C₂.

What is 25 °C in Fahrenheit?

(9/5 × 25) + 32 = 77 °F.

props.title: Dilutions and CFU
props.subject: Professional Skills for Biosciences
props.summary: 6.5 × 10⁹ cells mL⁻¹ through four 1 in 10 dilutions: 6.5 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁴ = 6.5 × 10⁵ cells mL⁻¹
props.source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Maths Workbook 2024/25 (Word); answers worked here

01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosci.html:
Dilutions and CFU

Professional Skills for Biosciences › Maths for Biologists

Source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Maths Workbook 2024/25 (Word); answers worked here

  • 6.5 × 10⁹ cells mL⁻¹ through four 1 in 10 dilutions: 6.5 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁴ = 6.5 × 10⁵ cells mL⁻¹
  • From 10⁷ to 10² cells mL⁻¹ is a 10⁻⁵ dilution
  • 10⁸ cells mL⁻¹ diluted 10⁻⁵ gives 10³ cells mL⁻¹

Counting bacteria in soil (CFU g⁻¹)

0.1 g soil in 1.0 mL water, diluted 10⁻¹ to 10⁻⁶, 50 μL plated from each (the workbook prints 50 ml, which must mean 50 μL). Counts: 7983 (10⁻³), 638 (10⁻⁴), 57 (10⁻⁵), 3 (10⁻⁶).

  • Countable range is roughly 30 to 300 colonies, so the 10⁻⁵ plate (57) is used
  • CFU per mL of that dilution = 57 ÷ 0.05 mL = 1140
  • CFU per mL of the original suspension = 1140 × 10⁵ = 1.14 × 10⁸
  • That 1 mL held 0.1 g soil, so 1.14 × 10⁸ ÷ 0.1 = 1.1 × 10⁹ CFU g⁻¹

The neighbouring plates give 1.3 × 10⁹ (10⁻⁴) and 6 × 10⁸ (10⁻⁶). Crowded plates undercount as colonies merge, and very low counts are dominated by chance, so replicate plates of the chosen dilution raise confidence.

Scale bars and maps

  • 1.5 cm bar at ×10,000: 1.5 cm ÷ 10,000 = 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ cm = 1.5 μm
  • 0.8 cm bar at ×1500: 0.8 ÷ 1500 cm = 5.3 μm
  • 300 km shown as 30 cm: 3 × 10⁷ cm : 30 cm = 1 : 1,000,000

Questions

A 10⁻⁵ plate (50 μL plated) has 57 colonies; the suspension held 0.1 g soil in 1 mL. What is the CFU g⁻¹?

57 ÷ 0.05 = 1140 mL⁻¹; × 10⁵ = 1.14 × 10⁸ mL⁻¹; ÷ 0.1 g = 1.1 × 10⁹ CFU g⁻¹.

What scale shows 300 km as 30 cm?

1 : 1,000,000.

Countable range is roughly 30 to 300 colonies, so the 10⁻⁵ plate (57) is used CFU per mL of that dilution = 57 ÷ 0.05 mL = 1140 CFU per mL of the original suspension = 1140 × 10⁵ = 1.14 × 10⁸ That 1 mL held 0.1 g soil, so 1.14 × 10⁸ ÷ 0.1 = 1.1 × 10⁹ CFU g⁻¹ The neighbouring plates give 1.3 × 10⁹ (10⁻⁴) and 6 × 10⁸ (10⁻⁶). Crowded plates undercount as colonies merge, and very low counts are dominated by chance, so replicate plates of the chosen dilution raise confidence. Scale bars and maps 1.5 cm bar at ×10,000: 1.5 cm ÷ 10,000 = 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ cm = 1.5 μm 0.8 cm bar at ×1500: 0.8 ÷ 1500 cm = 5.3 μm 300 km shown as 30 cm: 3 × 10⁷ cm : 30 cm = 1 : 1,000,000 Questions A 10⁻⁵ plate (50 μL plated) has 57 colonies; the suspension held 0.1 g soil in 1 mL. What is the CFU g⁻¹? 57 ÷ 0.05 = 1140 mL⁻¹; × 10⁵ = 1.14 × 10⁸ mL⁻¹; ÷ 0.1 g = 1.1 × 10⁹ CFU g⁻¹. What scale shows 300 km as 30 cm? 1 : 1,000,000.

01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosci.html:
Moles and molarity

Professional Skills for Biosciences › Maths for Biologists

Source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Maths Workbook 2024/25 (Word); answers worked here

Moles = mass ÷ molar mass (n = m / M). Molarity = moles ÷ volume in litres (M = mol L⁻¹).

Question Working Answer
Molar mass of KOH (2 mol = 112.22 g) 112.22 ÷ 2 56.11 g mol⁻¹
Moles in 3.2 mg NaCl 3.2 × 10⁻³ ÷ 58.44 5.48 × 10⁻⁵ mol
Moles in 1.4 μg glucose 1.4 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ 180 7.8 × 10⁻⁹ mol
Mass of 0.25 μmol ZnCl₂ 0.25 × 10⁻⁶ × 136 34 μg
9.4 g Na₂CO₃ in 100 mL 9.4 ÷ 106 = 0.0887 mol; ÷ 0.1 L 0.887 M
0.58 mg NaCl in 0.25 mL 9.92 × 10⁻⁶ mol ÷ 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ L 0.040 M

Dilutions with C₁V₁ = C₂V₂

  • 0.7 L of 0.04 M NaCl from 0.25 M stock: V₁ = 0.04 × 0.7 / 0.25 = 0.112 L (112 mL)
  • 30 mL with 5 mM CaCl₂ (from 3.0 M) and 80 mM MgSO₄ (from 1.5 M): 0.05 mL (50 μL) CaCl₂, 1.6 mL MgSO₄, and 28.35 mL water
  • 50 mL of 0.2 M TRIS from 0.5 M: 20 mL stock
  • 500 mL of 5 mM CaCl₂ from 1 M: 2.5 mL stock

% (w/v) and TRIS

  • % (w/v) = mass in g / volume in mL × 100, so 80 mL of 15% glucose holds 12 g
  • TRIS (121.1 g mol⁻¹): 200 mL of 1 M needs 24.22 g; 1 L of 0.5 M needs 60.55 g; 5 mL of 1 mM needs 0.61 mg
  • 1 L of TBS with 87.7 g NaCl and 74.2 g TRIS: NaCl 1.50 M, TRIS 0.613 M

Questions

What is the molarity of 9.4 g Na₂CO₃ (106 g mol⁻¹) in 100 mL?

0.0887 mol ÷ 0.1 L = 0.887 M.

How much 0.25 M NaCl stock makes 0.7 L of 0.04 M?

V₁ = 0.04 × 0.7 / 0.25 = 0.112 L (112 mL).

How much TRIS (121.1 g mol⁻¹) makes 200 mL of 1 M?

0.2 mol × 121.1 = 24.22 g.
