props.title: Logarithms and pH
props.subject: Professional Skills for Biosciences
props.summary: A logarithm answers 'what power?': log₁₀(1000) = 3 because 10³ = 1000. Biology uses base 10 (pH, dilution series, log scales) and base e, the natural log ln (growth and decay).
props.source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Maths Workbook 2024/25 (Word); answers worked here

01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosci.html:
Logarithms and pH

Professional Skills for Biosciences › Maths for Biologists

Source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Maths Workbook 2024/25 (Word); answers worked here

A logarithm answers 'what power?': log₁₀(1000) = 3 because 10³ = 1000. Biology uses base 10 (pH, dilution series, log scales) and base e, the natural log ln (growth and decay).

  • log a + log b = log ab
  • log a − log b = log (a/b)
  • n log a = log aⁿ
  • e.g. log x + log 4 = log 4x; log 15 + log 3 − log 9 = log 5
Lengths from 2 × 10⁻⁴ m to 3 × 10⁶ m fit on one log scale, each unit being ×10

The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation

pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), where A⁻ is the base form and HA the acid form. More acid than base gives a pH below the pKa; more base gives a pH above it. This is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.

  • 0.2 M acetic acid + 0.05 M acetate (pKa 4.7): pH = 4.7 + log(0.25) = 4.10
  • 0.05 M H₂PO₄⁻ + 0.2 M HPO₄²⁻ (pKa 7.21): pH = 7.21 + log(4) = 7.81
  • Acetate buffer at pH 5.1 with 0.8 M acetic acid: log([A⁻]/0.8) = 0.4, so [A⁻] = 0.8 × 10⁰·⁴ = 2.0 M

Exponential growth and decline

  • Population P = 245(1.03)ⁿ thousand, n years after 2010: in 2015 P = 245 × 1.03⁵ = 284,000
  • It reaches 400,000 when 1.03ⁿ = 1.633, so n = log 1.633 / log 1.03 = 16.6: during 2027
  • 5% growth would be 245(1.05)ⁿ
  • Hedgehogs falling 4% a year from 200,000 in 2022: N = 200,000 × 0.96ⁿ, giving about 156,500 in 2028

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 52

As explained in Panel 2–2, to avoid the use of unwieldy numbers the concentration of H3O+ is expressed using a logarithmic scale called the pH scale.

Panel 2–2: Water and Its Influence on the Behavior of Biological Molecules, pH (Alberts 7e, p. 97)

Questions

pH of 0.2 M acetic acid + 0.05 M acetate (pKa 4.7)?

4.7 + log(0.05/0.2) = 4.7 − 0.60 = 4.10.

pH of 0.05 M H₂PO₄⁻ + 0.2 M HPO₄²⁻ (pKa 7.21)?

7.21 + log 4 = 7.81.

Simplify log 15 + log 3 − log 9.

log (15 × 3 / 9) = log 5.

props.title: Linear graphs
props.subject: Professional Skills for Biosciences
props.summary: A straight line is y = mx + c, where the gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) and c is the y-intercept. A perpendicular line has gradient −1/m.
props.source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Maths Workbook 2024/25 (Word); answers worked here

01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosci.html:
Linear graphs

Professional Skills for Biosciences › Maths for Biologists

Source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Maths Workbook 2024/25 (Word); answers worked here

A straight line is y = mx + c, where the gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) and c is the y-intercept. A perpendicular line has gradient −1/m.

  • Through A(3, 6) and B(0.2, 4): m = 2/2.8 = 0.71; c = 6 − 0.71 × 3 = 3.86; y = 0.71x + 3.86
  • Through A(0.4, 5) and B(3, 1): m = −4/2.6 = −1.54; c = 5.62; y = −1.54x + 5.62
  • DMSP 2.8 at 5 min and 5.6 at 10 min: m = 0.56, c = 0; y = 0.56x

Questions

What is the gradient of the line through (3, 6) and (0.2, 4)?

(6 − 4)/(3 − 0.2) = 2/2.8 = 0.71.

props.title: Non-linear graphs and enzyme kinetics
props.subject: Professional Skills for Biosciences
props.summary: Many biological curves can be turned into straight lines. Exponential growth N = N₀eᵏᵗ becomes ln N = ln N₀ + kt: a straight line of ln N against t with gradient k.
props.source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Maths Workbook 2024/25 (Word); answers worked here

01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosci.html:
Non-linear graphs and enzyme kinetics

Professional Skills for Biosciences › Maths for Biologists

Source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Maths Workbook 2024/25 (Word); answers worked here

Many biological curves can be turned into straight lines. Exponential growth N = N₀eᵏᵗ becomes ln N = ln N₀ + kt: a straight line of ln N against t with gradient k.

The Michaelis-Menten equation v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]) gives a curve. Rearranging gives three straight-line plots, the best known being the Lineweaver-Burk plot:

Plot y x y intercept x intercept
Lineweaver-Burk 1/v 1/[S] 1/Vmax −1/Km
Eadie-Hofstee v v/[S] Vmax Vmax/Km
Hanes-Woolf [S]/v [S] Km/Vmax −Km

The same idea applies in pharmacology: the drug-receptor saturation equation rearranges into the straight-line Scatchard plot.

From the textbook (Alberts 7e)

Alberts 7e, p. 151

In general, a lower value of Km means tighter substrate binding.

Panel 3–2: Some of the Methods Used to Study Enzymes, Steady-state enzyme kinetics (Alberts 7e, p. 150)

Panel 3–2: Some of the Methods Used to Study Enzymes, The double-reciprocal plot (Alberts 7e, p. 151)

Questions

What are the axes and intercepts of a Lineweaver-Burk plot?

y = 1/v, x = 1/[S]; y intercept 1/Vmax, x intercept −1/Km.

props.title: Calculus basics
props.subject: Professional Skills for Biosciences
props.summary: Differentiation gives the rate of change (gradient) of a curve. Power rule: d/dx (axⁿ) = naxⁿ⁻¹, so y = 3x² gives dy/dx = 6x
props.source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Maths Workbook 2024/25 (Word); answers worked here

01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosci.html:
Calculus basics

Professional Skills for Biosciences › Maths for Biologists

Source: Skills for Biologists (BIO-4008Y): Maths Workbook 2024/25 (Word); answers worked here

  • Differentiation gives the rate of change (gradient) of a curve. Power rule: d/dx (axⁿ) = naxⁿ⁻¹, so y = 3x² gives dy/dx = 6x
  • A maximum or minimum is where dy/dx = 0, such as the month starling numbers peak
  • Integration is the reverse: ∫axⁿ dx = axⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C, so ∫3x² dx = x³ + C
  • A definite integral gives the area under a curve, such as total oxygen consumed from a rate curve

Questions

Differentiate y = 3x², then integrate 3x².

dy/dx = 6x. ∫3x² dx = x³ + C.

Maths for Biologists: questions

Professional Skills for Biosciences › Maths for Biologists

14 questions

Rearranging equations

Make V₂ the subject of C₁V₁ = C₂V₂.

V₂ = C₁V₁ / C₂.

What is 25 °C in Fahrenheit?

(9/5 × 25) + 32 = 77 °F.

Measurements, volumes and densities

What is the volume of a sphere 24 mm across?

r = 12 mm; 4/3 × π × 12³ = 7238 mm³ (7.24 cm³).

Dilutions and CFU

A 10⁻⁵ plate (50 μL plated) has 57 colonies; the suspension held 0.1 g soil in 1 mL. What is the CFU g⁻¹?

57 ÷ 0.05 = 1140 mL⁻¹; × 10⁵ = 1.14 × 10⁸ mL⁻¹; ÷ 0.1 g = 1.1 × 10⁹ CFU g⁻¹.

What scale shows 300 km as 30 cm?

1 : 1,000,000.

Moles and molarity

What is the molarity of 9.4 g Na₂CO₃ (106 g mol⁻¹) in 100 mL?

0.0887 mol ÷ 0.1 L = 0.887 M.

How much 0.25 M NaCl stock makes 0.7 L of 0.04 M?

V₁ = 0.04 × 0.7 / 0.25 = 0.112 L (112 mL).

How much TRIS (121.1 g mol⁻¹) makes 200 mL of 1 M?

0.2 mol × 121.1 = 24.22 g.

Logarithms and pH

pH of 0.2 M acetic acid + 0.05 M acetate (pKa 4.7)?

4.7 + log(0.05/0.2) = 4.7 − 0.60 = 4.10.

pH of 0.05 M H₂PO₄⁻ + 0.2 M HPO₄²⁻ (pKa 7.21)?

7.21 + log 4 = 7.81.

Simplify log 15 + log 3 − log 9.

log (15 × 3 / 9) = log 5.

Linear graphs

What is the gradient of the line through (3, 6) and (0.2, 4)?

(6 − 4)/(3 − 0.2) = 2/2.8 = 0.71.

Non-linear graphs and enzyme kinetics

What are the axes and intercepts of a Lineweaver-Burk plot?

y = 1/v, x = 1/[S]; y intercept 1/Vmax, x intercept −1/Km.

Calculus basics

Differentiate y = 3x², then integrate 3x².

dy/dx = 6x. ∫3x² dx = x³ + C.

Measurements and Dilutions: questions

Professional Skills for Biosciences › Measurements and Dilutions

10 questions

Why units matter

How should twenty five milligrams be written?

25 mg: value, space, then prefix and unit.

SI units

Name the seven SI base units.

Metre (m), second (s), kilogram (kg), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd).

Is the litre an SI unit?

No, but it is accepted with SI: 1 L = 1 dm³ = 1/1000 m³.

Converting units

Convert 5 nL to mL.

5 × 10⁻⁶ mL (nL and mL are 10⁶ apart).

Convert 2.5 μL to nL.

2500 nL (2.5 × 10³ nL).

Convert 150 m² to mm².

1 m² = 10⁶ mm², so 1.5 × 10⁸ mm².

Scale and scale bars

A mitochondrion measures 0.8 mm in a picture at 10,000:1. What is its real size?

0.8 mm ÷ 10,000 = 8 × 10⁻⁵ mm = 80 nm.

Dilutions

How is a 1 in 5 dilution made, and what does it do to 10⁵ bacteria mL⁻¹?

1 part culture + 4 parts medium. It gives 2 × 10⁴ bacteria mL⁻¹.

Serial dilutions

A 10⁸ cells mL⁻¹ culture goes through four 1 in 10 dilutions. What is the final concentration?

10⁴ cells mL⁻¹.

What does a 1 in 2 dilution of 10⁸ cells mL⁻¹ give?

5 × 10⁷ cells mL⁻¹ (equal volumes of culture and medium).

02 Key Terms/Agrobacterium tumefaciens.title: Agrobacterium tumefaciens
02 Key Terms/Agrobacterium tumefaciens.html:
Agrobacterium tumefaciens

Definition

A soil bacterium that causes crown gall disease by inserting part of its own DNA (the T-DNA from its Ti plasmid) into a plant's genome.

Where this comes up

  • Natural transformation · Molecular Biology and Genetics

Test

What is T-DNA, and what does Agrobacterium do with it?

T-DNA is the segment of the Ti plasmid that gets physically transferred into a plant cell's genome during infection, hijacking its growth to form a gall.

02 Key Terms/Alkane.title: Alkane
02 Key Terms/Alkane.html:
Alkane

Definition

A chain of carbon and hydrogen with only single bonds: saturated.

Where this comes up

  • Alkanes · Biological Chemistry
  • Alkyl and aryl groups · Biological Chemistry
  • Alkenes · Biological Chemistry
  • Lecture checklist (Functional Groups in Biology) · Biological Chemistry

Questions

What makes an alkane saturated?

Only single bonds, so every carbon has its maximum number of bonded hydrogens.

What is an alkyl group?

An alkane with one hydrogen removed so it can attach to another molecule, e.g. methyl –CH₃.

What is the difference between an alkane and an alkene?

An alkene has a C=C double bond (two fewer H), so it is unsaturated.

02 Key Terms/Amino group.title: Amino group
02 Key Terms/Amino group.html:
Amino group

Definition

–NH₂. Found in every amino acid; amines are primary, secondary or tertiary.

Where this comes up

  • Amino groups and amines · Biological Chemistry
  • Peptide bonds · Biological Chemistry
  • Amino acids · Biological Chemistry

Questions

What are primary, secondary and tertiary amines?

N bonded to 1, 2 or 3 carbons, e.g. methylamine, dimethylamine, trimethylamine.

How does a peptide bond form?

The carboxyl group of one amino acid joins the amino group of the next, releasing water.

Why is TRIS useful, and roughly what pH does it buffer?

Its amino group gains and loses H⁺, so it resists pH change. It buffers around pH 8.

Questions

How many aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases are there?

02 Key Terms/Central dogma.title: Central dogma
02 Key Terms/Central dogma.html:
Central dogma

Definition

Crick's 1970 statement that sequence information flows from DNA to RNA to protein and cannot be transferred back from protein to protein or nucleic acid. Often put as 'DNA makes RNA and RNA makes protein'.

Where this comes up

  • Further reading (The Genetic Code) · Molecular Biology and Genetics
  • Information flow: DNA to mRNA to protein · Molecular Biology and Genetics

Questions

State the central dogma of molecular biology.

Information flows one-way: DNA → RNA → protein. It cannot flow back from protein to nucleic acid.

What is the central dogma of molecular biology?

Information flows DNA → RNA → protein (Crick, 1970). Sequence information cannot be transferred back from protein to protein or nucleic acid. Often put as 'DNA makes RNA and RNA makes protein'.

What does the central dogma say can never happen?

Information can pass between nucleic acids and from nucleic acid to protein, but never back from protein to nucleic acid or to another protein (Crick, 1970).

02 Key Terms/Chargaff's rule.title: Chargaff's rule
02 Key Terms/Chargaff's rule.html:
Chargaff's rule

Definition

In DNA the amount of A equals T and the amount of G equals C, whatever the species, even though the overall A+T versus G+C ratio varies widely between species.

Where this comes up

  • Discovering the structure: Franklin, Chargaff, Watson and Crick · Molecular Biology and Genetics

Test

What is Chargaff's rule, and why was it an important clue?

%A is roughly equal to %T and %G roughly equal to %C in every species, even though the overall A+T versus G+C ratio varies widely. It was a direct clue toward complementary base pairing.

Sarcina DNA is about 13% A and 37% G. What does that show about Chargaff's rule?

A is still roughly equal to T (13.4 and 12.4) and G equal to C (37.1 and 37.1), even though the balance of A+T to G+C is very different from other species.

What is the mRNA and the peptide? mRNA 5′-AUGCUUUUGCCAAUU-3′, read as AUG CUU UUG CCA AUU: Met, Leu, Leu, Pro, Ile.

02 Key Terms/Codon.title: Codon
02 Key Terms/Codon.html:
Codon

Definition

Three consecutive mRNA nucleotides that specify one amino acid or a stop signal. There are 64 codons.

Where this comes up

Questions

How did Khorana's repeating copolymers assign codons? Give an example.

A repeat read in different frames gives a known set of codons. Repeating UC gives UCU and CUC, and the product contained leucine and serine.

Which codons did Khorana's GUA, GAU and GUAA repeats reveal?

The stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA: these repeats did not prime synthesis of a polypeptide product.

What is the start codon, and what is the first amino acid in bacteria?

AUG, which encodes methionine. In bacteria the first amino acid is the modified form N-formylmethionine (fMet).

mRNA 5′-UGAUUCCUAGGAGGUUUGACCUAUGCGAUCUGUUGGU-3′ has one start codon. What are the first five amino acids?

Met, Arg, Ser, Val, Gly: reading from AUG gives AUG CGA UCU GUU GGU.

02 Key Terms/Competence.title: Competence
02 Key Terms/Competence.html:
Competence

Definition

The physiological state a bacterial cell needs to take up foreign DNA. In the lab it is induced with calcium chloride and a heat shock.

Where this comes up

  • Transformation in the lab · Molecular Biology and Genetics

Test

Why does CaCl₂ make E. coli 'competent'?

It provides positive ions that neutralise the negative charge on both the cell membrane and DNA's phosphate backbone, reducing repulsion so DNA can approach the cell.

How is competency induced in the practical?

Artificially, with calcium chloride. Cells sit on ice with the plasmid, then get a brief heat shock at 42°C that lets the plasmid cross into the cell.

02 Key Terms/Covalent bond.title: Covalent bond
02 Key Terms/Covalent bond.html:
Covalent bond

Definition

A bond where two atoms share a pair of electrons. A double bond shares two pairs, a triple bond three.

Where this comes up

  • Dative (coordinate) bonds · Biological Chemistry
  • Electronegativity · Biological Chemistry

Questions

How does an ionic bond differ from a covalent bond?

Ionic: electrons are transferred, forming cations and anions held by electrostatic attraction. Covalent: a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.

What is a dative bond? Give an example.

A covalent bond where both electrons come from one atom's lone pair, e.g. N–H in NH₄⁺ formed when NH₃ bonds to H⁺.

What is electronegativity and what affects it?

An atom's ability to pull electrons in a covalent bond towards itself. It depends on the number of protons and the distance of the outer electrons from the nucleus.

How did Avery, MacLeod and McCarty identify the transforming principle as DNA?

Only the DNase-treated batch of IIIS filtrate failed to transform IIR cells. RNase and protease treatment didn't stop transformation. By elimination, DNA is the active factor.

What is T-DNA, and what does Agrobacterium do with it?

T-DNA is the segment of the Ti plasmid that gets physically transferred into a plant cell's genome during infection, hijacking its growth to form a gall.

What does 'antiparallel' mean for the two DNA strands?

One strand runs 5′→3′, the other runs 3′→5′: opposite directions.

What direction is DNA/RNA always synthesised, transcribed, and translated in?

5′ to 3′, in all three processes.

02 Key Terms/Electronegativity.title: Electronegativity
02 Key Terms/Electronegativity.html:
Electronegativity

Definition

An atom's ability to pull the electrons of a covalent bond towards itself. Fluorine is highest; it rises across a period and falls down a group.

Where this comes up

  • Electronegativity · Biological Chemistry
  • Polar bonds · Biological Chemistry
  • Oxygen makes molecules polar · Biological Chemistry
  • Nucleophilic attack and polar bonds · Biological Chemistry

Questions

What is electronegativity and what affects it?

An atom's ability to pull electrons in a covalent bond towards itself. It depends on the number of protons and the distance of the outer electrons from the nucleus.

Why is water polar, and what does that allow?

O is much more electronegative than H, so O is δ− and the H atoms δ+. Water molecules attract each other through hydrogen bonds.

Why do oxygen-containing groups make molecules polar?

Oxygen is much more electronegative than C and H, so C–O and O–H bonds are polar. C–H bonds are not.

02 Key Terms/Elimination.title: Elimination
02 Key Terms/Elimination.html:
Elimination

Definition

Reduction to zero (or a very low target rate) of new cases within a defined area through deliberate effort, with continued measures still needed to stop transmission re-establishing. Example: measles.

Where this comes up

  • Proving DNA is the hereditary material · Molecular Biology and Genetics
  • Vaccination: success stories · Introduction to Biomedicine

Test

What's the difference between disease eradication and disease elimination? Give an example of each.

Eradication is a complete, permanent, worldwide reduction to zero new cases, with no further control measures needed (e.g. smallpox). Elimination is reduction to zero or a very low rate within a defined area, but continued measures are still needed to prevent it re-establishing (e.g. measles).

Inserting or deleting 1 or 2 nucleotides abolished gene function, but 3 often did not, because three restores the reading frame. So the code is read in triplets.

02 Key Terms/Fungi.title: Fungi
02 Key Terms/Fungi.html:
Fungi

Definition

A very diverse group (moulds, mushrooms, yeasts) found in almost any habitat. Most are harmless to humans, and a few cause disease, especially in immune-compromised people.

Where this comes up

  • Case study: pneumonia · Introduction to Biomedicine
  • Microorganisms: fungi and parasites · Introduction to Biomedicine
  • What an infectious disease actually is · Introduction to Biomedicine

Test

Are most fungi harmful to humans? Who is most at risk from fungal infections?

No. Most are harmless and only a few cause disease (for example athlete's foot and ringworm). Fungal infections can become serious in immune-compromised people, such as with HIV/AIDS or during cancer treatment.

Give two ways fungi benefit humans.

Fermentation (yeast for bread and beer) and antibiotics such as penicillin.

02 Key Terms/Gram-negative bacteria.title: Gram-negative bacteria
02 Key Terms/Gram-negative bacteria.html:
Gram-negative bacteria

Definition

Bacteria with a thinner peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane. They lose the crystal violet stain and look pink after the safranin counterstain.

Where this comes up

  • Microorganisms: bacteria · Introduction to Biomedicine

Test

What's the key structural difference between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria?

Gram-positive cells have several thick layers of peptidoglycan and retain crystal violet stain (purple). Gram-negative cells have a thinner peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane, lose the stain, and appear pink when counterstained with safranin.

02 Key Terms/HAART.title: HAART
02 Key Terms/HAART.html:
HAART

Definition

Highly active anti-retroviral therapy: three or more antiretroviral drugs that suppress HIV to undetectable levels. It does not cure HIV, but lets the immune system recover.

Where this comes up

  • Case study: HIV/AIDS · Introduction to Biomedicine

Test

What is HAART, and what does it actually do?

Highly active anti-retroviral therapy: 3 or more antiretroviral drugs aiming to reduce HIV viral load to undetectable levels. It doesn't cure HIV, but suppresses it and lets the immune system recover.

02 Key Terms/Heat shock.title: Heat shock

Heat shock

Definition

A brief jump to 42 degrees C after the cells and DNA have sat on ice. It helps the plasmid cross into the cell.

  • Aim and background (Transformation) · Molecular Biology and Genetics

Test

What are the heat shock conditions?

42°C for precisely 50 seconds, then straight back onto ice for 2 minutes.

Why is a separate 10⁻² tube set aside before the heat shock?

To work out how many living cells were used in total. It is 990 µL LB broth plus 10 µL of the original E. coli cells.

02 Key Terms/Hybridisation.title: Hybridisation
02 Key Terms/Hybridisation.html:
Hybridisation

Definition

Mixing an atom's s and p orbitals into equal hybrid orbitals before bonding: sp (180°), sp² (120°) or sp³ (109.5°).

Where this comes up

  • Carbon and its electrons · Biological Chemistry
  • Hybridisation · Biological Chemistry
  • Sigma and pi bonds · Biological Chemistry

Questions

How can carbon make four identical bonds if its 2s and 2p electrons differ?

Hybridisation: the 2s and three 2p orbitals mix into four identical sp³ orbitals pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron.

What are sp, sp² and sp³ hybridisation, with angles?

sp: 2 hybrids, 180°. sp²: 3 hybrids, 120°. sp³: 4 hybrids, 109.5°.

02 Key Terms/Hydrogen bond.title: Hydrogen bond
02 Key Terms/Hydrogen bond.html:
Hydrogen bond

Definition

A weak attraction between a δ+ hydrogen and a lone pair on a nearby O or N. Holds water molecules together and DNA's two strands.

Where this comes up

  • Polar molecules and water · Biological Chemistry

Questions

Why is water polar, and what does that allow?

O is much more electronegative than H, so O is δ− and the H atoms δ+. Water molecules attract each other through hydrogen bonds.

02 Key Terms/Infectious disease.title: Infectious disease
02 Key Terms/Infectious disease.html:
Infectious disease

Definition

Disease caused by a pathogenic microorganism: bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites. Examples: tetanus, influenza, measles.

Where this comes up

  • The Grand Challenges in Biomedicine · Introduction to Biomedicine
  • Microorganisms: bacteria · Introduction to Biomedicine
  • What an infectious disease actually is · Introduction to Biomedicine
  • Why this is a Grand Challenge · Introduction to Biomedicine

Test

What are the 'big three' infectious diseases, and roughly how many people do they affect?

TB (~10 million ill, 1.4 million deaths in 2019), HIV (37.6 million living with it in 2020), Malaria (229 million cases, 409,000 deaths in 2019).

Why do infectious diseases hit low-income countries harder?

6 of the leading causes of death in low-income countries are communicable diseases, versus only 2 in high-income countries.

Which 3 infectious diseases appear in the WHO's top 10 global causes of death (as opposed to the 'big three')?

COVID-19, lower respiratory infections, and tuberculosis. Note this is a different list from the 'big three' (TB, HIV, Malaria), which are the three biggest infectious disease burdens specifically, not the overall top 10 causes of death.

Which four groups of microorganism can cause infectious disease?

Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites.

02 Key Terms/Ionic bond.title: Ionic bond
02 Key Terms/Ionic bond.html:
Ionic bond

Definition

A bond formed when one atom transfers electrons to another, so the resulting cation and anion attract.

Where this comes up

  • Ionic bonding · Biological Chemistry
  • Ionic or covalent? · Biological Chemistry
  • Lecture checklist (How Atoms Form Molecules) · Biological Chemistry
  • Polar bonds · Biological Chemistry

Questions

How does an ionic bond differ from a covalent bond?

Ionic: electrons are transferred, forming cations and anions held by electrostatic attraction. Covalent: a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.

Is KCl ionic or covalent, and why?

Ionic: K easily loses an electron and Cl easily gains one, so K⁺ and Cl⁻ form.

What happens when atoms with very different electronegativities bond?

A very large difference gives an ionic bond. A smaller but significant difference gives a polar covalent bond with δ+ and δ− ends.

02 Key Terms/Lagging strand.title: Lagging strand
02 Key Terms/Lagging strand.html:
Lagging strand

Definition

The new strand made discontinuously, as short Okazaki fragments running against the direction of the fork, because DNA polymerase only builds 5' to 3'.

Where this comes up

  • Extra depth: semiconservative replication · Molecular Biology and Genetics
  • Replication forks: leading and lagging strands · Molecular Biology and Genetics

Test

Why is the lagging strand synthesised in fragments (Okazaki fragments)?

DNA polymerase only builds in the 5′→3′ direction, so the strand running the wrong way relative to the replication fork has to be copied backwards in short pieces.

What's the difference between the leading strand and the lagging strand?

The leading strand is synthesised continuously in the same direction the replication fork moves. The lagging strand is synthesised discontinuously, in short Okazaki fragments, running in the opposite direction to fork movement.

Lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond > bond–bond.

02 Key Terms/Major groove.title: Major groove
02 Key Terms/Major groove.html:
Major groove

Definition

The wider groove of the double helix. It exposes more of each base pair's chemical detail, so sequence-reading proteins such as transcription factors typically bind there.

Where this comes up

  • The double helix: full structure · Molecular Biology and Genetics

A 5-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base.

02 Key Terms/Okazaki fragments.html:
Okazaki fragments

Definition

The short pieces in which the lagging strand is made, roughly 1,000 to 2,000 nucleotides long in bacteria and 150 to 200 in eukaryotes. Ligase joins them up.

Test

Why is the lagging strand synthesised in fragments (Okazaki fragments)?

DNA polymerase only builds in the 5′→3′ direction, so the strand running the wrong way relative to the replication fork has to be copied backwards in short pieces.

Which enzyme removes the RNA primers, and which seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments?

DNA polymerase I removes the primers and replaces them with DNA. DNA ligase seals the phosphodiester bonds joining the Okazaki fragments.

02 Key Terms/Operator.title: Operator
02 Key Terms/Operator.html:
Operator

Definition

The DNA site next to a promoter where a repressor binds to block RNA polymerase.

Where this comes up

  • Repression and induction · Molecular Biology and Genetics

Questions

How does lactose switch on the lac operon?

Without lactose the lacI repressor sits on the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. Lactose (strictly allolactose) binds the repressor so it releases the operator.

What do lacI mutants that can't bind the operator, and operator Oᶜ mutants, have in common?

Both give constitutive expression: the repressor can't block transcription, so the genes are always on.

What happens with a lacI mutant whose repressor can't bind lactose?

The operon stays repressed even with lactose present, because the repressor never leaves the operator.

Operon

Questions

What is an operon? Name the lac operon genes and their products.

Linked genes under one promoter. lacZ: β-galactosidase (splits lactose). lacY: permease (brings lactose in). lacA: transacetylase.

How does lactose switch on the lac operon?

Without lactose the lacI repressor sits on the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. Lactose (strictly allolactose) binds the repressor so it releases the operator.

How does glucose control the lac operon?

No glucose: cAMP rises, binds CAP, and cAMP-CAP binds next to the promoter to strongly activate transcription. With glucose, cAMP is low and activation is weak.

02 Key Terms/Promoter.title: Promoter
02 Key Terms/Promoter.html:
Promoter

Definition

The DNA sequence upstream of a gene where RNA polymerase binds and transcription starts. In E. coli it has −35 (TTGACA) and −10 (TATAAT) boxes.

Where this comes up

  • Gene and mRNA structure · Molecular Biology and Genetics
  • Prokaryotic promoters and RNA polymerase · Molecular Biology and Genetics

  • Summary (Transcription) · Molecular Biology and Genetics

Questions

What do 'cis-acting' and 'trans-acting' mean for a promoter and RNA polymerase?

The promoter is cis-acting: a DNA sequence that only controls its own gene. RNA polymerase is trans-acting: a protein that can act on any matching promoter.

What are the −10 and −35 consensus sequences of an E. coli promoter?

−35: TTGACA. −10: TATAAT. They are 15 to 20 bp apart, and the −10 box is 5 to 9 bp before +1.

What does the sigma factor do?

It binds the −10 and −35 boxes so RNA polymerase starts at the right place. Different sigma factors recognise different sets of promoters.

Which DNA strand does RNA polymerase read, and which strand does the mRNA match?

It reads the template strand. The mRNA is complementary to the template and has the same sequence as the coding strand, with U in place of T.

What do 'cis-acting' and 'trans-acting' mean for a promoter and RNA polymerase?

The promoter is cis-acting: a DNA sequence that only controls its own gene. RNA polymerase is trans-acting: a protein that can act on any matching promoter.

2 α, 1 β, 1 β′ and 1 σ (sigma) subunit.

Repressor

Definition

Questions

How does lactose switch on the lac operon?

Without lactose the lacI repressor sits on the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. Lactose (strictly allolactose) binds the repressor so it releases the operator.

Lactose present, glucose present: what happens to lac gene expression and why?

Low. The repressor is released, but with little cAMP, CAP does not activate, so transcription is weak.

What do lacI mutants that can't bind the operator, and operator Oᶜ mutants, have in common?

Both give constitutive expression: the repressor can't block transcription, so the genes are always on.

Test

What is semiconservative replication?

DNA replication where each daughter molecule contains one original (old) strand and one newly synthesised strand.

What banding pattern did Meselson and Stahl actually observe, and why did it confirm semiconservative replication?

Generation 0 gave one heavy band; Generation I gave one intermediate band; Generation II gave one intermediate and one light band. This matches semiconservative replication exactly, since each new duplex should contain one old (heavy) and one new (light) strand.

Standard curve

What's the purpose of building a standard curve in the DNA concentration practical?

To convert an absorbance reading into a DNA concentration, by measuring several samples of known concentration, plotting concentration against absorbance, and fitting a line through the points.

How many tubes are made for the standard curve, and why?

Six dilutions of sample A, each made in triplicate, so 18 tubes in total.

What do you plot for the standard curve, and what do you do with the line?

Concentration (or the volume of DNA standard added) on the x-axis against absorbance on the y-axis gives a straight line. Its equation, y = mx + c, converts a new absorbance reading into a concentration.

Because of how lagging-strand synthesis works, a linear chromosome would lose a little DNA from its ends with every round of replication. Telomerase solves this by adding new repeat sequences onto the chromosome ends, using its own internal RNA template.

02 Key Terms/Transformation.title: Transformation
02 Key Terms/Transformation.html:
Transformation

Definition

The uptake of foreign DNA by a cell. Rare in nature, and the basis of both the experiments that identified DNA and modern genetic engineering.

Where this comes up

  • Proving DNA is the hereditary material · Molecular Biology and Genetics
  • Aim and background (Transformation) · Molecular Biology and Genetics
  • Calculating transformation efficiency · Molecular Biology and Genetics

Test

Why does the transformation experiment include a control plate of untransformed cells on ampicillin?

To confirm the bacteria weren't already ampicillin-resistant before transformation, so any growth on the actual transformation's ampicillin plate can be attributed to the plasmid.

How do you calculate the frequency of transformation?

Divide the number of transformed cells (CFU/mL) by the total number of cells (CFU/mL) used in the transformation.

02 Key Terms/Triplet code.title: Triplet code
02 Key Terms/Triplet code.html:
Triplet code

Definition

The genetic code is read in groups of three bases. Three bases give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons, enough for 20 amino acids; one or two bases would give only 4 or 16.

Where this comes up

  • Summary (The Genetic Code) · Molecular Biology and Genetics
  • Why the code must be a triplet · Molecular Biology and Genetics

Questions

Why must the genetic code be read in triplets?

DNA has 4 bases. Singles give 4 combinations and pairs give 16, too few for 20 amino acids. Triplets give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons, enough with redundancy (Brenner).

02 Key Terms/Virus.title: Virus
02 Key Terms/Virus.html:
Virus

Definition

An infectious nucleic acid (RNA or DNA) surrounded by protein. It can only replicate inside a host cell, and is not considered alive.

Where this comes up

  • Proving DNA is the hereditary material · Molecular Biology and Genetics
  • Case study: HIV/AIDS · Introduction to Biomedicine
  • Case study: pneumonia · Introduction to Biomedicine
  • Microorganisms: viruses · Introduction to Biomedicine
  • Vaccination: approaches · Introduction to Biomedicine
  • What an infectious disease actually is · Introduction to Biomedicine

Test

Why are viruses not considered to be alive?

They're obligate intracellular parasites: they can only replicate inside a host cell, relying on it for energy, metabolic intermediates and protein synthesis.

What's the difference between a naked virus and an enveloped virus?

A naked virus has just a protein capsid (mainly infects bacteria). An enveloped virus has a capsid plus an outer phospholipid envelope derived from the host cell (mainly infects animals).

Name the four outcomes a virus can have once inside a host cell.

Lytic infection (replicates and destroys the host cell), persistent infection (replicates and buds out without destroying the cell), latent infection (viral DNA present but not replicating), and transformation (converts the host cell into a tumour cell).

Test

What did Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction photographs show?

They distinguished A-form from B-form DNA and suggested the molecule was probably helical. Watson and Crick used this data, shared via Maurice Wilkins, to build the double-helix model in 1953.

02 Key Terms/Zoonotic disease.title: Zoonotic disease
02 Key Terms/Zoonotic disease.html:
Zoonotic disease

Definition

An infectious disease of animals that can cause disease when transmitted to humans, such as avian influenza or COVID-19.

Where this comes up

  • What an infectious disease actually is · Introduction to Biomedicine

Test

What's the difference between an infectious, a communicable, and a zoonotic disease?

Infectious: caused by a pathogenic microorganism. Communicable: an infectious disease spread person to person. Zoonotic: an animal infectious disease that can transmit to humans.

02 Key Terms/cAMP.title: cAMP
02 Key Terms/cAMP.html:
cAMP

Definition

Cyclic AMP: made from ATP when glucose is low. It binds CAP to switch on the lac operon, and is a signalling molecule in many cells.

Where this comes up

  • Glucose control: cAMP and CAP · Molecular Biology and Genetics

Questions

How does glucose control the lac operon?

No glucose: cAMP rises, binds CAP, and cAMP-CAP binds next to the promoter to strongly activate transcription. With glucose, cAMP is low and activation is weak.

Lactose present, glucose present: what happens to lac gene expression and why?

Low. The repressor is released, but with little cAMP, CAP does not activate, so transcription is weak.

How do ATP and cAMP differ?

ATP has three phosphates in a chain on carbon 5 of ribose. In cAMP a single phosphate bridges carbons 3 and 5, making a ring.

02 Key Terms/oriC.title: oriC
02 Key Terms/oriC.html:
oriC

Definition

The E. coli origin of replication: 245 bp long, with three repeats of a 13 bp sequence and four repeats of a 9 bp sequence.

Where this comes up

  • Origins of replication: oriC · Molecular Biology and Genetics

Test

What is oriC, and what does it consist of?

The E. coli chromosomal origin of replication: 245 bp, containing three repeats of a 13 bp sequence and four repeats of a 9 bp sequence.

Describe the three stages of initiation at oriC.

(a) Around 20 DnaA proteins, each bound to ATP, bind the four 9 bp repeats and wrap the DNA around the complex. (b) The three 13 bp repeats are denatured in sequence. (c) DnaB helicase hexamers, helped by DnaC, bind each strand and start unwinding, ready for priming and synthesis.

02 Key Terms/pKa.title: pKa
02 Key Terms/pKa.html:
pKa

Definition

The pH at which an acid is half in its acid form and half in its base form. Buffers work best near their pKa.

Where this comes up

  • Logarithms and pH · Professional Skills for Biosciences

Questions

pH of 0.2 M acetic acid + 0.05 M acetate (pKa 4.7)?

4.7 + log(0.05/0.2) = 4.7 − 0.60 = 4.10.

pH of 0.05 M H₂PO₄⁻ + 0.2 M HPO₄²⁻ (pKa 7.21)?

7.21 + log 4 = 7.81.
